body.text: śāstrasaṃgrahaḥ prathamo 'dhyāyaḥ 1
body.translated_text: <s>Śāstrasaṃgraha</s> (Compendium of Sciences). First Chapter. 1.

body.text: kāvyamīmāṃsā 'prakāśa' atha kavirahasyam prathamo 'dhyāyaḥ 1
body.translated_text: <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> '<s>Prakāśa</s>' — Now [begins] the <s>Kavirahasya</s> (Poet's Secret). First Chapter. 1.

body.text:
śāstrasaṃgrahaḥ
athātaḥ kāvyaṃ mīmāṃsiṣyāmahe, yathopadideśa śrīkaṇṭhaḥ parameṣṭhivaikuṇṭhādibhyaśtuḥṣaṣṭayoḥ /
so 'pi bhagavānsvayambhūricchājanmabhyaḥ svāntevāsibhyaḥ /
teṣu sāgasvateyo vṛndīyasāmapi vandyaḥ kāvyapuruṣa āsīt /
body.translated_text: <s>Śāstrasaṃgraha</s> (Compendium of Sciences). Now then, we shall inquire into poetry (<s>kāvya</s>), as <s>Śrīkaṇṭha</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) taught it to sixty-two [disciples] beginning with <s>Parameṣṭhin</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>) and <s>Vaikuṇṭha</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>). And he too, the blessed <s>Svayambhū</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>), [taught it] to his own students, born of his will. Among them, the son of <s>Sārasvatī</s>, worthy of veneration even by <s>Vṛndīya</s> (<s>Bṛhaspati</s>) and the rest, was the <s>Kāvyapuruṣa</s> (Poetry Personified).

body.text:
taṃ ca sarvasamayavidaṃ divyena cakṣuṣā bhaviṣyadarthadaśinaṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsvastritayavarttinīṣu prajāsu hatikāmyayā prajāpatiḥ kāvyavidyāpravarttanāyai prāyuṅkta /
so 'ṣṭādaśādhikaraṇīṃ divyebhyaḥ kāvyavidyāsnātakebhyaḥ saprapañcaṃ provāca /
tatra kavirahasyaṃ sahasrākṣaḥ samāmnāsīt, auktikamuktigarbhaḥ, rītinirṇayaṃ suvarṇanābhaḥ, ānuprāsikaṃ pracetā, yamakaṃ yamaḥ, citraṃ citrāṅgadaḥ, śabdaśleṣaṃ śeṣaḥ, vāstuvaṃ pulastyaḥ, aupabhyamaupakāyanaḥ, atiśayaṃ parāśaraḥ, arthaśleṣamrutathyaḥ, ubhayālaṅkārikaṃ kuberaḥ, vainodikaṃ kāmadevaḥ, rupakanirupaṇīyaṃ bharataḥ, rasādhikārikaṃ nandikeśvaraḥ, doṣādhikaraṇaṃ dhiṣaṇaḥ, guṇopādānikamupamanyuḥ, aupaniṣadikaṃ kucucāraḥ, iti /
tataste pṛthak pṛthak svaśāstrāṇi viracayāñcakruḥ /
itthaṅkārañca prakīrṇatvātvāt sā kiñciduccicacchide /
itīyaṃ prayojakāṅgavatī saṅkṣipya sarvamarthamalpagranthena aṣṭādaśaprakaraṇī praṇītā /

children.translated_text: Of that [science], this is the enumeration of topics and sections:

children.text: 1 śāstrasaṃgrahaḥ, 2 śāstranirdeśaḥ, 3 kāvyapuruṣotpattiḥ, 4 śiṣyapratibhe, 5 vyutpatti-vipākāḥ, 6 padavākyavivekaḥ, 7 vākyavidhayaḥ, 8 kākuprakārāḥ, 9 pāṭhapratiṣṭhā, 10 kāvyārthayonayaḥ, 11 arthānuśāsanaṃ, 12 kavicaryāḥ, 13 rājacaryā, 14 śabdārthaharaṇopāyāḥ, 15 kavi viśeṣaḥ, 16 kavisamayaḥ, 17 deśakālavibhāgaḥ, 18 bhruvanakośaḥ, iti kavirahasyaṃ prathamamadhikaraṇamityādi /
children.translated_text: 1 <s>Śāstrasaṃgraha</s> (Compendium of Sciences), 2 <s>Śāstranirdeśa</s> (Designation of Sciences), 3 <s>Kāvyapuruṣotpatti</s> (Origin of the Poetry Person), 4 <s>Śiṣyapratibhā</s> (Students' Genius), 5 <s>Vyutpatti-vipāka</s> (Maturation of Learning), 6 <s>Padavākyaviveka</s> (Discrimination of Words and Sentences), 7 <s>Vākyavidhaya</s> (Modes of Sentence), 8 <s>Kākuprakāra</s> (Types of Intonation), 9 <s>Pāṭhapratiṣṭhā</s> (Establishment of Recitation), 10 <s>Kāvyārthayonaya</s> (Sources of Poetic Meaning), 11 <s>Arthānuśāsana</s> (Instruction on Meaning), 12 <s>Kavicaryā</s> (Conduct of Poets), 13 <s>Rājacaryā</s> (Conduct of Kings), 14 <s>Śabdārthaharaṇopāya</s> (Means of Appropriating Words and Meanings), 15 <s>Kaviviśeṣa</s> (Distinctions among Poets), 16 <s>Kavisamaya</s> (Conventions of Poets), 17 <s>Deśa</s> (Regional [conventions]),
These are the <s>sūtras</s> (aphorisms). Now there will be a commentary-exposition (<s>vyākhyābhāṣya</s>) on them.
This presentation — concise and elaborate in arrangement — is by us for the benefit of students.

body.translated_text: And <s>Prajāpati</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>), knowing him to be omniscient in all doctrines, seeing future purposes with divine vision, desiring the welfare of creatures dwelling in the three worlds of <s>Bhūḥ</s>, <s>Bhuvaḥ</s>, and <s>Svaḥ</s>, appointed him for the propagation of the science of poetry (<s>kāvyavidyā</s>). He (<s>Kāvyapuruṣa</s>) expounded to those divine graduates of the science of poetry the [treatise] with its eighteen sections (<s>adhikaraṇa</s>), in full detail. Therein, the thousand-eyed <s>Indra</s> collected the <s>Kavirahasya</s> (Poet's Secret), which contained the essence of reasoned arguments and liberating insights,

children.translated_text: With striking examples, weighty [in content] yet light in text —
this is our <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> (Inquiry into Poetry), the cause of poetic learning.

children.text: iyaṃ sā kāvyamīmāṃsā mīmāṃsā yatra vāglavaḥ /
children.translated_text: This <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> is an inquiry where economy of expression (<s>vāglava</s>) [is prized];

children.text: vāglavaṃ na sa jānāti na vijānāti yastvimām //
children.translated_text: one who does not know this [work] does not know economy of expression.
The <s>Yāyāvarīya</s> [i.e., <s>Rājaśekhara</s>], condensing the extensive opinions of the sages,
composed this <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> for the sake of poets.

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe prathamo 'dhyāyaḥ śāstrasaṅgrahaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the first chapter, <s>Śāstrasaṅgraha</s>, in the first section of the <s>Kavirahasya</s> in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.
Chapter 2

body.text: śāstranirdeśaḥ dvitīyo 'dhyāyaḥ 2
body.translated_text: <s>Śāstranirdeśa</s> (Designation of Sciences). Second Chapter. 2.

body.text:
śāstranirdeśaḥ iha vāṅmayamubhayathā śāstraṃ kāvyaṃ ca /
śāstrapūrvakatvāt kāvyānāṃ pūrva śāstreṣvabhiniviśeta /
tacca dvidhā apauruṣeyaṃ pauruṣeyaṃ ca /
aphauruṣeya śrutiḥ /
sā ca mantrabrāhmaṇo /
vivṛtakriyātantrā manantrāḥ /
mantrāṇāṃ stutinindāvyākhyānaviniyogādigrantho brāhmaṇam /
ṛgyajuḥsāmavedastrayī /
atharva turīyam /
tatrārthavyavasthitapādā ṛcaḥ /
tāḥ sagīkayaḥ sāmāni /
acchandāṃsyagītāni yajūṃṣi /
ṛco yajūṃṣi sāmāni cārtharvāṇi ta ime catvārobedāḥ /
itihāsavedadhanurvedau gāndharvāyurvedāvapi copavedāḥ /
'vedopavedātmā sārvavarṇikaḥ pañcamo nāṭyavedaḥ' iti drauhiṇiḥ /
'śikṣā, kalpo, vyākaraṇaṃ, niruktaṃ, chandovicitiḥ, jyautiṣaṃ ca ṣaḍaṅgāni' ityācāryāḥ /
upakārakatvādalaṅkāraḥ satpamamaṅgam 'iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
ṛte ca tatsarupaparijñānādvedārthānavagatiḥ' /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by this verse]:

children.text: 'dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā samānaṃ vṛkṣaṃ pariṣasvajāte /
children.translated_text: 'Two birds, companions, joined together, clasp the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other, not eating, merely looks on.'

body.translated_text: <s>Śāstranirdeśa</s>. Here the world of words (<s>vāṅmaya</s>) is twofold: <s>śāstra</s> (science) and <s>kāvya</s> (poetry). Since poetry is preceded by science, one should first immerse oneself in the sciences. And that [science] is of two kinds: <s>apauruṣeya</s> (not of human authorship) and <s>pauruṣeya</s> (of human authorship). The non-human-authored [science] is <s>śruti</s> (Vedic revelation). And that comprises <s>mantra</s> and <s>brāhmaṇa</s>. [The portions] whose ritual application is explicitly stated are the <s>mantras</s>. The text dealing with the praise, blame, explanation, and ritual application of the <s>mantras</s> is the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>. The <s>Ṛg</s>, <s>Yajus</s>, <s>Sāma</s>, and <s>Atharva</s> [Vedas] —

body.text:
seyaṃ śāstroktiḥ /
pratyadhikaraṇaṃ ca ṛcaṃ yajuḥ sāmātharvaṇāṃ brāhmaṇaṃ cādāhṛtya bhāṣāmudāhariṣyāmaḥ /
tatra varṇānāṃ sthānakaraṇaprayatnādibhiḥ niṣpattinirṇayinī śikṣā āpiśalīyādikā /
nānāśākhādhītānāṃ mantrāṇāṃ viniyojakaṃ sūtraṃ kalpaḥ /
sā ca yajurvidyā /
śabdānāmanvākhyānaṃ vyākaraṇam /
nirvacanaṃ niruktam /
chandasāṃ pratipādiyitrīchandovicitiḥ /
grahagaṇitaṃ jyautiṣam, alaṅkāravyākhyānaṃ tu purastāt /
pauruṣeyaṃ tu purāṇam, ānvīkṣikī, mīmāṃsā, smṛtitantramiti catvāri śāstrāṇi /
tatra vedākhyānopanibandhanaprāyaṃ purāṇamaṣṭādaśadhā /

children.translated_text: As they say:
'Creation, dissolution, the cosmic age, the periods of the <s>Manus</s>, the genealogical chronicles —
that in which the world's [history] is recorded, that is to be known as <s>Purāṇa</s>.'

body.translated_text: This is a statement from <s>śāstra</s> (scripture). And for each section, having cited a verse from the <s>Ṛk</s>, <s>Yajus</s>, <s>Sāma</s>, or <s>Atharva</s> and the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, we shall illustrate with [examples in] the vernacular. Therein, <s>Śikṣā</s> (phonetics), such as that of <s>Āpiśali</s> and others, determines the production of sounds through place of articulation, instrument, effort, and the like. The <s>Kalpa</s> (ritual <s>sūtra</s>) prescribes the ritual application of <s>mantras</s> studied in various branches. And that is the <s>Yajurveda</s> tradition. <s>Vyākaraṇa</s> (grammar) is the etymological explanation of words.

body.text:
"purāṇapravibheda evetihāsaḥ' ityeke /
sa ca dvidhā parakriyāpurākalpābhyām /

children.translated_text: As they say:
'The course of <s>Itihāsa</s> is twofold: <s>parakriyā</s> (deeds of others) and <s>purākalpa</s> (ancient events).
The former has one hero; the latter has many heroes.'

body.translated_text: 'The differentiation of <s>Purāṇa</s> itself is <s>Itihāsa</s> (Epic)' — say some. And that is of two kinds: based on the deeds of others (<s>parakriyā</s>) and based on ancient events (<s>purākalpa</s>).

body.text:
tatra rāmāyaṇaṃ bhārataṃ codāharaṇe /
ānvīkṣikīṃ tu vidyāvasare vakṣyāmaḥ /
nigamavākyānāṃ nyāyaiḥ sahasreṇa vivektrī mīmāṃsā /
sā ca dvividhā vidhivivecanī brahmanidarśanī ca /
aṣṭādaśaiva śrutyarthasmaraṇātsmṛtayaḥ /
'tānīmāni caturdaśa vidyāsthānāni, yaduta vedāśratvāraḥ, ṣaḍaṅgāni, catvāri śāstrāṇi' ityācāryāḥ /
tānyetāni kṛtsnāmapi bhrūrbhuvaḥsvastrayīṃ vyāsajya varttante /

children.translated_text: They say:

children.text: 'vidyāsthānānāṃ gantumantaṃ na śakto jīvedvarṣaṇāṃ yo 'pi sāgraṃ sahasram /
children.translated_text: 'One who were to live even a full thousand years would not be able to reach the end of the seats of knowledge.
Therefore, the essence of their meaning has been stated in summary — <s>Vyāsa</s> set aside prolixity for the sake of those who fear long texts.'

body.translated_text: Therein, the <s>Rāmāyaṇa</s> and the <s>Bhārata</s> are examples. We shall discuss <s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic/philosophy) in the appropriate section on learning. <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> is that which discriminates the meaning of Vedic statements by means of a thousand [rules of] reasoning. And that is of two kinds: that which analyzes injunctions (<s>vidhivivecanī</s>) and that which reveals <s>Brahman</s> (<s>brahmanidarśanī</s>). The <s>Smṛtis</s> are eighteen in number, arising from the remembrance of Vedic meaning. 'These are the fourteen seats of knowledge: namely, the four <s>Vedas</s>, the six <s>Vedāṅgas</s>, and the four <s>Śāstras</s>,

body.text:
"sakalavidyāsthānaikāyatanaṃ pañcadaśaṃ kāvyaṃ vidyāsthānam' iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
gadyapadyamayatvāt kavidharmatvāt hitoradeśakatvācca /
tadvi śāstraṇyanudhāvati /
'vārttā kāmasūtraṃ śilpaśāstraṃ daṇḍanītiriti pūrvaiḥ sahāṣṭādaśa vidyāsthānāni'ityapare /
ānvīkṣikī trayī vārttā daṇḍanītiśceti vidyāḥ ' /
daṇḍanītirevaikā vidyā'ityauśanasāḥ /
daṇḍabhayādvi kṛtsno lokaḥ sveṣu sveṣu karmasvavatiṣṭhate /
'vārttā daṇḍanītirdve vidye' iti bārhaspatyāḥ /
vṛttirvinayagrahaṇaṃ ca sthitiheturlokayātrāyāḥ /
'trayīvārttādaṇḍanītayastisro vidyāḥ' iti mānavāḥ /
trayī hi vārttādaṇḍanītyorupadeṣṭrī /
'ānvīkṣikītrayīvārttādaṇḍanītayaścatasro vidyāḥ'iti kauṭalyaḥ /
ānvīkṣikyā hi vivecitā trayī vārttādaṇḍanītyoḥ prabhavati /
'pañcamī sāhityavidyā' iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
sā hi vacasṛṇāmapi vidyānāṃ nisyandaḥ /
ābhirddharmārthau yadvidyāttadvidyānāṃ vidyātvam /
tatra trayī vyākhyātā /
dvidhā cānvīkṣikī pūrvotrarapakṣābhyām /
arhadbhadantadarśane lokāyattaṃ ca pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ /
saṅkhayaṃ nyāyavaiśeṣikau cottaraḥ /
ta ime ṣaṭ tarkāḥ /
tatra ca tisraḥ kathā bhavanti vādo, jalpo, vitaṇḍā ca /
madhyasthayostattvāvabodhāya vastutattvaparāmarśo vādaḥ /
vijigīṣoḥ svapakṣasiddhaye chalajātinigrahādiparigraho jalpaḥ /
svapakṣasyāparigrahitrī parapakṣasya dūṣayitrī vitaṇḍā /
kṛṣipāśupālye vaṇijyā ca vārttā /
ānvīkṣikītrayīvārttānāṃ yogakṣemasādhano daṇḍastasya nītirdaṇḍanītiḥ /
tasyāmāyattā lokayātreti śāstrāṇi /

children.translated_text: And the general definition of these [sciences] is:
'Like the currents of rivers — trivial at first, progressively broader —

children.text: ye śāstrasamārambhā bhavanti lokasya te vandyāḥ' //
children.translated_text: those commencements of sciences that benefit the world are worthy of reverence.'

body.translated_text: 'The sole repository of all seats of knowledge, the fifteenth seat of knowledge, is poetry (<s>kāvya</s>)' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s> [<s>Rājaśekhara</s>]. Because it consists of prose and verse, because it partakes of the nature of the poet, and because it instructs in what is beneficial. It pursues [the truths of] the [other] sciences. 'Commerce (<s>Vārttā</s>), the <s>Kāmasūtra</s>, the <s>Śilpaśāstra</s> (science of crafts), and <s>Daṇḍanīti</s> (political science) — together with the former [fourteen], these make eighteen seats of knowledge' — say others. '<s>Ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic), <s>Trayī</s> (the three Vedas), <s>Vārttā</s> (economics), and <s>Daṇḍanīti</s> (politics) — these are the [four] sciences.'

body.text:
sūtrādibhiścaiṣāṃ praṇayanam /
tatra sūtraṇāt sūtram /

children.translated_text: As they say:
'Of few syllables, unambiguous, essential, comprehensive,
without filler-words, and faultless — this is what the authors of <s>sūtras</s> know as a <s>sūtra</s>.'

body.translated_text: And these are composed through <s>sūtras</s> and the like. Therein, a <s>sūtra</s> [is so called] from the act of stringing together (<s>sūtraṇa</s>).

body.text:
sūtrāṇāṃ sakalasāravivaraṇaṃ vṛttiḥ /
sūtravṛttivivecanaṃ paddhatiḥ /
ākṣipya bhāṣaṇādbhāṣyam /
antarbhāṣyaṃ samīkṣā /
avāntarārthavicchedaśca sā /
yathāsambhavamarthasya ṭīkanaṃ ṭīkā /
viṣamapadabhañjikā pañjikā /

children.translated_text: A <s>kārikā</s> (memorial verse) is a verse that displays the meaning.
A <s>vārttika</s> (critical supplement) is the consideration of what has been said, what has not been said, and what has been poorly said — thus [are described] the divisions of <s>śāstra</s>.
'One who, making manifest the hidden meaning, clarifying the obscured,
composing much from little and [reducing] the extensive to the brief — that is a <s>śāstrakavi</s> (scientific author).'

body.translated_text: A <s>vṛtti</s> (gloss) is the elucidation of the complete essence of the <s>sūtras</s>. A <s>paddhati</s> (manual) is the examination of the <s>sūtra</s> and its <s>vṛtti</s>. A <s>bhāṣya</s> (commentary) [is so called] from the act of speaking after raising [objections]. A <s>samīkṣā</s> (critical review) is a sub-commentary. And that is the subdivision of subsidiary meanings. A <s>ṭīkā</s> (annotation) is the annotation of meaning as far as possible. A <s>pañjikā</s> (detailed commentary) is the breaking down of difficult words.

body.text:
śāstraikadeśasya prakriyā prakaraṇam /
adhyāyādayastvavāntaravicchedāḥ kvatibhiḥ svatantratayā praṇītā ityaparisaṅkhyeyā anākhyeyāśca /
śābdārthayoryathāvatsahabhāvena vidyā sāhityavidyā /
upavidyāstu catuḥṣaṣṭhiḥ /
tāśca kalā iti vidagdhavādaḥ /

children.translated_text: That is the livelihood (<s>ājīva</s>) of poetry.
We shall discuss that in the <s>Aupaniṣadika</s> [section].
Thus the elaboration of those who are devoted [to learning] in this [subject] is endless;
[yet] it can be grasped by a sharp intellect, [even when] omitted, because of the weightiness of [a full] text.

body.translated_text: A <s>prakaraṇa</s> (topic) is the treatment of one part of a science. Chapters (<s>adhyāya</s>) and the like are subordinate divisions; since they are composed independently by various [authors], they are innumerable and cannot be fully listed. <s>Sāhityavidyā</s> (the science of literary composition) is [the study of] the proper co-existence of word and meaning. The subsidiary arts (<s>upavidyā</s>) number sixty-four. And these are called <s>kalās</s> (arts) — thus say the learned.

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau
body.translated_text: Thus in the work composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>,

body.text: kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe dvitīyo 'dhyāyaḥ śāstranirdeśaḥ //
body.translated_text: in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s>, in the <s>Kavirahasya</s>, in the first section — the second chapter, <s>Śāstranirdeśa</s>, ends.
Chapter 3

body.text: kāvyapuruṣotpattiḥ tṛtīyo 'dhyāyaḥ 3
body.translated_text: <s>Kāvyapuruṣotpatti</s> (Origin of the Poetry Person). Third Chapter. 3.

body.text:
kāvyapuruṣotpattiḥ evaṃ gurubhyo giraḥ puṇyāḥ purāṇīḥ śṛṇumaḥ sma, yatkiladhiśaṣaṇaṃ śiṣyāḥ kathāprasaṅge papracchuḥ, kīdṛśaḥ punarasau sārasvateyaḥ kābyapuruṣo vo guruḥ ? iti /
sa tān bṛhatāmpatiruce /
purā putrīyantī sarasvatī tuṣāragirau tapasyāmāsa /
body.translated_text: <s>Kāvyapuruṣotpatti</s>. Thus we used to hear these ancient and sacred words from our teachers: that the students of <s>Adhiśeṣaṇa</s>, in the course of conversation, asked: 'What manner of person is that son of <s>Sārasvatī</s>, the <s>Kāvyapuruṣa</s> (Poetry Person), who is your teacher?' He, the Lord of Hymns (<s>Bṛhatāmpati</s>), told them: 'Long ago, <s>Sarasvatī</s>, desiring a son, performed austerities on the <s>Tuṣāragiri</s> (Snow Mountain).

body.text:
prītena manasā tāṃ viriñcaḥ provāca-'putraṃ te sṛjāmi ' /
athaiṣā kāvyapuruṣaṃ suṣuve /
so 'bhyutthāya sapādopagrahaṃ chandasvartī vācamudacīcarat-
body.translated_text: With a pleased mind, <s>Viriñci</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>) said to her: "I shall create a son for you." Thereupon she gave birth to the <s>Kāvyapuruṣa</s> (Poetry Person). He, rising up, touching [his mother's] feet in reverence, uttered speech moving in meter:

children.translated_text: 'This entire world of words manifests in the form of meaning —
I am that Poetry Person, O Mother; I bow at your feet.'

body.text:
tāmāmnāyadṛṣṭacarīmupalabhya bhāṣāviṣaye chandomudrāṃ devī sasaṃmadamaṅkaparyaṅkenādāya tamudalāpayat /
'vatsa ! sacchandaskāyā giraḥ praṇetaḥ ! vāṅmayamātaramapi mātaraṃ māṃ vicayase /
praśasyatamaṃ cedamudāharanti yaduta ''putrātparājayo dvitīyaṃ putrajanma'iti /
tvattaḥ pūrve hi vidvāṃso gadyaṃ dadṛśurna padyam /
tvadupajñamathātaḥ chandasvadvacaḥ pravartsyati /
aho ślāghanīyo 'si /
śabdārthau te śarīraṃ, saṃskṛtaṃ mukhaṃ, prakṛtaṃ bāhuḥ, jaghanamaparbhraṃśaḥ, paiśācaṃ pādau, uro miśram /
samaḥ prasanno madhura udāra ojasvī cāsi /
ukticaṇaṃ te vaco, rasa ātmā, rāmāṇi chandāṃsi, praśnottarapravahlikādikaṃ ca vākkeliḥ, anuprāsopamādayaśca tvāmalaṅkurvanti /
bhaviṣyato 'rthasyābhidhātrī śrurirapi bhavantamabhistauti-
body.translated_text:
Finding him of conduct observed in tradition, in the domain of language, the goddess <s>Chandomudrā</s>, with delight, taking him on her lap, addressed him:
"Child! O creator of speech endowed with meter! You seek even your mother — the mother of all literature — me.
They declare this to be most praiseworthy: that 'defeat by one's son is a second birth of the son.'
For the learned ones before you saw only prose, not verse.
From your invention, henceforth metrical speech shall proceed.
Ah, you are praiseworthy!
Word and meaning are your body; Sanskrit is your face; Prakrit is your arms; the vulgar dialects (<s>apabhraṃśa</s>) are your loins; <s>Paiśāca</s> is your feet; and the mixed [language] is your chest.
You are even, clear, sweet, noble, and possessed of vigor.
Your speech is sharp in expression; <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) is your soul; meters are your pleasures; riddles, questions-and-answers, and the like are your play of words; and <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), <s>upamā</s> (simile), and other [figures] adorn you.
Even <s>śruti</s> (sacred scripture), which proclaims things yet to come, praises you —"

children.translated_text: "Four are its horns, three its feet, two its heads, seven its hands;

children.text: tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti maho debo martyānāviveśa' //
children.translated_text: bound threefold, the bull roars mightily — the great god has entered mortals."

body.text:
'tathāpi saṃvṛṇu pragalbhasya puṃsaḥ karma, bālocitaṃ ceṣṭasva' iti nigadya niveśya cainamanokahāśrayiṇī gaṇḍaśailatalatalpe snātumabhragaṅgāṃ jagāmaṃ /
tāvacca kuśān samidhaśca samāhattuṃ niḥsṛto mahāmuniruśanāḥ parivṛtte pūṣaṇyūṣmopaṣlutaṃ tamadrākṣīt /
kasyāyamanātho bāla iti cintayansvamāśramapadamanaiṣīt /
kṣaṇādāśvastaśca sa sārasvateyastasmai chandasvatīṃ vācaṃ samacārayat /
akasmādvismāpayansa cābhyuvāca-
body.translated_text:
"Nevertheless, conceal the deeds of a precocious man; conduct yourself as befits a child" — having said this and having settled him, she who dwelt in a mountain cave went to bathe in the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s>.
Meanwhile, the great sage <s>Uśanas</s>, who had gone out to gather <s>kuśa</s> grass and firewood, upon returning saw him splashed with warm milk by <s>Pūṣan</s> (the Sun).
Wondering "Whose is this unprotected child?" he brought him to his own hermitage.
After a moment, the child of <s>Sarasvatī</s>, having recovered, uttered metrical speech to him.
Astonishing him without warning, he spoke:

children.translated_text: "She who, though milked daily by poet-milkers, appears as if unmilked —

children.text: hṛdi naḥ sannidhattāṃ sā dūktidhenuḥ sarasvatī' //
children.translated_text: may that cow of fine speech, <s>Sarasvatī</s>, abide in our hearts!"

body.text: iti /
body.translated_text: (Thus.)

body.text:
tatpūrvakamadhyetṛṇāṃ ca sucedhastvamādideśa /
tataḥ prabhṛti tamuśanasaṃ santaḥ kavirityācakṣate /
tadupacārāñca kavayaḥ kavaya iti lokayātrā /
kaviśabdaśca 'kavṛvarṇane' ityasya dhātoḥ kāvyakarmaṇo rupame /
kāvyaikarupatvācca sārasvateye 'pi kāvyapuruṣa iti bhaktyā prayuñjate /
tataśca vinivṛttā vāgdevī tatra putramapaśyantī madhyehṛdayaṃ cakranda /
prasaṅgāgataśca vālpīkirmunivṛṣā sapraśrayaṃ tamudantamudāhṛtya bhagavatyai, bhṛgusūterāśramapadamadarśayat /
sāpi prastutapayodharā putrāyāṅkapālīṃ dadānā śirasi ca cumbantī svastimatā cetasā prācetasāyāpi maharṣaye nibhṛtaṃ sacchandāṃsi vacāṃsi prāyacchate /

children.text: anupreṣitaśca sa tayā niṣādanihatasahatasahacarīṃ krauñcayuvarti karuṇakreṅkārayā girā krandantīmudīkṣya śokavān ślokamujjagāda-
children.translated_text: And he, sent forth by her, seeing a female <s>krauñca</s> (curlew) — whose mate had been killed by a <s>Niṣāda</s> (hunter) — crying out with a piteous wail, was overcome with grief and uttered a verse:
"O <s>Niṣāda</s>! May you never find lasting fame for all eternity,
for you have killed one of the <s>krauñca</s> pair, who was stricken with desire!"

body.translated_text:
And prior to that, he instructed the students in the art of recitation.
From that time onward, the good call that <s>Uśanas</s> a "<s>kavi</s>" (poet).
And by extension from him, poets are called "<s>kavis</s>" — such is the worldly convention.
The word "<s>kavi</s>" is a form of the root "<s>kav</s>" meaning "to describe," with "poetry" (<s>kāvya</s>) as its object.
And because of his identity with poetry, the term "<s>Kāvyapuruṣa</s>" (Poetry-Person) is applied with devotion even to the son of <s>Sarasvatī</s>.
Then the goddess of speech returned and, not seeing her son there, wept from the depths of her heart.
And <s>Vālmīki</s>, the bull among sages, who came upon [her] by chance, reverentially narrating that account to the goddess, showed her the hermitage of the son of <s>Bhṛgu</s> (<s>Uśanas</s>).
And she, with her breasts full [of milk], offering her lap to her son and kissing him on the head, with a blessed heart, secretly gave metrical speeches to the great sage <s>Prācetasa</s> (<s>Vālmīki</s>) as well.

body.text:
'tato divyadṛṣṭirdevī tasmā api ślokāya varamadāt, yadutānyadanadhīyāno yaḥ prathamamenamadhyeṣyate sa sārasvataḥ kaviḥ saṃpatsyata iti /
sa tu mahāmuniḥ pravṛttavacano rāmāyaṇamidihāsaṃ samadṛbhat ; dvaipāyanastu ślokaprathamādhyāyī tatprabhāveṇa śatasāhasrīṃ saṃhitāṃ bhāratam /
ekadā tu brahmarṣivṛndārakayoḥ śrutivivāde dākṣiṇyavāndevaḥ svayambhūstāmimāṃ nirṇotrīmuddideśa /
upaśrutavṛttāntaśca mātaraṃ vrajantīṃ so 'nuvavrāja /
vatsa!parameṣṭhinānanumatasya te na brahmalokayātraghā niḥśreyasāyetyabhidadhānā haṭhānnyavartayadenamātmanā tu pravartate /
tataḥ sa kāvyapuruṣo ruṣā niścakrāma /
priyaṃ mitramasya ca kumāraḥ sākrandaṃ rudannabhyadhīyata gauryā tāta! tūṣṇīmāḥsva sāhameṣā niṣedhāmītinigadandī samacintayat /
prāyaḥ prāṇabhṛtāṃ premāṇamantareṇa nānyadvandhanamasti, tadetasyavaśīkaraṇaṃ kāmapi striyaṃ sṛjāmīti vicintayantī sāhityavidyāvadhūmrudapādayadādiśañcaināmeṣa te ruṣā dharmapatiḥ puraḥ pratiṣṭhate tadanuvarttasvainaṃ nivarttaya ca /
bhavanto 'pi hanta! munayaḥ!kāvyavidyāsnātakāścaritametayoḥ studhvametaddhi vaḥ kāvyasarvasvaṃ bhaviṣyatītyabhidhāya bhagavatī bhavānī joṣamāsiṣṭa /
te 'pi tathākarttumavatasthire /
atha sarve prathamaṃ prācīṃ diśaṃ śiśriyuryatrāṅgavaṅgasuhnabrahmapuṇḍrādyā janapadā;, tatrābhiyujjānā tamaumeyī yaṃ veṣaṃ yatheṣṭamseviṣṭa, sa tatratyābhiḥ strībhiranvakriyata /
sā pravṛttī raudramāgadhī /
tāṃ te munayo 'bhituṣṭuvuḥ-
body.translated_text:
Then the divine-sighted goddess gave a boon for that verse too — namely, that whoever would first study this [verse], even without having studied anything else, would become a poet endowed with <s>Sarasvatī</s>'s [grace].
That great sage, having commenced speech, composed the <s>Rāmāyaṇa</s>, the epic. And <s>Dvaipāyana</s> (<s>Vyāsa</s>), being the first student of the <s>śloka</s>, by its power [composed] the hundred-thousand-verse compilation, the <s>Bhārata</s>.
Once, in a dispute over learning between the two foremost <s>brahmarṣis</s>, the gracious lord <s>Svayambhū</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>) himself appointed her [<s>Sarasvatī</s>] as the arbiter.
Having heard the whole affair, he (<s>Kāvyapuruṣa</s>) followed his mother as she was departing.
"Child! Since you are not approved by <s>Parameṣṭhin</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>), the journey to the <s>Brahma</s>-world is not for your highest good" — saying this, she forcibly turned him back, while she herself proceeded.
Then that <s>Kāvyapuruṣa</s> departed in anger.
And his dear friend <s>Kumāra</s> (<s>Skanda</s>), weeping loudly, studied [poetry], while <s>Gaurī</s> (<s>Pārvatī</s>), saying "My son! Be silent — I shall stop him," pondered.
"Surely, for living beings, there is no bond other than love; therefore, to bring him under control, I shall create some woman" — thinking thus, she produced the maiden <s>Sāhityavidyā</s> (the Science of Literature) and instructed her: "This angry one, your rightful husband, stands before you — follow him and bring him back."
"And you too, O sages! Having bathed in the knowledge of poetry, celebrate the conduct of these two, for this will become the entire treasure of your poetry!" — having said this, the goddess <s>Bhavānī</s> fell silent.
They too resolved to do so.
Then all first proceeded to the eastern direction, where the countries of <s>Aṅga</s>, <s>Vaṅga</s>, <s>Suhma</s>, <s>Brahmapuṇḍra</s>, and others [are found]. There, as the daughter of <s>Umā</s> (<s>Sāhityavidyā</s>) was wooing him, whatever costume she assumed at will was adopted by the women of that region.
That manner became the <s>Raudra-Māgadhī</s> (the fierce <s>Māgadha</s> style).
The sages praised it:

children.translated_text: "With pearl-strings painted on breasts smeared with moist sandalwood paste, with hair-partings kissed by clusters [of flowers], with exposed shoulders —
may this costume long shine among the women of <s>Gauḍa</s>, beautiful with limbs [smooth] as <s>dūrvā</s> grass stalks and heavy ornaments!"

body.text:
yadṛcchayāpi yādṛṅnepathyaḥ sa sārasvateya āsīt tadveṣāśca puruṣā babhūvuḥ /
sāpi saiva pravṛttiḥ /
yadaparaṃ nṛttavādyādikameṣā cakre sā bhārattī vṛttiḥ /
tāṃ te munaya iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
tathāvidhākalpayāpi tayā yadavaśaṃvadīkṛtaḥ samāsavadanuprāsavadyogavṛttiparabhparātadgarbhaṃ (vākyaṃ) jagāda sā gauḍīyā rītiḥ /
tāṃ te munaya iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
vṛttirītisvarupaṃ yathāvasaraṃ vakṣyāmaḥ /
tataśca sa, pañcālānpratyuñcacāla /
yatra pāñcālaśūrasenahastināpurakāśmīravāhīkabāhlikabāhlaveyādayo janapadāḥ /
tatrābhiyuñjānā tamaumeyīti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
sā pāñcālamadhyamāpravṛttiḥ /

children.translated_text: The sages praised it:
"With cheek-lines rippled by the play of swinging earrings, with pearl necklaces dangling from the prominence of the breasts and swaying,
with the lower garment draped in a full circle from hip to ankle — bow to the costume of the women of <s>Mahodaya</s>!"

body.translated_text:
Whatever costume that son of <s>Sarasvatī</s> happened to assume, men [of that region] adopted that costume.
That too was the same manner (<s>pravṛtti</s>).
Whatever dance, music, and the like she performed — that was the <s>Bhāratī vṛtti</s> (the <s>Bhāratī</s> dramatic mode).
The sages [praised] it — the same as before.
And by such attire, when she brought him under her spell, the speech he uttered — with compounds, alliteration, and word-play embedded — that was the <s>Gauḍīyā rīti</s> (the <s>Gauḍa</s> style).
The sages [praised] it — the same as before.
The nature of <s>vṛtti</s> and <s>rīti</s> we shall explain at the appropriate time.
Then he proceeded toward the <s>Pañcāla</s> [country],
where the regions of <s>Pāñcāla</s>, <s>Śūrasena</s>, <s>Hastināpura</s>, <s>Kāśmīra</s>, <s>Vāhīka</s>, <s>Bāhlika</s>, <s>Bāhlaveya</s>, and others [are found].
There, as the daughter of <s>Umā</s> was wooing him — the same as before.
That manner became the <s>Pāñcāla-Madhyamā</s> (the middle <s>Pāñcāla</s> style).

body.text:
kiñcidārdramanā yannepathyaḥ sa sārasvateya āsīditi samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
sāpi saiveti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
yadīṣannṛttagītavādyavilāsādikameṣā darśayāṃbabhūva sā sātvatī vṛttiḥ /
āviddhagatimattvātsā cārabhaṭī /
tāṃ te munaya iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
tathāvidhākalpayāpi tayā yadīṣadūśaṃvadīkṛta īṣadasamāsamīṣadanuprāsamupacāragarbhañca (vākyaṃ) jagāda sā pāñcālī rītiḥ /
tāṃ te munaya iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
tataḥ so 'vantīnpratyuccacāla /
yatrāvantīvaidiśasurāṣṭramālavārbudabhṛgukacchādayo janapadāḥ /
janapadāḥ /
tatrābhiyuñjanā tamaumeyīti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
sā pravṛttirāvantī /
pāñcālamadhyamādākṣiṇātyayorantaracāriṇī hi sā /
ata eva sātvatīkaiśikyau tatra vṛttī /
tāṃ te munayo 'bhituṣṭuvuḥ-
body.translated_text:
He whose heart was slightly moist, whatever costume that son of <s>Sarasvatī</s> assumed — the same as before.
That too was the same — as before.
Whatever slight dance, song, music, and graceful display she showed — that was the <s>Sātvatī vṛtti</s> (the <s>Sātvatī</s> dramatic mode).
Being of the nature of piercing movement, that was also <s>Ārabhaṭī</s>.
The sages [praised] it — the same as before.
And by such attire, when she brought him slightly under her spell, the speech he uttered — with few compounds, few alliterations, and embedded with courteous [expressions] — that was the <s>Pāñcālī rīti</s> (the <s>Pāñcāla</s> style).
The sages [praised] it — the same as before.
Then he proceeded toward <s>Avantī</s>,
where the regions of <s>Avantī</s>, <s>Vaidiśa</s>, <s>Surāṣṭra</s>, <s>Mālava</s>, <s>Ārbuda</s>, <s>Bhṛgukaccha</s>, and others [are found].
The daughter of <s>Umā</s> wooing him there — the same as before.
That manner was <s>Āvantī</s> — for it moves between the <s>Pāñcāla-Madhyamā</s> and the <s>Dākṣiṇātya</s>.
Therefore the <s>Sātvatī</s> and <s>Kaiśikī</s> are the dramatic modes there.
The sages praised it:

children.translated_text: "The <s>Pāñcāla</s> costume for men, and for women the <s>Dākṣiṇātya</s> — let them delight!
Whatever is spoken, whatever is acted, and the rest — in the <s>Avanti</s> region they are mutually blended."

body.text:
tataśca sa dakṣiṇāṃ diśamāsasāda /
yatra masayamekalapālamañjarāḥ parvatāḥ /
kuntalakeralamahārāṣṭragāṅgakaliṅgādayo janapadāḥ /
tatrābhiyuñjānā tamaumeyīti, samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
sā dākṣiṇātyā pravṛttiḥ /
tāṃ te munayo 'bhituṣṭuvuḥ /
body.translated_text:
Then he reached the southern direction,
where the mountains <s>Masaya</s>, <s>Ekalapa</s>, and <s>Mālamanjarā</s> [are found];
where the regions of <s>Kuntala</s>, <s>Kerala</s>, <s>Mahārāṣṭra</s>, <s>Gāṅga</s>, <s>Kaliṅga</s>, and others [are found].
The daughter of <s>Umā</s> wooing him there — the same as before.
That was the <s>Dākṣiṇātya</s> (southern) manner.
The sages praised it:

children.translated_text: "With beautiful crests of hair curled from the root, with foreheads marked by masses of powder-locks,
with the garment tightly gathered from the hip to the ankle — may the costume of <s>Kerala</s> women long be victorious!"

body.text:
tāmanuraktamanāḥ sa yannepathyaḥ sārasvateya āsīditi samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
sāpi saiveti masānaṃ pūrveṇa /
yadvicitranṛttagītavādyavilāsādikameṣāvirbhāvayāmāsa sā kaiśikī vṛttiḥ /
tāṃ te munaya iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
yadatyarthaṃ ca sa tayā vaśaṃvadīkṛtaḥ sthānānuprāsavadasamāsaṃ yogavṛttigarbhaṃ ca (vākyaṃ)jagāda sā vaidarbhī rītiḥ /
tāṃ te munaya iti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
tatra veṣavinyāsakramaḥ pravṛttiḥ, vilāsavinyāsakramo vṛttiḥ, vacanavinyāsakramo rītiḥ /
'catuṣṭayī gatirvṛttīnāṃ pravṛttināṃ ca deśānāṃ punarānantyaṃ tatkathamiva kārtsnyena parigrahaḥ' ityācāryāḥ /
anantānapi hi deśāścaturdhaivākalpya kalpayanti 'cakravartikṣetraṃ sāmānyena tadavāntaraviśeṣaiḥ punaranantā eva'iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
dakṣiṇātsamudrādudīcīṃ diśaṃ prati yojanasahasraṃ cakravartikṣetraṃ, tatraiva nepathyavidhiḥ /
tataḥ paraṃ divyādyā api yaṃ deśamadhivaseyustaddeśyaṃ veṣamāśrayanto nibandhanīyāḥ /
svabhūmau tu kāmacāraḥ /
dvīpāntarabhavānāṃ tadanusāreṇa vṛttipravṛttī /
rītayastu tisraghastāstu purastāt /
tatrāsti manojanmano devasya krīḍāvāso vidarbheṣu vatsagulmaṃ nāma nagaram /
tatra sārasvateyastāmaumeyīṃ gandharvavatpariṇināya /
tatastadūdhūvaraṃ vinivṛttya teṣu pradeśeṣu viharamāṇaṃ tuṣāragirimevājagāma, yatra gaurī sarasvatī ca mithaḥ sambandhinyau tasthatuḥ /

children.text: tau ca kṛtavandanau dampatīdattvāśiṣaṃ prabhāvamayena vapuṣā kavimānasanivāsinau cakratuḥ /
children.translated_text: Those two [goddesses], having received the salutations of the couple, gave their blessings and, with a form endowed with power, made them dwell in the minds of poets.

children.text: tayośca taṃ sargaṃ kavibhyaḥ svargalokamakalpatāṃ, yatra kāvyamayena śarīreṇa marttyamadhivasanto divyena dehena kavaya ākalpaṃ modante /
children.translated_text: And that creation of theirs became a paradise for poets — where, dwelling among mortals with a body made of poetry, poets delight forever with a divine body.
Thus this <s>Kāvyapuruṣa</s> (Poetry-Person) was created of old by <s>Svayambhū</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>).

children.text: evaṃ vibhajya jānānaḥ pretya ceha ca nandati //
children.translated_text: One who, knowing this division, rejoices both in this world and in the next.

body.translated_text:
He whose heart was deeply enamored, whatever costume that son of <s>Sarasvatī</s> assumed — the same as before.
That too was the same — as before.
Whatever elaborate dance, song, music, and graceful display she manifested — that was the <s>Kaiśikī vṛtti</s> (the <s>Kaiśikī</s> dramatic mode).
The sages [praised] it — the same as before.
And when she brought him excessively under her spell by such attire, the speech he uttered — with few compounds, abundant alliteration, and embedded with figurative [expressions] — that was the <s>Vaidarbhī rīti</s> (the <s>Vidarbha</s> style).
The sages [praised] it — the same as before.
Therein, the sequence of costume-arrangement is <s>pravṛtti</s> (manner); the sequence of grace-arrangement is <s>vṛtti</s> (dramatic mode); the sequence of diction-arrangement is <s>rīti</s> (style).
"The four are the courses of the <s>vṛttis</s> and <s>pravṛttis</s>; but the regions are infinite — how then can there be complete enumeration?" — so say the teachers.
"Even infinite regions are arranged fourfold by arrangement" — "The domain of the <s>Cakravartin</s> (universal emperor) is [defined] in general terms; by its internal distinctions, they are indeed infinite" — thus says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s> (<s>Rājaśekhara</s>).
The domain of the <s>Cakravartin</s> extends a thousand <s>yojanas</s> from the southern ocean to the northern direction; the costume-rules [apply] within that domain.
Beyond that, even divine beings and others, dwelling in whatever region, should be represented wearing the costume of that region.
But in one's own land, there is freedom.
For those from other continents, the <s>vṛtti</s> and <s>pravṛtti</s> follow [the conventions of] that [place].
The styles (<s>rīti</s>) are three — these will be [discussed] ahead.
Therein, there is a city called <s>Vatsagulma</s> in <s>Vidarbha</s>, which is the pleasure-ground of the god born of the mind (<s>Kāmadeva</s>).
There, the son of <s>Sarasvatī</s> married the daughter of <s>Umā</s> in the <s>Gāndharva</s> manner.
Then, returning from that wedding procession, while wandering in those regions, he came to <s>Tuṣāragiri</s> (the Snowy Mountain / <s>Himālaya</s>), where <s>Gaurī</s> and <s>Sarasvatī</s>, who were related to each other, stood.

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe tṛtīyo 'dhyāyaḥ kāvyapuruṣotpattiḥ
body.translated_text: Thus ends the Third Chapter, "The Origin of the Poetry-Person" (<s>Kāvyapuruṣotpatti</s>), in the First Section of the <s>Kavirahasya</s> (Secret of Poets), in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.

body.text: śiṣyapratibhe caturtho 'dhyāyaḥ
body.translated_text: Fourth Chapter: "The Talent of the Student" (<s>Śiṣyapratiibhā</s>).

body.text:
śiṣyapratibhe dvividhaṃ śiṣyamācakṣate yaduta buddhimānāhāryabuddhiśca /
yasya nisargataḥ śāstramanudhāvati buddhiḥ sa buddhimān /
yasya ca śāstrābhyāsaḥ saṃskurute buddhimasāvāhāryabudhdiḥ /
tridhā ca sā, smṛtirmatiḥ prajñeti /
atikrāntasyārthasya smartrīsmṛtiḥ /
varttamānasya mantrī matiḥ /
anāgatasya prajñātrī prajñeti /
sā triprakārāpi kavīnāmupakartrī /
tayorbuddhimān śuśrūṣate śṛṇoti gṛhṇīte dhārayati vijānātyūhate 'pohati tattvaṃ cābhiniviśate /
āhāryabuddherapyeta eva guṇāḥ kintu praśāstāramapekṣante /
aharahaḥ sugurupāsanā tayoḥ prakṛṣṭe guṇaḥ /
sā hi buddhivikāsakāmadhenuḥ /
tadāhuḥ-
body.translated_text: On the talent of disciples: They describe two kinds of disciples — namely, the naturally intelligent and the one with acquired intelligence. He whose intellect naturally follows the treatise is the naturally intelligent one. He whose intellect is cultivated through the practice of the treatise — he is of acquired intelligence. And that [intelligence] is of three kinds: <s>smṛti</s> (memory), <s>mati</s> (deliberation), and <s>prajñā</s> (foresight). <s>Smṛti</s> is the faculty of remembering what is past. <s>Mati</s> is the faculty of deliberating on what is present. <s>Prajñā</s> is the faculty of foreseeing what is yet to come. All three of these are helpful to poets. Of the two, the naturally intelligent one serves [the teacher], listens, grasps, retains, understands, reasons, refutes, and arrives at the truth. The one of acquired intelligence also has these same qualities, but he requires a guide. Daily service to a good teacher is the supreme quality of both, for that [service] is the wish-fulfilling cow that develops the intellect. Thus they say —

children.translated_text: 'It first spreads the light of wisdom for the proper comprehension of meaning; then it produces a mind clear in the operations of reasoning and refutation;

children.text: abhainiviśate tasmāttattvaṃ tadekamukhodayaṃ saha paricayo vidyāvṛddhaiḥ kramādamṛtāyate' //
children.translated_text: from that, one arrives at the truth, which arises from that single source — familiarity with the learned in knowledge gradually becomes nectar-like.'

body.text:
tābhyāmanyathābuddhirdurbuddhiḥ /
tatra buddhimataḥ pratipattiḥ /
sa khalu sakṛdabhidhānapratipannārthaḥ kavimārgaṃ mṛgayituṃ gurukulamupāsīta /
āhāryabuddhestu dvayamapratipattiḥ sandehaśca /
sa khalvapratipannamarthaṃ pratipattuṃ sandehaṃ ca nirākartumācāryānupatiṣṭheta /
durbuddhestu sarvatra mativiparyāsa eva /
sa hi nīlīmecakitasicayakalpo 'nādheyaguṇāntaratvāt taṃ yadi sārasvato 'nubhāvaḥ prasādayati tamaupaniṣadike vakṣyāmaḥ /
'kāvyakarmaṇi kaveḥ samādhiḥ paraṃ vyāpriyate iti śyāmadevaḥ /
manasa ekāgratā samādhiḥ' /

children.translated_text: A concentrated mind perceives meanings. And it has been said —

children.text: 'sārasvataṃ kimapi tatsumahārahasyaṃ dadgocaraṃ ca viduṣāṃ nipuṇaikasevyam /
children.translated_text: 'That which pertains to <s>Sarasvatī</s>, that great secret somehow within the range of sight of the learned, accessible only to the most diligent —

children.text: tatsiddhaye paramayaṃ paramo 'bhyapāyo yaccetaso viditavedyavidheḥ samādhiḥ //
children.translated_text: for the attainment of that, the supreme means is <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), the discipline of one who has mastered the method of what is to be known.'

body.translated_text: Different from both of these is the one of wrong understanding — the dull-witted. In that regard, the comprehension of the naturally intelligent one [is described]: he indeed, having grasped the meaning from a single statement, should attend the guru's school to explore the path of poetry. For the one of acquired intelligence, there are two [problems]: non-comprehension and doubt. He indeed should attend upon teachers to comprehend what is not comprehended and to remove doubt. For the dull-witted, there is always perversion of understanding. He is like a heap dyed with indigo — incapable of receiving any other quality. If the grace of <s>Sarasvatī</s> should illuminate him, we shall speak of him in the <s>Aupaniṣadika</s> chapter. '<s>Samādhi</s> (concentration) is the supreme occupation of the poet in the work of poetry' — thus says <s>Śyāmadeva</s>. '<s>Samādhi</s> is one-pointedness of mind.'

body.text:
''abhyāsaḥ' iti maṅgalaḥ /
avicchedena śīlanamabhyāsaḥ /
sa hi sarvagāmī sarvatra niratiśayaṃ kauśalamādhatte /
samādhirāntaraḥ prayatno bāhyastvabhyāsaḥ /
tāvubhāvapi śaktimudbhāsayataḥ /
'sā kevalaṃ hetuḥ' iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
viprasṛtiśca sā pratibhāvyutpattibhyām /
śaktikartṛkehi pratibhāvyutpattikarmaṇī /
śaktasya pratibhāti śaktaśca vyutpadyate /
yā śabdagrāmamarthasārthamalaṅkāratantramuktimārgamanyadapi tathāvidhamadhihṛdayaṃ pratibhāsayati sā pratibhā /
apratibhasya padārthasārthaḥ parokṣa iva, pratibhāvataḥ punarapaśyato 'pi pratyakṣa iva /
yato meghāvirudrakumāradāsādayo jātyandhāḥ kavayaḥ śrūyante /
kiñcana mahākavayo 'pi deśadvīpāntarakathāpuruṣādidarśanena tatratyāṃ vyavahṛrti nibadhnantisma /

children.translated_text: In that regard, the portrayal of customs of another country —

children.text: 'prāṇānāmanilena vṛttirucitā satkalpavṛkṣe vane toye kāñcanapadmareṇukapiśe puṇyābhiṣekakriyā /
children.translated_text: 'The breath is sustained by the wind; in the forest of wish-fulfilling trees, the proper activity is ritual bathing in water tinged with the pollen of golden lotuses;

children.text: dhyānaṃ ratnaśilāgṛheṣu vibudhastrīsannidhau saṃyamo yatkāṅkṣanti tapobhiranyamunayastarsmistapasyantyamī //
children.translated_text: meditation in houses of jeweled rock-slabs, self-control in the presence of divine women — what other sages seek through austerities, these [sages] practice their austerities in that [paradise].'

body.translated_text: 'Practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>)' — thus says <s>Maṅgala</s>. <s>Abhyāsa</s> is uninterrupted cultivation. For it is all-pervading and everywhere brings about unsurpassable skill. <s>Samādhi</s> is the inner effort; <s>abhyāsa</s> is the outer. Both of these bring the creative power to light. 'That [power] is merely the cause' — thus says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. And its manifestation is through <s>pratibhā</s> (creative intuition) and <s>vyutpatti</s> (erudition). For the creative power is the agent, while <s>pratibhā</s> and <s>vyutpatti</s> are the actions. The capable one has intuition, and the capable one acquires erudition. That which makes manifest in the heart the host of words, the caravan of meanings, the system of ornaments, the path of expression, and other such things — that is <s>pratibhā</s> (creative intuition). For one without intuition, the caravan of word-meanings is as if invisible; but for one with intuition, even without seeing, it is as if directly perceived. For we hear that <s>Meghāvir</s>, <s>Rudra</s>, <s>Kumāradāsa</s>, and others were blind-born poets. Moreover, even great poets, through [merely] hearing the descriptions of other countries, islands, legendary persons, and the like, would compose accounts of the local customs there.

body.text: dvīpāntaravyavahāraḥ-
body.translated_text: The portrayal of customs of another island —

children.translated_text: 'I shall sport with him on the shores of the ocean, in the rustling groves of <s>tāḍī</s> palms,
[cooled] by breezes that have taken away the drops of sweat with clove-flowers brought from other islands.'

body.text: kathāpuruṣavyavahāraḥ-
body.translated_text: The portrayal of legendary persons —

children.translated_text: 'Even <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), his composure abandoned, like the ocean at the onset of moonrise,
directed his eyes upon the face of <s>Umā</s>, whose lower lip was like a <s>bimba</s> fruit.'

body.text: ādigrahaṇāt-
body.translated_text: From the word 'and others' [in the preceding statement] —

children.translated_text: 'A friend addressed her friend, the staff-bearer, who had arrived, beginning with a joke —
'Dear child, let us go elsewhere' — and then the bride looked at her with a sidelong glance crooked with jealousy.'

body.text:
sā ca dvidhā kārayitrī bhāvayitrī ca /
kaverupakurvāṇā kārayitrī /
sāpi trividhā sahajā'hāryaupadeśikī ca /
janmāntarasaṃskārāpekṣiṇī sahajā /
iha janmasaṃskārayonirāhāryā /
mantratantrādyupadeśaprabhavā aupadeśikī /
aihikena kiyatāpi saṃskāreṇa prathamāṃ tāṃ sahajeti vyapadiśanti /
mahatā punarāhāryā /
aupadeśikyāḥ punaraihika eva upadeśakālaḥ, aihika eva saṃskārakālaḥ /
ta ime trayo 'pi kavayaḥ sārasvataḥ, ābhyāsikaḥ, aupadeśikaśca /
janmāntarasaṃskārapravṛttasarasvatīko buddhimānsārasvataḥ /
iha janmābhyāsodbhāsitabhāratīka āhāryabuddhirābhyāsikaḥ /
upadeśitadarśitavāgvibhavā durbuddhiraupadeśikaḥ /
tasmānnetarau tantraśeṣamanutiṣṭhatām /
'nahi prakṛtimadhurā drākṣā phāṇitatasaṃskāramapekṣate' ityācāryāḥ /
'na'iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
body.translated_text: And that [<s>pratibhā</s>] is twofold: <s>kārayitrī</s> (productive, enabling the poet) and <s>bhāvayitrī</s> (appreciative, enabling the connoisseur). That which assists the poet in creating is <s>kārayitrī</s>. And it is of three kinds: innate (<s>sahajā</s>), acquired (<s>āhāryā</s>), and taught (<s>aupadeśikī</s>). That which depends on the impressions of previous births is innate. That born of cultivation in this very life is acquired. That arising from instruction in mantras, tantras, and the like is taught. With even some amount of cultivation in this life, they designate the first as 'innate.' The acquired, however, [requires] great [cultivation]. For the taught, both the time of instruction and the time of cultivation are in this very life. These then are the three types of poets: the <s>sārasvata</s> (divinely inspired), the <s>ābhyāsika</s> (trained through practice), and the <s>aupadeśika</s> (taught). The naturally intelligent one, in whom <s>Sarasvatī</s> operates through the impressions of previous births, is the <s>sārasvata</s>. The one of acquired intelligence, whose power of speech is brought to light through practice in this life, is the <s>ābhyāsika</s>. The dull-witted one, whose verbal power is shown through instruction, is the <s>aupadeśika</s>. Therefore, let not the other two [types] merely follow the remainder of the treatise. 'For a grape that is naturally sweet does not require the refinement of treacle' — thus say the teachers. 'No [that is not so]' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>.

body.text:
ekārthaṃ hi kriyādvayaṃ dvaiguṇyāya sampadyate /
'teṣāṃ pūrvaḥ pūrvaḥ śreyān' iti śyāmadevaḥ /
body.translated_text: For a twofold action toward a single goal produces a doubled result. 'Of these, the former is successively better' — says <s>Śyāmadeva</s>.

children.translated_text: The <s>sārasvata</s> (divinely inspired) poet is independent and profound; the <s>ābhyāsika</s> (practice-trained) would be moderate;
the <s>aupadeśika</s> (taught) poet, however, though his work may be charming, is also insubstantial and superficial.

body.text:
'utkarṣaḥ śreyān' iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
sa cānekaguṇasannipāte bhavati /

children.translated_text: Moreover —
'Intelligence, practice in the ancillary sciences of poetry,
and the mystic power [of <s>Sarasvatī</s>] — these three combined in one person are rare for a poet.

body.translated_text: 'The one who excels is better' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. And that [excellence] arises from the conjunction of many qualities.

children.translated_text: For the intelligent one who has practiced the sciences ancillary to poetry
and who is devoted to the performance of mantras — the kingship of poetry is nearest.'

body.text: kavīnāṃ tāratamyataścaiṣa prāyovādaḥ /

children.translated_text: As it is said —

children.text: 'ekasya tiṣṭhati kavergṛha eva kāvyam anyasya gacchati suhṛdbhavanāni yāvat /
children.translated_text: 'The poetry of one poet remains in his own house; another's travels as far as the houses of friends;

children.text: nyasyāvidagdhavadaneṣu padāni śaścat kasyāpi sañcarati viścakutūhalīva' //
children.translated_text: but someone's [poetry], constantly placing its feet in the mouths of even the unlearned, wanders about like a curiosity belonging to the whole world.'

body.translated_text: And this is a general statement about the gradation among poets.

body.text:
seyaṃ kārayitrī /
bhāvakasyopakurvāṇā bhāvayitrī /
sā hi kaveḥ śramamabhiprāyaṃ ca bhāvayati /
tayā khalu phalitaḥ kavervyāpārataruḥ /
anyathā so 'vakeśī syāt 'kaḥ punaranayorbhedo yatkavirbhāvayati bhāvakaśca kaviḥ' ityācāryāḥ /

children.translated_text: Thus they say —
'According to the gradation of intuition, fame is established in abundance upon the brow [of poets];

children.text: bhāvakastu kaviḥ prāyo na bhajatyadhamāṃ daśam //
children.translated_text: but the appreciative poet generally does not descend to the lowest state.'

body.translated_text: This is the <s>kārayitrī</s> (productive intuition). That which assists the connoisseur (<s>bhāvaka</s>) is <s>bhāvayitrī</s> (appreciative intuition). For it makes one experience (<s>bhāvayati</s>) the effort and intention of the poet. Through it indeed the tree of the poet's labor bears fruit. Otherwise it would be fruitless. 'But what is the difference between them, since the poet also appreciates and the appreciator is also a poet?' — thus say the teachers.

body.text:
"na'iti kālidāsaḥ /
pṛthageva hi kavitvābhdāvakatvaṃ, bhāvakatvācca kavitvam /
svarupabhedādviṣayabhedācca /

children.translated_text: as they say —

children.text: 'kaścidvācaṃ racayitumalaṃ śrotumevāparastāṃ kalyāṇī te matirubhayathā vismayaṃ nastanoti /
children.translated_text: 'One person is able to compose speech, another merely to hear it; your auspicious intellect amazes us in both respects;

children.text: nahyekasminnatiśayavatāṃ sannipāto guṇānām ekaḥ sūte kanakamrupalastatparīkṣākṣamo 'nyaḥ //
children.translated_text: for the conjunction of excellent qualities does not occur in a single person — one produces gold, another has the ability to test it.'

body.translated_text: 'No [that is not so]' — says <s>Kālidāsa</s>. For poetic creation and appreciation are distinct; and from appreciation comes [recognition of] poetry. By the difference in their essential nature and in their objects,

body.text:
"te ca dvidhārocakinaḥ, satṛṇābhyavahāriṇaśca' iti maṅgalaḥ /
'kavayopi bhavanti'iti vāmanīyāḥ ' /
caturdhā' iti yāyāvarīyaḥ 'matsariṇastattvābhiniveśinaśca' /
'tatra vivekinaḥ pūrve tadviparītāstu tato 'nantarāḥ'iti vāmanīyāḥ /
'arocakitā hi teṣāṃ naisargikī, jñānayonirvā /
naisirgikīṃ hi saṃskāraśatenāpi vaṅgamiva kālikāṃ te na jahati /
jñānayonau tu tasyāṃ viśiṣṭajñāyavati vacasi rocakitāvṛttireva' iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
. kiñca satṛṇābhyavahāritā sarvasādhāraṇī /
tathāhi-vyutpitsoḥ kautukinaḥ sarvasya sarvatra prathamaṃ sā /
pratibhāvivekavikalatā hi na guṇāguṇayorvibhāgasūtraṃ pātayati /
tato bahu tyajati bahu ca gṛhṇāti /
vivekānusāreṇa hi buddhayo madhu niṣyandante /
pariṇāme tu yathārthadarśī syāt /
vibhramabhraṃśaśca niḥśreyasaṃ santidhatte /
matsariṇastu pratibhātamapi na pratibhātaṃ, paraguṇeṣu vācaṃyamatvāt /
sa punaramatsarī jñātā ca viralaḥ /

children.translated_text: Thus it has been said —

children.text: 'kastvaṃ bhoḥ kavirasmi kāpyabhinavā sūktiḥ sakhe paṭhyatāṃ tyaktā kāvyakathaiva samprati mayā kasmādidaṃ śruyatām /
children.translated_text: 'Who are you, sir?' 'I am a poet.' 'Friend, recite some fresh verse.' 'I have given up the very talk of poetry now.' 'Why? Let this be heard —

children.text: yaḥ sampagvivinakti doṣaguṇayoḥ sāraṃ, svayaṃ satkaviḥ so 'sminbhāvaka eva nāstyatha bhaveddaivānna nirmatsaraḥ' //
children.translated_text: he who himself distinguishes the essence among faults and merits, being a good poet — as for him, there is no appreciator; and should there be one, by fate he would not be free from envy.'

body.translated_text: 'And they [the connoisseurs] are of two kinds: those with refined taste and those who consume [everything] including the chaff' — says <s>Maṅgala</s>. 'Poets too may be [connoisseurs]' — say the followers of <s>Vāmana</s>. 'Of four kinds' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s> — 'the envious and those devoted to truth [are also included].' 'Among these, the discriminating ones come first; those opposite to them come next' — say the followers of <s>Vāmana</s>. 'For the lack of taste in them is either natural or born of knowledge. That which is natural — even with a hundred refinements, they do not abandon it, like the blackness of tin. But when it is born of knowledge, then when confronted with a distinguished utterance, the disposition of refined taste returns' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. Moreover, consuming [everything] including the chaff is common to all. For indeed, for anyone curious and eager to learn, that [undiscriminating taste] is at first universal everywhere. For the lack of discrimination through intuition does not allow the thread of distinction between merits and faults to be drawn. Therefore one rejects much and accepts much. But with the guidance of discrimination, the intellect flows like honey. In the end, one becomes a seer of truth. And the fall from delusion bestows the highest good. But the envious person [claims] even what has been intuitively grasped to be not grasped, because of his silence regarding others' virtues. Such a one who is free from envy and also a knower is rare.

children.translated_text: But one devoted to truth, if even one among a thousand — as it has been said —

children.text: 'śabdānāṃ vivinakti gumphanavidhīnāmodate sūktibhiḥ sāndaṃ leḍhi rasāmṛtaṃ vicinute tātparyamrudrāṃ ca yaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'He who discriminates the methods of word-arrangement, delights in fine sayings, intensely licks the nectar of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion), discerns the deeper meaning, and the profound sense —

children.text: puṇyaiḥ saṅghaṭate vivektṛvirahādantarmukhaṃ tāmyatāṃ keṣāmeva kadācideva sudhiyāṃ kāvyaśramajño janaḥ //
children.translated_text: such a person, knowledgeable about the labor of poetry, comes together only through merit; in the absence of a discerning critic, let the inward-directed [poets] suffer — for only occasionally, among only a few wise ones, is there such a person.'

children.text: svānī mitraṃ ca mantrī ca śiṣyaśyācārya eva ca /
children.translated_text: His own self, friend, counselor, disciple, teacher as well —

children.text: kaverbhavati hī titraṃ kiṃ hi tadyanna bhāvakaḥ //
children.translated_text: all of these the poet possesses as a trusted companion — for what is there that the connoisseur is not?
What use is a poem to a poet if it exists only in the confines of his own mind?

children.text: nīyante bhāvakairyasya na nibandhā diśo daśa //
children.translated_text: He whose compositions are not carried by connoisseurs to the ten directions [of the world is of no account].
Poetic compositions inscribed in books exist in every household;
but only two or three are those whose [compositions] are pounded on the stone slab of the connoisseur's mind.
Some transformations of the connoisseur shine forth in fine poetry —
those which were not seen even by the creator of drama [<s>Bharata</s>], though determined through all modes of dramatic representation.
Some are connoisseurs of speech; some are connoisseurs of the heart;
some are connoisseurs through <s>sāttvika</s> (involuntary emotional) responses, through bodily gestures, and through consequent expressions.
Some are inclined to perceive merits; others to perceive faults;
and some connoisseurs are devoted to both accepting merits and rejecting faults.
Even when the application is the same, this sequence is varied;
thereby we know that the cause of people's delight in this [poetry] is superhuman.

children.text: na nisargakaviḥ śāstre na kṣuṇṇaḥ kavate ca yaḥ /
children.translated_text: He who is not a poet by nature, nor well-versed in the science [of poetry], yet composes —
he merely mocks himself, being seized by obstinate attachment.

children.text: kavitvaṃ na sthitaṃ yasya kāvye ca kṛtakaitukaḥ /
children.translated_text: He in whom poetic talent does not reside, yet who is eager about poetry —
his success in [the art of] <s>Sarasvatī</s> [comes] from the application of tantric and mantra practices.
When the wise person knows the difference between his own words and those of others,

children.text: tadā sa siddho mantavyaḥ, kukaviḥ kavireva vā //
children.translated_text: then he should be considered accomplished — whether a bad poet or a true poet.
The <s>kārayitrī</s> (productive) and the <s>bhāvayitrī</s> (appreciative) — these are the two divisions of <s>pratibhā</s> (intuition).
Now hereafter we shall describe <s>vyutpatti</s> (erudition), the mother of poetry.'

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe śiṣyapratibhāvyākhyānaḥ caturtho 'dhyāyaḥ
body.translated_text: Thus ends the fourth chapter, entitled 'The Exposition of the Disciple's Intuition,' in the first section of the <s>Kavirahsya</s> (Secrets of the Poet) in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.
Chapter 5

body.text: vyutpattikavipākāḥ
body.translated_text: Erudition and the Types of Poets (<s>vyutpattikavipākāḥ</s>)

body.text: pañcamo 'dhyāyaḥ 5.
body.translated_text: Fifth chapter, section 5.

body.text:
vyutpattikavipākāḥ 'bahujñātā vyutpattiḥ' ityācāryāḥ /
sarvatodikkā hi kavivācaḥ /

children.translated_text: Thus it has been said —

children.text: 'prasarati kimapi kathañcana nābhyaste gocare vacaḥ kasya /
children.translated_text: 'The speech of one who has not practiced hardly extends at all, somehow, to any sphere;
that alone is true poetic art — that one's words reach in all directions.'

body.translated_text: '<s>Vyutpatti</s> (erudition) is extensive knowledge' — thus say the teachers. For the words of a poet range in all directions.

body.text:
"ucitānucitaviveko vyutpattiḥ' iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
'pratibhāvyutpattyoḥ pratibhā śreyasī' ityānandaḥ /
sā hi kaveravyutpattikṛtaṃ doṣamaśeṣamācchādayati /

children.translated_text: Thus he says —
'The fault arising from lack of erudition is covered by the poet's power (<s>śakti</s>);
but the fault arising from lack of power appears like a blemish [that cannot be hidden].'

body.translated_text: 'The discrimination between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate is <s>vyutpatti</s> (erudition)' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. '<s>Pratibhā</s> (intuition) is superior to <s>vyutpatti</s> (erudition) between the two' — says <s>Ānanda</s>. For it conceals completely the faults that arise from a poet's lack of erudition.

body.text: śaktiśabdaścāyamupacaritaḥ pratibhāne varttate /

children.translated_text: <s>Pratibhā</s> (intuition) is illustrated as follows —

children.text: 'etatkiṃ śirasi sthitaṃ mama pituḥ, khaṇḍaṃ sudhājanmano lālāṭaṃ kimidaṃ vilocanamidaṃ, haste 'sya kiṃ pannagāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'What is this on my father's head — a fragment born of nectar? What is this on his forehead? Is this an eye? What are these in his hand — serpents?'

children.text: itthaṃ krauñcaripoḥ kramādupagate digvāsasaḥ śūlinaḥ praśne vāmakaroparodhasubhagaṃ devyāḥ smitaṃ pātu vaḥ //
children.translated_text: When <s>Krauñcaripu</s> (the enemy of Mount <s>Krauñca</s>, i.e., <s>Kārttikeya</s>) thus questioned the trident-bearing, sky-clad one (<s>Śiva</s>) step by step — may the smile of the Goddess (<s>Devī</s>), made beautiful by the restraint of her left hand [over her mouth], protect you!'

body.translated_text: And the word <s>śakti</s> (power) here is used figuratively to denote <s>pratibhā</s> (intuition).

body.text:
"vyutpattiḥ śreyasī' iti maṅgalaḥ /
sā hi kaveraśaktikṛtaṃ doṣamaśeṣamācchādayati /

children.translated_text: As for instance —
'The poet's lack of power is covered by erudition on the path of poetry;
the clever-minded should avoid [mere] stringing together of words [without substance].'

body.translated_text: '<s>Vyutpatti</s> (erudition) is superior' — says <s>Maṅgala</s>. For it conceals completely the fault caused by the poet's lack of creative power.

children.translated_text: <s>Vyutpatti</s> (erudition) is illustrated as follows —

children.text: 'kṛtaḥ kaṇṭhe niṣko nahi kimuta tanvī maṇilatā kṛśaṃ līlāpatraṃ śravasi nihitaṃ kuṇḍalamraci /
children.translated_text: 'No necklace was placed on her neck, nor a delicate string of gems; no playful ornamental leaf was set on her ear, nor an earring for beauty;

children.text: na kauśeyaṃ citraṃ vasanamavadātaṃ tu vasitaṃ samāsannībhūte nidhuvanavilāse vanītayā //
children.translated_text: no colorful silken garment was worn, but only a spotless white one — by the young woman, when the delights of lovemaking drew near.'

body.text:
"pratibhāvyutpattī mithaḥ samavete śreyasyau iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
na khalu lāvaṇyalābhādṛte rupasampadṛte rupasampado vā lāvaṇyalabdhirmahate saundaryāya /

children.translated_text: The combination of both is illustrated as follows —
'With <s>golāṅgūla</s> monkeys (langurs), whose swaying tail-creepers encircle the trunks of <s>bakula</s> trees, chattering in the reverberant old mountain caves,

in the groves where the serpent-hoods of cobras are raised erect — by whom the breezes, the kinsmen of the <s>tāla</s> palms with bursting sheaths, overleap the tide-line — the novel foot-ornament of <s>Bhavānī</s> (<s>Pārvatī</s>), presenting the beauty of a lotus born from the naturally clear pool of her own bodily grace, triumphs in her lord's imitation of [cosmic] dance.'

body.translated_text: '<s>Pratibhā</s> (intuition) and <s>vyutpatti</s> (erudition), when mutually united, are the best' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. For indeed, without the acquisition of charm (<s>lāvaṇya</s>) there is no beauty of form, nor without beauty of form is there acquisition of charm — for great loveliness.

body.text:
pratibhāvyutpattimāṃśca kaviḥ kavirityucyate /
sa ca tridhā /
śāstrakaviḥ kāvyakavirubhayakaviśca /
'teṣāmuttarottarīyo garīyān' iti śyāmadevaḥ /
'na'iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
yathāsvaviṣaye sarvo garīyān /
nahi rājahaṃsaścandrikāpānāya prabhavati, nāpi cakoro 'dbhayaḥ kṣīroddharaṇāya /
yacchāstrakaviḥ kāvye rasasampadaṃ vicchinatti /
yatkāvyakaviḥśāstre tarkakarkaśamapyarthamuktivaicitryeṇa ślathayati /
ubhayakavistūbhayorapi varīyānyadyubhayatra paraṃ pravīṇaḥ syāt /
tasmāttulyaprabhāvāveva śāstrakāvyakavī /
upakāryopakārakabhāvaṃ tu mithaḥ śāstrakāvyoranumanyāmahe /
yacchāstrasaṃskāraḥ kāvyamanugṛhṇāti śāstraikapravaṇatā tu nigṛhṇāti /
kāvyasaṃskāro 'pi śāstraghavākyapākamanuruṇaddhi kāvyaikapravaṇatā tu viruṇaddhi /
tatragha tridhā śāstrakaviḥ /
yaḥ śāstraṃ vidhatte, yaśca śāstre kāvyaṃ saṃvalidhatte, yo 'pi kāvye śāstrārthaṃ nidhatte /
kāvyakaviḥ punaraṣṭadhā /
tadyathā-racanākaviḥ, śabda-kaviḥ, arthakaviḥ, alaṅkārakaviḥ, uktikaviḥ, rasakaviḥ, mārgakaviḥ, śāstrārthakaviriti /

children.translated_text: Among these, the poet of composition (<s>racanākavi</s>) —
'With <s>golāṅgūla</s> monkeys, whose swaying tail-vines encircle the trunks of <s>bakula</s> trees, chattering in the reverberant old mountain caves,
in groves where cobras raise erect their expanded hoods — by whom the wind, kinsman of <s>tāla</s> palms with bursting sheaths, overleaps the tide-line.'

body.translated_text: And a poet possessing both <s>pratibhā</s> (intuition) and <s>vyutpatti</s> (erudition) is truly called a poet. And he is of three kinds: a <s>śāstrakavi</s> (scientific poet), a <s>kāvyakavi</s> (literary poet), and an <s>ubhayakavi</s> (poet of both). 'Of these, each succeeding one is greater' — says <s>Śyāmadeva</s>. 'No' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s> — each is greatest in his own domain. For the royal swan cannot drink moonlight, nor can the <s>cakora</s> bird extract milk from water. A <s>śāstrakavi</s> in poetry disrupts the richness of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion). A <s>kāvyakavi</s> in a treatise softens even an argument that is harsh with logic through the variety of his expression. But an <s>ubhayakavi</s> is superior to both, if he is supremely skilled in both. Therefore the scientific and literary poets are of equal power. But we acknowledge the mutual relationship of beneficiary and benefactor between science and literature. For the cultivation of science benefits literature, but exclusive devotion to science hinders it. Similarly, literary cultivation furthers the maturity of scientific prose, but exclusive devotion to literature obstructs it. Among these, the <s>śāstrakavi</s> (scientific poet) is of three kinds: one who composes a treatise, one who blends poetry into a treatise, and one who introduces the content of a treatise into poetry. The <s>kāvyakavi</s> (literary poet), however, is of eight kinds, namely: the poet of composition (<s>racanākavi</s>), the poet of words (<s>śabdakavi</s>), the poet of meaning (<s>arthakavi</s>), the poet of ornament (<s>alaṅkārakavi</s>), the poet of expression (<s>uktikavi</s>), the poet of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) (<s>rasakavi</s>), the poet of style (<s>mārgakavi</s>), and the poet of philosophical content (<s>śāstrārthakavi</s>).

body.text: tridhā ca śabdakavirnāmākhyātobhayabhedena /

children.translated_text: Among these, the poet of nouns (<s>nāmakavi</s>) —

children.text: 'vidyeva puṃso mahimeva rājñaḥ prajñeva vaidyasya dayeva sādhoḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Like knowledge for a man, majesty for a king, wisdom for a physician, compassion for a saint,

children.text: lajjeva śūrasya mṛjeva yūno vibhūṣaṇaṃ tasya nṛpasya saiva' //
children.translated_text: modesty for a hero, grooming for a youth — she alone was the ornament of that king.'

body.translated_text: And the poet of words (<s>śabdakavi</s>) is of three kinds, distinguished by nouns, verbs, and both.

children.translated_text: The poet of verbs (<s>ākhyātakavi</s>) —
'They laughed aloud, were thrilled, roared, struck with their massive flashing arms,

children.text: santuṣṭuvurmumudire bahu menire ca vācaṃ guroramṛtasambhavalābhagarbhām' //
children.translated_text: praised, rejoiced, and greatly esteemed the words of the teacher, pregnant with the gain of nectar.'
The poet of both nouns and verbs (<s>nāmākhyātakavi</s>) —
'Deprived of luster, blind, with shoulders and arms gone limp, the women, as if unconscious with despair,

children.text: na cukruśurno rurudurna sasvanurna celurāsurlikhitā iva kṣaṇam' //
children.translated_text: did not cry out, nor weep, nor make a sound, nor stir — they were motionless, as if painted, for a moment.'
The poet of meaning (<s>arthakavi</s>) —

children.text: 'devī putramasūta nṛtyata gaṇāḥ kiṃ tiṣṭhatetyudbhuje harṣādbhṛṅgiriṭāhṛtagirā cāmuṇḍayāliṅgite /
children.translated_text: 'The Goddess has borne a son! Dance, O <s>Gaṇas</s>! Why are you standing?' — at this, with arms upraised, when <s>Cāmuṇḍā</s> embraced [them] with words spoken [ecstatically] by <s>Bhṛṅgiriṭa</s> in his joy,

may the sound protect you — [a sound] that arose from the impact of their bodies against each other, born from the striking of their massive bones, overpowering even the music of the <s>dundubhi</s> drums of the gods.'

body.text: dvidhālaṅkārakaviḥ śabdārthabhedena /

children.translated_text: Of these, verbal ornament (<s>śabdālaṅkāra</s>) —

children.text: 'na prātpaṃ viṣamaraṇaṃ prātpaṃ pāpena karmaṇā viṣamaraṇaṃ ca /
children.translated_text: 'No death by poison was obtained; but death by poison was obtained through sinful deeds;

children.text: na mṛto bhāgīrathyāṃ mṛto 'hamupaguhya mandabhāgī rathyām' //
children.translated_text: I did not die in the <s>Gaṅgā</s> (<s>Bhāgīrathī</s>); I, ill-fated one, died embracing [the corpse on] the road.'

body.translated_text: The poet of ornament (<s>alaṅkārakavi</s>) is of two kinds, distinguished by verbal ornament and ornament of meaning.

children.translated_text: Ornament of meaning (<s>arthālaṅkāra</s>) —
'Of <s>Vāsuki</s>, whose flickering tongue is like a banner, whose hood is like an umbrella,
my arm is capable of reducing [even] his fang-pegs to poverty [i.e., rendering them useless].'
The poet of expression (<s>uktikavi</s>) —
'This belly is contemptible; the sighs of the proud woman are to be sipped; the slope of her breasts [sets] the boundary for the embrace of the arm-creeper;

children.text: sphurati ca vadanendurddakpraṇālīnipeyastad iha sudṛśi kalyāḥ kelayo yauvanasya' //
children.translated_text: and the moon of her face shines, to be drunk through the channel of the gaze — such, in this beautiful-eyed woman, are the delightful sports of youth.'
Or again —
'The lower lip accepts the <s>aśoka</s> sprout-like hue of red; the cheek, from its pallor, descends to the maturity of the <s>tāḍī</s> palm;

children.text: parimlānaprāyāmanuvadati dṛṣṭiḥ kamalinīm itīyaṃ mādhuryaṃ spṛśati ca tanutvaṃ ca bhajate' //
children.translated_text: the gaze, almost withered, imitates the lotus — thus she touches sweetness and also assumes thinness.'
The poet of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) (<s>rasakavi</s>) —
'Look at this river <s>Tāmraparṇī</s>, O slender-waisted one — the pearls extracted from opened oyster-shells in the ocean,

children.text: yasyāḥ payāṃsi pariṇāhiṣu hāramūrttyā vāmabhruvāṃ pariṇamanti payodhareṣu' //
children.translated_text: whose waters, in the form of necklaces, ripen upon the full breasts of beautiful-browed women.'
The poet of style (<s>mārgakavi</s>) —

children.text: 'mūlaṃ bālakavīrudhāṃ surabhayo jātītaruṇāṃ tvacaḥ sāraścandanaśāśināṃ kisalayānyārdrāṇyaśokasya ca /
children.translated_text: 'The roots of young tender herbs, the fragrant barks of <s>jātī</s> saplings, the heartwood of <s>candana</s> (sandalwood) and moonstone trees, the fresh shoots of <s>aśoka</s>,

children.text: śairīṣī kusumogdatiḥ pariṇamanmocaṃ ca so 'yaṃ gaṇo grīṣmeṇoṣmaharaḥ purā kila dade dagdhāya pañcaṣave' //
children.translated_text: the blossom-tip of <s>śirīṣa</s>, and the ripening plantain — this group, heat-removing in summer, was once offered to the burnt <s>Pañcaśara</s> (<s>Kāma</s>, the five-arrowed god of love).'
The poet of philosophical content (<s>śāstrārthakavi</s>) —

'Those who delight in the Self, who have attained bliss in the thought-free <s>samādhi</s> (meditation), whose knots of darkness are untied by the surge of knowledge, who are established in <s>sattva</s> (pure being) —

children.text: yaṃ vīkṣinte kamapi tamasāṃ jyotiṣāṃ vā parastāt taṃ mohāndhaḥ kathamayamamuṃ vetti devaṃ purāṇam' //
children.translated_text: Him whom they behold, [that being] beyond darkness and beyond light — how can this one, blinded by delusion, know that ancient God?'

body.text:
eṣāṃ dvitrairguṇaiḥ kanīyān, pañcakairmadhyamaḥ, sarvaguṇayogī mahākaviḥ /
daśa ca kaveravasthā bhavanti /
tatra ca buddhimadāhāryabuddhayoḥ satpa, tistraśca aupadeśikasya /
tadyathā-kāvyavidyāsnātako, hṛdayakaviḥ, anyāpadeśī, sevitā, ghaṭamānaḥ, mahākaviḥ, kavirājaḥ, āvicchedī, saṅkrāmayitā ca /
yaḥ kavitvakāmaḥ kāvyavidyopavidyāgrahaṇāya gurukulānyupāste sa vidyāsnātakaḥ /
yo hṛdaya eva kavate nihnute ca sa hṛdayakaviḥ /
yaḥ svamapi kāvyaṃ doṣabhayādanyasyetyapadiśya paṭhati so 'nyāpadeśī /
yaḥ pravṛttavacanaḥ paurastyānāmanyatamacchāyāmabhyasyati sa sevitā /
yo 'navadyaṃ kavate na tu prabadhnāti sa ghaṭamānaḥ /
yo 'nyataraprabandhe pravīṇaḥ sa mahākaviḥ /
yastu tatra tatragha bhāṣāviśeṣe teṣu teṣu prabandheṣu tasmiṃstasmiṃśca rase svatantraḥ sa kavirājaḥ /
te yadi jagatyapi katipaye /
yo mantrādyupadeśavaśāllabdhasiddhirāveśasamakālaṃ kavate sa āviśikaḥ /
yo yadaivecchati tadaivāvicchinnavacanaḥ so 'vicchedī /
yaḥ kanyākumārādiṣu siddhamantraḥ sarasvatīṃ saṅkrāmayati sa saṅkrāmayitā /
satatamabhyāsavaśataḥ sukaveḥ vākyaṃ pākamāyāti /
'kaḥ punarayaṃ pākaḥ?' ityācāryāḥ /
'pariṇāmaḥ' iti maṅgalaḥ /
'kaḥ punarayaṃ pariṇāmaḥ?' ityācāryāḥ /
'supāṃ tiṅgāṃ ca śravaḥ saiṣā vyutpattiḥ'iti maṅgalaḥ /
sauśabdyametat /
'padaniveśaniṣkampatā pākaḥ'ityācāryāḥ /

children.translated_text: Thus they say —
'As long as the mind oscillates in the insertion and removal [of words],

children.text: padānāṃ sthāpite sthairye hanta siddhā sarasvatī //
children.translated_text: when firmness of words is established — behold, <s>Sarasvatī</s> is accomplished!'

body.translated_text: Among these, one who possesses two or three qualities is a minor [poet]; one with five is a middling [poet]; one who combines all qualities is a <s>mahākavi</s> (great poet). And there are ten stages of a poet. Among these, seven belong to the naturally intelligent and the one of acquired intelligence, and three to the taught one. They are: the student of poetry (<s>kāvyavidyāsnātaka</s>), the poet of the heart (<s>hṛdayakavi</s>), the pseudonymous one (<s>anyāpadeśin</s>), the imitator (<s>sevitṛ</s>), the striving one (<s>ghaṭamāna</s>), the great poet (<s>mahākavi</s>), the king of poets (<s>kavirāja</s>), the uninterrupted one (<s>āvicchedin</s>), and the transmitter (<s>saṅkrāmayitṛ</s>). He who, desiring poetic art, attends the schools of teachers for the acquisition of poetry and its ancillary sciences — he is the student (<s>vidyāsnātaka</s>). He who composes only in his heart and conceals [his work] — he is the poet of the heart (<s>hṛdayakavi</s>). He who, out of fear of criticism, recites even his own poetry attributing it to someone else — he is the pseudonymous one (<s>anyāpadeśin</s>). He who, having begun to speak, practices the style of one or another of the ancients — he is the imitator (<s>sevitṛ</s>). He who composes faultlessly but does not bind [his work into a composition] — he is the striving one (<s>ghaṭamāna</s>). He who is accomplished in one type of literary composition — he is the great poet (<s>mahākavi</s>). But he who is independent in various languages, in various types of compositions, and in various <s>rasas</s> — he is the king of poets (<s>kavirāja</s>). Such persons are few even in the world. He who, through instruction in mantras and the like, attains accomplishment and composes at the time of [divine] possession — he is the one possessed (<s>āviśika</s>). He who, whenever he wishes, speaks without interruption — he is the uninterrupted one (<s>āvicchedin</s>). He who, having accomplished mantras at [sacred sites like] <s>Kanyākumārī</s> and the like, transmits <s>Sarasvatī</s> [to others] — he is the transmitter (<s>saṅkrāmayitṛ</s>). Through constant practice, the speech of a good poet attains maturity (<s>pāka</s>). 'But what is this maturity?' — ask the teachers. 'Transformation' — says <s>Maṅgala</s>. 'But what is this transformation?' — ask the teachers. 'The knowledge of nominal and verbal forms — that is <s>vyutpatti</s> (erudition)' — says <s>Maṅgala</s>. This amounts to mere grammatical correctness. 'Maturity is the unshakeable placement of words' — say the teachers.

body.text: "āgrahaparigrahādapi padasthairyaparyavasāyastasmātpadānāṃ parivṛttivaimukhyaṃ pākaḥ'iti vāmanīyāḥ /

children.translated_text: Thus they say —
'When words themselves abandon the capacity for replacement,
those skilled in the arrangement of words call that the maturity of words.'

body.translated_text: 'Even beyond obstinate attachment, the final settlement of word-firmness — therefore, maturity is the aversion of words to being replaced' — say the followers of <s>Vāmana</s>.

body.text:
"iyamaśaktirna punaḥ pākaḥ'ityavantisundarī /
yadekasminvastuni mahākavīnāmineko 'pi pāṭhaḥ paripākavānbhavati, tasmādrasocitaśabdārthasūktinibandhanaḥ pākaḥ /

children.translated_text: As she says —
'That arrangement of qualities, ornaments, style, expression, words, and meaning

children.text: svadate sudhiyāṃ yena vākyapākaḥ sa māṃ prati' //
children.translated_text: which delights the wise — that is maturity of speech, in my view.'

body.translated_text: 'This is [merely] inability, not maturity' — says <s>Avantisundarī</s>. Since among great poets, even a single reading on a single subject attains full ripeness, therefore maturity is the composition of fine sayings with words and meanings appropriate to the <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion).

children.translated_text: Thus it has been said —

children.text: 'sati vaktari satyarthe śabde sati rase sati /
children.translated_text: 'When the speaker exists, when the meaning is true, when the word exists, when <s>rasa</s> exists,

children.text: asti tanna vinā yena paristravati vāṅmadhu //
children.translated_text: there is still something without which the honey of speech does not flow.'

body.text:
"kāryānumeyatayā yattacchabdanivedyaḥ paraṃ pāko 'bhidhāviṣayastatsahṛdayaprasiddhisiddha eva vyavahārāṅgamasau'iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
sa ca kavigrāmasyakāvyamabhyasyate navadhā bhavati /
tatrādyantayorasvādu picumandapākam, ādāvasvādu pariṇāme madhyamaṃ badarapākam, ādāvasvādu pariṇāme svādu mṛdvīkāpākam, ādau madhyamamante cāsvādu vārttākapākam, ādyantayormadhyamaṃ tintiḍīkapākam, ādau madhyamamante svādu sahakārapākam, ādāvuttamamante cāsvādu kramukapākam, ādāvuttamamante madhyamaṃ trapusapākam, ādyantayoḥ svādu nālikerapākamiti /
teṣāṃ triṣvapi trikeṣu pākāḥ prathame tyājyāḥ /
varamakavirna punaḥ kukaviḥ syāt /
kukavitā hi socchravāsaṃ maraṇam /
madhyamāḥ saṃskāryāḥ /
saṃskāro hi sarvasya guṇamutkarṣayati /
dvādaśavarṇamapi suvarṇaṃ pāvakapākena hemībhavati /
śeṣā grāhyāḥ /
svabhāvaśuddhaṃ hi na saṃskāramapaikṣate /
na muktāmaṇeḥ śāṇastāratāyai prabhavati /

children.translated_text: That which has an unsettled maturity they call <s>kapitthapāka</s> (wood-apple ripening).
In that, the obtaining of fine sayings is like obtaining grains of rice by winnowing chaff.
When one properly practices poetry, it ripens in nine ways;
the wise person should discriminate among them by the principle of rejection and acceptance.

body.translated_text: 'That which is to be inferred from the effect [on the listener], that which is communicated beyond the literal words — that is the supreme maturity in the domain of denotation; and this is established by the experience of the sensitive reader (<s>sahṛdaya</s>) and is a component of [literary] convention' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. And [maturity] as practiced by the community of poets becomes ninefold in poetry.
