children.translated_text: Thus they say:
"<s>Vaidarbhī</s>, <s>Gauḍīyā</s>, and <s>Pāñcālī</s> — these are the three <s>rītis</s> (styles).

children.text: āśu ca sākṣānnivasati sarasvatī tena lakṣyante" //
children.translated_text: In these, <s>Sarasvatī</s> (the goddess of speech) directly and swiftly resides — hence they are recognized."

body.translated_text: "Why then is there exposition of the two unteachable speech-paths, the <s>Brāhya</s> and the <s>Pārameśvara</s>?" — thus the teachers [ask]. "That too is meant for the instruction of poets" — thus says the <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. Because in dramas and similar [works], when gods like <s>Īśvara</s> and others enter, speeches possessing the character of those [types] should be composed — hence [the term] 'divine.' Here the main discussion concerns the speech of <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>Vāsudeva</s>, who delights in worldly conduct through mortal incarnation — that is <s>Vaiṣṇava</s>, and they designate it as 'human.' And that is threefold according to the three <s>rītis</s> (styles).

children.translated_text: The three types of sentences in the form of <s>rīti</s> (style) — but <s>kāku</s> (tonal expression) multiplies [them] greatly.
"<s>Kāku</s> (tonal modulation) is named <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) — it is a verbal figure of speech" — thus says <s>Rudraṭa</s>.

body.text:
"abhiprāyāvānpāṭhadharmaḥ kākuḥ, sa kathamalaṅkārī syāt?" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
sā ca dvidhā sākāṅkṣā nirākāṅkṣā ca /
vākyāntarākāṅkṣiṇī sākāṅkṣā, vākyottarabhāvinī nirākāṅkṣā /
tadeva vākyaṃ kākuviśeṣeṇa sākāṅkṣam /
tadeva kākumantareṇanirākāṅkṣam /
ākṣepagarbhā, praśnagarbhā, vitarkagarbhā ceti sākāṅkṣā /
vidhirupā, uttararupā, nirṇayarupeti nirākāṅkṣā /

children.translated_text: Among these, containing objection:
"If his beloved is [my] messenger, then I too am [his] beloved;

children.text: yadi tasyāḥ priyā vācaḥ tanmamāpi priyapriyāḥ" //
children.translated_text: If her words are dear [to him], then [his] dear ones are also dear to me."

body.translated_text: "<s>Kāku</s> is the property of recitation that conveys intention — how can it be a figure of speech?" — thus says the <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. And it is twofold: <s>sākāṅkṣā</s> (expectant) and <s>nirākāṅkṣā</s> (non-expectant). That which desires another sentence is <s>sākāṅkṣā</s>; that which is complete in the subsequent sentence is <s>nirākāṅkṣā</s>. The same sentence, with a particular <s>kāku</s>, is expectant; the same sentence, without <s>kāku</s>, is non-expectant. [<s>Sākāṅkṣā</s> is of three kinds:] containing objection, containing question, and containing speculation. [<s>Nirākāṅkṣā</s> is of three kinds:] in the form of a command, in the form of a reply, and in the form of a conclusion.

body.text: evameva nirdeṣṭurvidhirupā /

children.translated_text: Containing question:
"Gone is that time when pearls were born on creepers;
Now the causes of those [pearls] are oyster-shells."

body.translated_text: When directed as instruction, the same [becomes] the command form.

body.text: iyamevopadeṣṭiruttararupā /

children.translated_text: Containing speculation:

children.text: "navajaladharaḥ sannaddho 'yaṃ na dṛtpaniśācaraḥ sukadhanuridaṃ dūrākṛṣṭaṃ na nāma śarāsanam /
children.translated_text: "This [must be] a new rain-cloud armed [for battle], not a dreadful night-wanderer (demon); this [must be] a rainbow drawn from afar, not indeed a bow;

children.text: ayamapi paṭurdhārāsāro na bāṇaparamparā kanakanikaṣasnigdhā vidyutpriyā na mamorvaśī" //
children.translated_text: This torrential shower [must be] a dense downpour, not a volley of arrows; this lightning, smooth as a golden touchstone, [must be my] beloved — not <s>Urvaśī</s>."

body.translated_text: This same [verse], when directed as instruction, is the reply form.

body.text:
iyamevopadeṣṭurnirṇayarupā /
tā imāstisro 'pi niyatanibandhāḥ /
tadviparītāḥ punaranantāḥ /

children.translated_text: Among those, the <s>kāku</s> of concession and entreaty:

children.text: "yuṣmacchāsanalaṅghanāmbhasi mayā magnena nāma sthitaṃ prātpā nāma vigarhaṇā sthitimatāṃ madhye 'nujāmāmapi /
children.translated_text: "By me who was submerged in the waters of transgressing your command, there was indeed reproach gained among the steadfast — [reproach even of] my younger brother.

children.text: krodhollāsitaśoṇitāruṇagadasyocchindataḥ kauravā-nadyaikaṃ divasaṃ mamāsi na gururnāhaṃ vidheyastava" //
children.translated_text: Yet, O destroyer of the <s>Kaurava</s> army, with your mace reddened by blood ignited in wrath — for one day you are not my elder, nor am I your subordinate."

body.translated_text: This same, when directed as instruction, is the conclusion form. These three [pairs] have fixed compositions. Their opposites, however, are endless.

children.translated_text: The <s>kāku</s> of permission and mockery:

children.text: "mathnāmi kauravaśataṃ samare na kopād duḥśāsanasya rudhiraṃ na pubāmyurastaḥ /
children.translated_text: "I shall not churn the hundred <s>Kauravas</s> in battle out of anger; I shall not drink the blood from <s>Duḥśāsana</s>'s chest;

children.text: sañcūrṇayāmi gadayā na suyodhanoru sandhiṃ karotu bhavatāṃ nṛpatiḥ paṇena" //
children.translated_text: I shall not crush <s>Suyodhana</s>'s thigh with my mace — let your king make peace by a wager!"

body.text: evaṃ tricaturakākuyogo 'pi /

children.translated_text: Among those, a triple combination:

children.text: "seyaṃ paśyati no kuraṅgakavadhūstrastaivamaradvīkṣate tasyāḥ pāṇirayaṃ na mārutavalatpatrāṅguliḥ pallavaḥ /
children.translated_text: "That deer-wife sees us — no, she gazes with such startled eyes; this is not [her] hand — [it is] a leaf-fingered sprout trembling in the wind;

children.text: tāraṃ roditi saiva naiṣa marutā veṇuḥ samāpūryate seyaṃ māmabhibhāṣate priyatamā no kokilaḥ kūjati" //
children.translated_text: She herself cries aloud — no, this is a bamboo flute being filled by the wind; she, my beloved, speaks to me — no, a cuckoo coos."

body.translated_text: Thus there can be a combination of three or four <s>kākus</s> as well.

children.translated_text: A quadruple combination:

children.text: "ucyatāṃ sa vacanīyamaśeṣaṃ neśvare paruṣatā sakhi sārdhvī /
children.translated_text: "Tell him everything that should be said — harshness toward a lord is not proper, friend;
Bring him back conciliated — but how can one who causes displeasure be conciliated?"
"In the speech of a female friend, or of a heroine, or of both friend and heroine,

children.text: sakhīnāṃ bhūyasīnāṃ vā vākye kākuriha sthitā" //
children.translated_text: Or of several female friends — <s>kāku</s> is established here."
Of those versed in word and sentence,
The path that is otherwise established —
<s>Kāku</s>, made manifest through bodily gesture, renders it otherwise.

children.text: ayaṃ kākukṛto loke vyavahāro na kevalam /
children.translated_text: This usage created by <s>kāku</s> is not [found] in the world alone;
It has sovereignty even in the sciences, and it is the very life of poetry.
<s>Kāku</s> zealously reveals an alternative meaning;
But it also makes clear the skill of emotional acting among the wise.
Thus should a poet compose, and thus should a learned person recite,
So that some shadow of the compositional chain is poured forth.

children.text: karoti kāvyaṃ prāyeṇa saṃskṛtātmā yathā tathā /
children.translated_text: A poet whose soul is refined composes poetry in whatever manner;

children.text: paṭhituṃ vetti sa paraṃ yasya siddhā sarasvatī //
children.translated_text: But only he whose eloquence is perfected knows how to recite it supremely.
Just as through practice in previous births, there is redness (beauty) in someone's throat,
So too the beauty of recitation is fashioned over many births.
One should recite Sanskrit and <s>Apabhraṃśa</s> (vernacular) embraced with grace,
And should utter <s>Prākṛta</s> and <s>Bhūtabhāṣā</s> (spirit-language) with excellent deportment.
In a calm [passage], one should lower the voice to a deep register, and raise it high in its opposite;
And in a sustained [passage], one should employ both deep and high registers in succession.
Graceful, accompanied by tonal modulation, brilliant, with divisions determined by meaning,
With pleasant sounds and distinct syllables — [such] recitation the poets praise.
Too hasty, too slow, with excessive sound, or lacking in sound,
With broken words, without repetition, and too soft or harsh — these they censure.
Depth, confidence, mastery of high and low registers,
And charm in combined syllables — these are remembered as the qualities of recitation.

children.text: yathā vyaghrī haretputrān daṃṣṭrābhiśca na pīḍayet /
children.translated_text: Just as a tigress carries her cubs with her fangs without hurting them,
Fearful of both dropping and crushing — so should one employ the syllables.
Where inflections are clear, where compounds are not distorted,
And where word-junctions are unfaded — there recitation is established.

children.text: na vyastapadayoraikyaṃ na bhidāṃ tu samastayoḥ /
children.translated_text: One should not unite separated words, nor divide compound ones,
Nor should a wise person reciting cause the fading of verb-words.
From cowherds to women — to that extent may this be enjoyed.
Thus a poet who recites poetry [in this manner] is exceedingly dear to <s>Vāgdevī</s> (the goddess of speech).
Those who are neither knowers of words nor skilled in meanings —
Even among those good poets, their recitation is truly a delight to the ears.

children.text: paṭhanti saṃskṛtaṃ suṣṭhu kuṇṭhāḥ prākṛtavāci tu /
children.translated_text: The <s>Kuṇṭhas</s> recite Sanskrit well, but in Prakrit speech,
those east of <s>Vārāṇasī</s>, the <s>Magadhas</s> and others, are poor."
He said:
"O Brahman, I petition you with the desire to relinquish my own domain.
Let the <s>Gauḍa</s> poet abandon his <s>gāthā</s> (verse), or let <s>Sarasvatī</s> be another altogether.

children.text: nātispaṣṭo na cāśliṣṭo na rukṣo nātikomalaḥ /
children.translated_text: Neither too distinct nor too slurred, neither harsh nor too soft,

children.text: na madro nātitāraśca pāṭhī gauḍeṣu vāḍavaḥ //
children.translated_text: neither slow nor too high-pitched — such is the <s>Vāḍava</s> style of recitation among the <s>Gauḍas</s>.

children.text: rasaḥ ko 'pyastu kāpyastu rītiḥ ko 'pyastu vā guṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: Whatever the <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment), whatever the <s>rīti</s> (style), whatever the <s>guṇa</s> (quality),
all the <s>Karṇāṭa</s> poets recite proudly with a vigorous, emphatic delivery.

children.text: gadye padye 'thavā miśre kāvye kāvyamanā api /
children.translated_text: Whether in prose, verse, or mixed <s>kāvya</s> (poetry), even those with poetic sensibility,

children.text: geyagarbhe sthitaḥ pāṭhe sarvo 'pi draviḍaḥ kaviḥ //
children.translated_text: every <s>Draviḍa</s> poet remains fixed in a recitation style embedded with song.
The <s>Lāṭas</s>, hostile to Sanskrit, recite in a <s>Lāṭa</s>-like manner of Prakrit,
with a tongue that has obtained the seal of beauty through graceful prattle.
Those of <s>Surāṣṭra</s>, <s>Travaṇa</s>, and other regions recite with offered elegance,
yet even their Sanskrit utterances are mere morsels of <s>Apabhraṃśa</s> (corrupt dialect).
By the grace of <s>Śāradā</s>, the <s>Kāśmīra</s> people are good poets;
their recitation is like a mouthful of <s>guḍūcī</s> (Tinospora) to the ear — what more need be said?
Then those poets who dwell further north on the <s>Uttarāpatha</s> (Northern Road),
even with great refinement, recite with a nasal quality.
Following the proper path of sound, a treasury of qualities, with fully formed syllables, divided by proper caesuras,

children.text: pāñcālamaṇlabhruvāṃ subhagaḥ kavīnāṃ śrotre madhu kṣarati kiñcana kāvyapāṭhaḥ //
children.translated_text: the poetry recitation of the <s>Pāñcāla</s> poets, charming to the arched-browed ladies, drips a certain honey into the ears.
With a tongue that rolls the letter 'la' and a speech in which the letter 'ra' is worn and distorted,

children.text: girā bhujaṅgāḥ pūjyante kāvyabhāvyadhiyo na tu //
children.translated_text: the <s>Bhujaṅgas</s> (serpent-people) are honored, but not those devoted to the essence of poetry.
The proper production of sounds arising from the five places of articulation,

children.text: arthavaśena ca viratiḥ sarvasvamidaṃ hi pāṭhasya" //
children.translated_text: and pausing according to the sense — this is the entirety of recitation."
This establishment of recitation, together with tonal modulation (<s>kāku</s>), has been set forth. Now the types of instruction on meaning shall be enumerated.
Now the types of instruction on meaning shall be enumerated.

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe satpamo 'dhyāyaḥ vākyaviśeṣāḥ kākukalanā pāṭhapratiṣṭhā ca //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the seventh chapter on special sentences, tonal modulation, and the establishment of recitation, in the first section of the <s>Kavirahasya</s> in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.

body.text: aṣṭamo 'dhyāyaḥ 8
body.translated_text: Eighth Chapter — 8

body.text:
vākyārthayonayaḥ "śrutiḥ, smṛtiḥ, itihāsaḥ, purāṇaṃ, pramāṇavidyā, rājasiddhāntatrayī, loko, viracanā, prakīrṇakaṃ ca kāvyārthānāṃ dvādaśa yonayaḥ" iti ācāryāḥ /
"ucitasaṃyogena, yoktṛsaṃyogena, utpādyasaṃyogena, saṃyogavikāreṇa ca saha ṣoḍaśa" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
tatra śrautaḥ /
"urvaśī hāpsarāḥ pururavasamaiḍaṃ cakame" /

children.translated_text: On this theme:
"From the Moon was born the illustrious <s>Budha</s>; O king, he begat the first <s>Purūravas</s>, son of <s>Iḍā</s>;

children.text: taṃ cāpsarāḥ smaravatī cakame kimanyad atrorvaśī smitavaśīkṛtaśakracetāḥ" //
children.translated_text: and the <s>Apsaras</s>, filled with love, desired him — what else? Here <s>Urvaśī</s>, who had subdued <s>Śakra</s>'s mind with her smile."

body.translated_text: The sources of sentence-meaning: "<s>Śruti</s> (Vedic revelation), <s>Smṛti</s> (tradition), <s>Itihāsa</s> (epic), <s>Purāṇa</s> (ancient lore), <s>Pramāṇavidyā</s> (science of valid knowledge), the triad of royal doctrines (<s>Rājasiddhāntatrayī</s>), the world (<s>Loka</s>), poetic invention (<s>Viracanā</s>), and miscellaneous (<s>Prakīrṇaka</s>) — these are the twelve sources of poetic content," say the teachers. "Together with appropriate combination (<s>ucitasaṃyoga</s>), combination through the author (<s>yoktṛsaṃyoga</s>), combination through the created (<s>utpādyasaṃyoga</s>), and modification of combination (<s>saṃyogavikāra</s>), they become sixteen," says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. Among these, the Vedic source: "The <s>Apsaras</s> <s>Urvaśī</s> desired <s>Purūravas</s>, son of <s>Iḍā</s>."

body.text:
yathā vā-
"yadetanmaṇḍalaṃ tapati tanmahadukthaṃ tā ṛcaḥ sa ṛcāṃ loko 'tha yadetadarcirdīpyate tanmahāvrataṃ tāni sāmāni sa sāmnāṃ loto 'tha ya eṣa tasminmaṇḍale puruṣaḥ so 'gnistāni yajūṃṣāṃ lokaḥ saiṣā trayyeva vidyā tapati" /

children.translated_text: On this theme:

children.text: "etadyanmaṇḍalaṃ khe tapati dinakṛtastā ṛco 'rcīṃṣi yāni dyotante tāni sāmānyayamapi puruṣo maṇḍale 'ṇuryajūṃṣi /
children.translated_text: "This disc that shines in the sky belongs to the sun — those are the <s>Ṛcs</s>; the rays that blaze are the <s>Sāmans</s>; and this subtle person within the disc is the <s>Yajus</s> formulae.

children.text: evaṃ yaṃ veda vedatriyamayamayaṃ vedavedī samagro vargaḥ svargāpavargaprakṛtiravikṛtiḥ so 'stu sūryaḥ śriye vaḥ" //
children.translated_text: Thus one who knows this threefold <s>Veda</s> is a complete knower of the <s>Veda</s>; may that <s>Sūrya</s>, the source of heaven and liberation, unchanging, be for your prosperity."

body.translated_text: Or as follows: "That disc which shines — that is the <s>Mahad Uktha</s>; those are the <s>Ṛcs</s>; that is the world of the <s>Ṛcs</s>. Now that flame which blazes — that is the <s>Mahāvrata</s>; those are the <s>Sāmans</s>; that is the world of the <s>Sāmans</s>. Now the person who is in that disc — he is <s>Agni</s>; those are the <s>Yajus</s> formulae; that is the world of the <s>Yajus</s>. This threefold knowledge indeed shines."

children.translated_text: This indeed is the appropriation of Vedic material, as they relate it thus:
"Salutation

children.text: stu tasyai śrutaye yāṃ duhanti pade pade /
children.translated_text: be to that <s>Śruti</s> (revelation) which, at every step,
the sages, the authors of <s>śāstras</s> (treatises), and the poets milk according to their understanding."
The <s>Smṛti</s>-based source:
"When one is charged by an accuser who is well-versed in many matters, who denies everything,
the accused must give what is demanded, even if only a part has been established."
On this theme:
"O <s>Haṃsa</s> (swan), give me back my beloved — you have stolen her gait!
When a part of the claim is established, the accused must give what is demanded."
The <s>Itihāsa</s>-based sources:

children.text: "na sa saṅkucitaḥ panthā yena vālī hato gataḥ /
children.translated_text: "That path by which <s>Vālī</s> went to his death is not a narrow one.
Abide by the agreement, O <s>Sugrīva</s> — do not follow the path of <s>Vālī</s>."
On this:

children.text: "madaṃ navaiśvaryalavena lambhitaṃ visṛjya pūrvaṃ samayo vimṛśyatām /
children.translated_text: "Cast aside the arrogance gained from a mere morsel of new sovereignty, and first reflect upon the agreement.
Death, whose throat itches with eagerness to devour the world, is not <s>Vālī</s> alone, nor does the Destroyer rest content after striking once."
The <s>Purāṇa</s>-based sources:
"The <s>Daitya</s> <s>Hiraṇyakaśipu</s>, whichever direction he glanced toward with a smile,

children.text: bhayabhrāntaiḥ suraiścakre tasyai tasyai diśe namaḥ" //
children.translated_text: to that very direction the gods, trembling with fear, paid obeisance."
On this:
"He who wandered through the three worlds, whom <s>Śrī</s> (Fortune) herself had spontaneously chosen as her abode,
to that direction the gods paid obeisance at the three junctions of the day, with hands from which their crown-jewels slipped."
On this they say:
"Thorough study of the <s>Śrutis</s> with their limbs and branches, of the <s>Itihāsa</s> and <s>Purāṇa</s>,
the reading of treatises on meaning and of narratives — this is the one remedy for poetic skill.
Through <s>Itihāsa</s> and <s>Purāṇa</s>, like two eyes
purified by the collyrium of discernment, a good poet perceives even the subtlest meaning.
Just as poets are praised for composing works based on the meaning of the <s>Vedas</s>,
so too for works based on the <s>Smṛtis</s>, the <s>Itihāsa</s>, and the <s>Purāṇa</s>."

body.text:
dvividhaḥ prāmāṇiko maimāṃsikastārkikaśca /
tatra prathamaḥ śabdasya sāmānyamabhidheyaṃ viśeṣaścārthaḥ /

children.translated_text: On this:
"Even a word denoting a general class, when uttered in reference to me, becomes fixed on a particular object of denotation;

children.text: strī kācidityabhihite satataṃ mano me tāmeva vāmanayanāṃ viṣayīkaroti" //
children.translated_text: when someone says 'a certain woman,' my mind invariably turns to that same lovely-eyed one."

body.translated_text: The <s>Pramāṇika</s> (logician) source is of two kinds: the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> (ritualist-exegete) and the <s>Tārkika</s> (dialectician). Of these, the first holds that a word's general meaning and its particular meaning are both signified.

children.translated_text: Among the dialecticians, the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> view:
"The unreal never comes into being, nor does the real ever cease to exist;
the boundary between these two has been perceived by the seers of truth."
On this:

children.text: "ya ete yajvānaḥ prathitamahaso ye 'pyavanipā mṛgākṣyo yāśvetāḥ kṛtamaparasaṃsārakathayā /
children.translated_text: "Those sacrificers of renowned glory, those kings of the earth, those doe-eyed fair women — enough of talk about further transmigration!

children.text: amī ye dṛśyante phalakusumanamrāśca taravo jagatyevaṃrupā vilasati mṛdeṣā bhagavatī" //
children.translated_text: These trees that are seen bending with fruit and flowers — the world manifests thus; this blessed <s>Earth</s> is but clay."

body.text:
nyāyavaiśeṣikīyaḥ-sa kiṃsāmagrīka īśvaraḥ karttā? iti pūrvapakṣaḥ /
niratiśayaiśvaryasya tasya kartṛtvamiti siddhāntaḥ /

children.translated_text: On this:

children.text: "kimīhaḥ kiṅkāyaḥ sa khalu kimupāyastribhuvanaṃ kimādhāro dhātā sṛjati kimupādāna iti ca /
children.translated_text: "What is his desire? What is his purpose? What indeed is his means for creating the three worlds? What is his support? From what material does the Creator create?

children.text: atarkyaiśvarye tvayyanavasaraduḥstho hṛtadhiyaḥ kutarko 'yaṃ kāṃśvanmukharayati mohāya jagataḥ" //
children.translated_text: In you, whose sovereignty is beyond reasoning, this futile speculation, finding no foothold, bewilders the minds of those whose understanding has been stolen — whom does it make prattle, for the delusion of the world?"

body.translated_text: The <s>Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika</s> view: "Is <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) the creator who requires material accessories?" — this is the prior objection (<s>pūrvapakṣa</s>). "His creatorship follows from his unsurpassed sovereignty" — this is the established conclusion (<s>siddhānta</s>).

body.text:
boddhīyaḥ-
vivakṣāpūrvā hi śabdāstāmeva vivakṣāṃ sūcayeyuḥ /

children.translated_text: On this:

children.text: "bhavatu viditaṃ śabdā vakturvivakṣitasūcakāḥ smaravati yataḥ kānte kāntāṃ balātparicumbati /
children.translated_text: "Granted, it is known that words indicate the speaker's intention; for when a lover, remembering his beloved, forcibly kisses her,

children.text: na na na ma ma mā mā māṃ sprākṣīrniṣedhaparaṃ vaco bhavati śithile mānagranthau tadeva vidhāyakam" //
children.translated_text: the words 'No, no, no! Stop, stop! Don't, don't touch me!' — speech meant as prohibition — when the knot of pride loosens, that very speech becomes an invitation."

body.translated_text: The Buddhist view: Words are preceded by the intention to speak (<s>vivakṣā</s>), and they indicate precisely that intention.

body.text:
laukāyatikaḥ -
bhūtebhyaśvaitanyaṃ madaśaktivat /

children.translated_text: On this:
"The various witness-philosophers proclaim that the soul is something other than the body;

children.text: api ca sudati te sacintakāḥ pralayaṃ yānti sahaiva cintayā" //
children.translated_text: but, O beautiful-toothed one, those who hold such views perish along with their very speculation."

body.translated_text: The <s>Lokāyatika</s> (materialist) view: Consciousness arises from the elements, like the power of intoxication from ingredients.

body.text:
ārhataḥ -
śarīraparimāṇa ātmā, anyathā śarīrāphalyamātmāphalyaṃ vā /

children.translated_text: On this:
"Those who declare the soul to be co-extensive with the body are victorious;
for even at the mere touch of her body, a horripilation of all my limbs has arisen."

body.translated_text: The <s>Jaina</s> (<s>Ārhata</s>) view: The soul is of the same extent as the body; otherwise, the body would be purposeless or the soul would be purposeless.

body.text: sarvapārṣadatvātkāvyavidyāyāḥ tānimānanyāṃścārthānvyutyattaye pratyavekṣeta /

children.translated_text: And they say:
"Those ideas which, harsh in dialectics, the poet cherishes in his <s>sūktis</s> (fine sayings),
like the rays of the sun reflected in the moon, they attain a certain loveliness."

body.translated_text: Since the science of poetry belongs to all schools, one should examine these and other ideas in order to deploy them.

children.translated_text: Among the doctrinal sciences, the <s>Śaiva Siddhānta</s> view:
"Transcending the <s>Ghora</s> (terrible), the <s>Ghoratara</s> (more terrible), <s>Brahmavidyā</s> (knowledge of Brahman), and <s>Kalā</s> (parts),
pervading both the higher and the lower states — may <s>Parameśvara</s> (the Supreme Lord) protect us."
The <s>Pañcarātra</s> view:
"Without beginning or end, the ancient sages, subtle yet vast, the sovereign teachers —
may <s>Aniruddha</s>, <s>Pradyumna</s>, <s>Saṅkarṣaṇa</s>, and <s>Vāsudeva</s> destroy all my fevers."
The Buddhist doctrinal view:

children.text: "kalikṛtakaluṣāṇi yāni loke mayi nipatantu vimucyatāṃ sa lokaḥ /
children.translated_text: "May whatever afflictions brought about by the <s>Kali</s> age in this world fall upon me; may that world be liberated.

children.text: mama hi sucaritena sarvasattvāḥ paramasukhena sukhāvanīṃ prayāntu" //
children.translated_text: Through my merit, may all beings proceed to the land of happiness with supreme bliss."

body.text: evaṃ siddhāntantāntareṣvapi /

children.translated_text: In the triad of royal doctrines, the <s>Arthaśāstra</s> (political science) source:

children.text: "śamavyāyāmābhyāṃ prativihitatantrasya nṛpateḥ paraṃ pratyuccairnama kuñcayāgracaraṇaṃ māṃ paśya tāvatsthitam /
children.translated_text: "For a king whose strategy is countered by conciliation and exertion, the enemy says: 'Bow deeply before me and bend your leading foot — just look at me standing thus!'

children.text: bahuvyājaṃ rājyaṃ na sukaramarājapraṇidhibhir durārādhā lakṣmīranavahidacittaṃ chalayati" //
children.translated_text: Kingship is full of pretexts; it is not easy for those without royal spies; <s>Lakṣmī</s> (Fortune), hard to propitiate, deceives the inattentive mind."

body.translated_text: Similarly in other doctrinal systems as well.

children.translated_text: The <s>Nāṭyaśāstra</s> (dramaturgy) source:

children.text: "evaṃ dhāraya devi bāhulatikāmevaṃ kuruṣvāṅgakaṃ mātyuccairnama kuñcayāgracaraṇaṃ māṃ paśya tāvatsthitam /
children.translated_text: "Thus hold this arm-creeper, O Queen; thus arrange your limbs; do not bow too deeply; bend your leading foot; just look at me standing thus.

children.text: devīṃ narttayataḥ svavakramurajenābhbhodharadhvāninā śabhbhorvaḥ paripāntu lambitalayacchedāhṛtāstālikāḥ" //
children.translated_text: As <s>Śambhu</s> (Śiva), with his own mouth's thunderous voice, teaches the Queen to dance, may his claps, drawn out with suspended rhythm, protect you."
The <s>Kāmasūtra</s> (erotics) source:
"It is no wonder that <s>Lakṣmī</s>, having cast her glance downward, came to you;
she was slow in love-play, but you were equally matched with her in passion."

body.text: laukikastu dvidhā prākṛto vyutpannaśca /

children.translated_text: Of these, the first:

children.text: "sphuṭitapiṭharībandhaślādhyo vipakṣagṛhepyabhūt priyatama yayoḥ snehagranthistathā prathamaṃ sa nau /
children.translated_text: "O dearest, the bond of affection between us two was once so praiseworthy that even in the enemy's house a cracked pot would be mended; such was our knot of love at first.

children.text: janavadadhunā sadmanyāvāṃ vasāva ihaiva tau dhigaparicite prema strīṇāṃ cirāya ca jīvitam" //
children.translated_text: Now people say, 'Let the two of you live here in this very house.' Fie upon the unfamiliar love of women, and upon a long life!"

body.translated_text: The worldly source is twofold: the common (<s>prākṛta</s>) and the learned (<s>vyutpanna</s>).

children.translated_text: Or as follows:
"Of sugarcane juice, of treacle, of curd, of pastry,

children.text: vārāhasya ca māṃsasya śeṣo gacchati phālgune" //
children.translated_text: and of boar's flesh — the remainder is consumed in the month of <s>Phālguna</s>."

body.text:
dvitīyo dvidhā samastajanajanyaḥ katipayajanajanyaśca /
tayoḥ prathamo 'nekadhā deśānāṃ bahutvāt /

children.translated_text: Among these, the southern (<s>Dākṣiṇātya</s>) source:
"Drinking and savoring pepper, with mouths made fresh by betel,
the <s>Draviḍa</s> women sip honeys that are mere morsels of a beloved's lip."

body.translated_text: The second is twofold: arising from all people collectively, and arising from particular people. Of these, the first is manifold due to the multiplicity of regions.

children.translated_text: Or as follows:

children.text: "virama madana kastvaṃ caitragha kā śakti rindor iha hi kusumabāṇāḥ kuṇṭhitāgrāḥ skhalanti /
children.translated_text: "Cease, O <s>Madana</s> (Love)! Who are you, O spring? What power has the moon here? For here the flower-arrows fall blunted at their tips.
These heart-brows of the <s>Kuntala</s> women's beloveds are hard as diamond, with knots toughened by striking."
The northern (<s>Udīcya</s>) source:
"The <s>Nepālī</s> women, adorned with moist <s>aiṇa</s>-musk, together with their lovers,
spend the summer nights on beds of <s>granthiparṇa</s> (patchouli) leaves."
The second (arising from particular people):
"As the doe-eyed woman's eye, with its falsely half-closed trembling lashes, turns upward, restless like a wave in the long river of her sidelong glance,

children.text: patyuḥ kelimataḥ kathāṃ viramayannanyonyapaṇkūyanāt ko 'yaṃ vyāharatītyudīrya niragātsavyājamālījanaḥ" //
children.translated_text: the maidservant, interrupting the tale of her husband's amorous exploits with mutual whispering, said 'Who is speaking?' and departed with a pretext — the clever attendant."

body.text: kavimanīṣānirmitaṃ kathātantramarthamātraṃ vā viracanā /

children.translated_text: Of these, the first (narrative framework):
"There is a lord of swordsmen named <s>Citraśikha</s>,
on the southern slope of <s>Malaya</s>, the master of the city <s>Ratnavatī</s>.

body.translated_text: <s>Viracanā</s> (poetic invention) is a narrative framework or a mere subject matter fashioned by the poet's intellect.

children.translated_text: His wife, <s>Citrasundarī</s>, daughter of the Ocean (mine of jewels), a sister of the goddess <s>Śrī</s>,
held a <s>svayaṃvara</s> (self-choice ceremony) as his consort."
The second (mere subject matter):

children.text: "jyostnāṃ limpati candanena sa pumānsiñcatyasau mālatīmālāṃ gandhajalairmadhīni kurute svādūnyasau phāṇitaiḥ /
children.translated_text: "That man smears moonlight with sandal paste; this one sprinkles the jasmine garland with fragrant water; this one makes sweets more delicious with molasses.

children.text: yastasya prathitānguṇanprathayati śrīvīracūḍāmaṇeḥ tāratvaṃ sa ca śāṇayā mṛgayate muktāphalānāmapi" //
children.translated_text: He who proclaims the renowned qualities of the glorious <s>Vīracūḍāmaṇi</s> — even he tests the genuineness of pearls with a touchstone."
On this they say:
"He whose creative imagination does not diminish in the canto of fictional narrative,
he is the chief among poets; the rest are merely his dependents."

body.text: abhihitebhyo yadanyattatprakīrṇakam /

children.translated_text: Among these, the source from <s>Hastiśikṣā</s> (the science of elephant training):
'The spray of clouds, having assumed the form of a momentary laugh, has become a scattered necklace across the directions, a slap upon the full breasts of celestial women gleaming in the sky,

children.text: kṣuṇṇaścandra ivolbaṇo madavaśādairāvaṇapreritaḥ pāyādūḥ paripākapāṇḍulavalīśrītaskaraḥ śīkaraḥ" //
children.translated_text: trampled like the fierce moon, impelled by intoxication from <s>Airāvaṇa</s>, may that spray — the thief of the beauty of ripened-pale creepers — protect you!'

body.translated_text: Whatever is other than what has been described — that is <s>Prakīrṇaka</s> (miscellaneous).

children.translated_text: From the science of gem-examination (<s>Ratnaparīkṣā</s>) —

children.text: "dvau vajravarṇau jagatīpatīnāṃ sadbhiḥ pradiṣṭau na tu sārvajanyau /
children.translated_text: 'Two colors of diamonds have been declared by the wise for kings, but they are not common to all:
one that is red like a broken <s>japā</s> flower or coral, and another that resembles the hue of turmeric extract.'
From the science of archery (<s>Dhanurveda</s>) —
'He saw, with fist placed at the right corner of the eye, shoulder bent, left foot drawn up,
having made the beautiful bow into a circle, his own progenitor raised up to strike.'
From the science of <s>Yoga</s> (<s>Yogaśāstra</s>) —

children.text: "yaḥ sarveṣāṃ hṛdayakamale prāṇināmekahaṃsas tvaṃ jāgarṣi svapiṣi ca muhurbudhyase nāpi buddhaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'You who are the one <s>Haṃsa</s> (swan-soul) in the heart-lotus of all living beings — you who wake and sleep repeatedly and are awakened yet not truly awakened —

children.text: taṃ tvārādhya pravitatadhiyo bandhabhedaṃ vidhāya dhvastātaṅkā vimalamahasaste bhavanto bhavanti" //
children.translated_text: having worshipped you, those of expanded intellect, having broken the bonds, free from distress, become that pure radiance and transcend <s>bhava</s> (worldly existence).'

body.text: evaṃ prakīrṇakāntaramapi /

children.translated_text: Appropriate conjunction (<s>ucitasaṃyoga</s>) —
'This <s>Pāṇḍya</s> king, with a long garland resting upon his shoulders, his body anointed with <s>haricandana</s> (yellow sandalwood),
shines like the king of mountains with its peaks reddened by the morning sun, as if pouring forth waterfalls.'

body.translated_text: Thus also for miscellaneous categories.

children.translated_text: Conjunction through the agent (<s>yoktṛsaṃyoga</s>) —

children.text: "kurvadbhiḥ suradantino madhulihāmasvādu dānodakaṃ tanvānairnamucidruho bhagavatāścakṣuḥ sahasravyathām /
children.translated_text: 'By those making the water of <s>dāna</s> (ichor) from the divine elephants unpleasant for the bees, inflicting a thousand-fold pain upon the eyes of the lord, the slayer of <s>Namuci</s>,

children.text: bhajjan svargataraṅgiṇījalabhare paṅkīkṛte pāṃsubhir yadyātrāvyasanaṃ nininda vimanāḥ svarlokanārījanaḥ" //
children.translated_text: when the waters of the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s> were muddied by dust — by that march-obsession the women of heaven, disheartened, reproached <s>Śakra</s> who even abandoned sleep due to the flapping of <s>Airāvaṇa</s>'s ears.'
Conjunction through the effect (<s>utpādyasaṃyoga</s>) —
'If both the waters of the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s> were to fall in separate streams through the sky,
then his chest, dark as a <s>tamāla</s> tree with released strings of pearls, could be compared to that.'
Transformation through conjunction (<s>saṃyogavikāra</s>) —
'Through your fame that spreads, mixed with the attraction of virtues,
a half-mark of <s>kuṅkuma</s> (saffron) has suddenly appeared on the faces of the goddesses of the directions.'
Or for instance —

children.text: "unmādyatyamburāśirvidalati kumudaṃ saṅkucantyambujāni syandante candrakāntāḥ patitasumanasaḥ santi śephālikāśca /
children.translated_text: 'The ocean becomes intoxicated, the water-lily splits open, the lotuses contract, the moonstones flow, the <s>śephālikā</s> flowers have fallen and lie scattered,

children.text: pīyante candrikāmbhaḥ kramasaralagalaṃ kiṃ ca kiñciñcakorāś candre karpūragauvadyutibhṛti nabhaso yāti cūḍāmaṇitvam" //
children.translated_text: the moonlight-waters are drunk gradually through smooth throats — and what more — the <s>cakora</s> birds [drink them]; when the moon, bearing the luster of camphor, traverses the sky, it attains the state of a crest-jewel.'
This has been told to poets, devoted to the origin of meaning;
for one who is bold of mind here, there is never any mishandling of meaning.

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe (arthānuśāsane)ṣoḍaśa kāvyārthanayaḥ aṣṭamo 'dhyāyaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the eighth chapter, entitled 'The Sixteen Sources of Poetic Meaning' (<s>kāvyārthanaya</s>), in the first section on 'Instruction in Meaning' (<s>arthānuśāsana</s>) of the <s>Kavirahsya</s> (Secrets of the Poet) in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.
Chapter 9

body.text: navamo 'dhyāyaḥ 9
body.translated_text: Ninth chapter, section 9.

body.text:
arthānuśāsanam (arthavyātpiḥ) "sa tridhā" iti drauhiṇiḥ;divyo, divyamānuśaṣo, mānuṣaśca /
"satpadhā"iti yāyāvarīyaḥ pātālīyo,; marttyapātālīyo, divyapātālīyo, divyamarttyapātālīyaśca /

children.translated_text: Of these, the divine (<s>divya</s>) —

children.text: "smṛtvā yannijavāravāsagatayā vīṇāsamaṃ tumburor udgītaṃ nalakūvarasya virahādutkañculaṃ rambhayā /
children.translated_text: 'Remembering the song of <s>Tumburu</s> sung in harmony with the <s>vīṇā</s> by his own course of movement to the harem, and <s>Rambhā</s>'s restlessness born of <s>Nalakūvara</s>'s separation —

children.text: tenairāvaṇakarṇacāpalamuṣā śakro 'pi nidrā jahad bhūyaḥ kārita eva hāsini śacīvaktre dṛśaṃ sambhramam" //
children.translated_text: by that, even <s>Śakra</s>, abandoning sleep at the flapping of <s>Airāvaṇa</s>'s ear, was again made to cast a startled glance at the smiling face of <s>Śacī</s>.'

body.translated_text: Instruction in Meaning: The Classification of Meaning (<s>arthavyāpti</s>). 'It is threefold' — says <s>Drauhiṇi</s>: divine (<s>divya</s>), divine-human (<s>divyamānuṣa</s>), and human (<s>mānuṣa</s>). 'It is sixfold' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>: of the netherworld (<s>pātālīya</s>), human-netherworld (<s>martyapātālīya</s>), divine-netherworld (<s>divyapātālīya</s>), and divine-human-netherworld (<s>divyamartyapātālīya</s>) [in addition to the three].

body.text:
divyamānuṣasti caturddhā /
divyasya martyāgamane, martyasya ca svargagamana ityeko bhedaḥ /
divyasya martyabhāve, martyasya ca divyabhāva iti dvitīyaḥ /
divyetivṛttaparikalpanayā tṛtīyaḥ /
prabhāvāvirbhūtadivyarupatayā caturthaḥ /

children.translated_text: Of these, the descent of a divine being to the mortal world —
'The lord of <s>Śrī</s>, glorious, to rule the world, dwelling in the abode of <s>Vasudeva</s> which is the residence of the lord of the universe,
<s>Hari</s>, appearing like the season of spring, descended from the sky to [visit] the sage born from the body of <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s>.'

body.translated_text: The divine-human (<s>divyamānuṣa</s>) is fourfold: the descent of a divine being to the mortal world, and a mortal's ascent to heaven — this is the first division. A divine being assuming mortal form, and a mortal assuming divine form — this is the second. Through the imagining of divine history — the third. Through the manifestation of divine form by [supernatural] power — the fourth.

children.translated_text: A mortal's ascent to heaven —

children.text: "pāṇḍornandana nandanaṃ vanamidaṃ saṅkalpajaiḥ śīdhubhiḥ kḷtpāpānakakelikalpataruṣu dvandvaiḥ sudhālehinām /
children.translated_text: 'O son of <s>Pāṇḍu</s>, this is the <s>Nandana</s> grove — where with wish-fulfilling liquors at the wish-granting trees, with the pairs of nectar-tasting [celestial beings] engaged in merrymaking,

children.text: apyatrenduśilālavālavalayaṃ santānakānāṃ tale jyotsnāsaṃgaladacchanirjharajalairyatnaṃ vinā pūryate" //
children.translated_text: and where beneath the <s>Santānaka</s> trees, the basin-rings of moonstone are filled effortlessly by the waters of cascades flowing from dissolving moonlight.'
A divine being assuming mortal form (<s>divyasya martyabhāva</s>) —

children.text: "iti vikasati tasminnanvavāye yadūnāṃ samajani vasudevo devakī yatkalatram /
children.translated_text: 'Thus, in that expanding lineage of the <s>Yādavas</s>, <s>Vasudeva</s> was born, whose wife was <s>Devakī</s> —
what more need be said? — from him, <s>Padmanābha</s> came to be, having bestowed embraces upon sixteen thousand wives.'
A mortal assuming divine form (<s>martyasya divyabhāva</s>) —
'Standing with one foot placed on the edge of the platform of the aerial chariot, grasping with their hands the pairs of its shafts,

children.text: kautūhalāttava taraṅgavighaṭṭitāni paśyanti devi manujāḥ svakalevarāṇi" //
children.translated_text: out of curiosity, O goddess, the mortals behold their own bodies struck by the waves [below].'
The imagining of divine history (<s>divyetivṛttaparikalpanā</s>) —
'On this sandy bank of the <s>Sarayū</s>, bright with the flood of moonlight, a game of dice took place for a long time between two <s>Siddha</s> youths.

children.text: eko brūte prathamanihataṃ kaiṭabhaṃ kaṃsamanyaḥ sa tvaṃ tattvaṃ kathaya bhavatā ko hatastatra pūrvam" //
children.translated_text: One says: "<s>Kaiṭabha</s> was slain first." The other: "<s>Kaṃsa</s>." "You tell the truth — who was slain first by you there?"'
The manifestation of divine form through [supernatural] power (<s>prabhāvāvirbhūtadivyabhāva</s>) —

children.text: "mā gāḥ pātālamurvi sphurasi kimaparaṃ pāṭyamānaḥ kudaityata? trailokyaṃ pādapītaprathima, nahi bale? pūrasyūnamaṅghreḥ /
children.translated_text: '"Do not go to the netherworld, O Earth! Why do you tremble further? Are you being split open by the demon?" "The three worlds are crushed under the weight of [your] foot — have you no strength? [Your] foot is still incomplete!"

Thus, while the world-bearer was dreaming, may <s>Yaśodā</s>, her cheeks smiling and horripilating with joy at the prostration of the <s>cakra</s>-marked foot of the child resting on [her] lap, protect you!'
The human (<s>martya</s>) —

children.text: "vadhūḥ śvaśrūsthāne vyavaharati putraḥ pitṛpade pade rikte rikte vinihitapadārthāntaramiti /
children.translated_text: 'The bride acts in the place of the mother-in-law, the son in the place of the father — in each vacant place, a substitute is installed for the one who held it.',

children.text: nadīsrotonyāyādakalitavivekakramaghanaṃ na ca pratyāvṛttiḥ pravahati jagatpūrṇamatha ca" //
children.translated_text: 'Like the course of a river's current, with undiscerned sequence of discrimination, there is no return — the world flows on, filling everything.'
Of the netherworld (<s>pātālīya</s>) —

children.text: "karkoṭaḥ koṭikṛtvaḥ praṇamati puratastakṣake dehi cakṣuḥ sajjaḥ sevājjaliste kapilakulikayoḥ staiti ca svastikastvāṃ /
children.translated_text: '<s>Karkoṭaka</s> bows before you ten million times! O <s>Takṣaka</s>, grant your gaze! <s>Jallista</s>, ready in service! The <s>Svastika</s> of the <s>Kapila</s> family stands before you!

children.text: padmaḥ sadmaiṣa bhakteravalagati puraḥ kambalo 'yaṃ balo 'yaṃ sotsarpaḥ sarparājo vrajatu nijagṛhaṃ preṣyatāṃ śaṅkhapālaḥ" //
children.translated_text: <s>Padma</s>, this is his abode of devotion, he stands before you — this is <s>Kambala</s>, this is <s>Bala</s>, the serpent-king rises up — let him return to his own dwelling — let <s>Śaṅkhapāla</s> be dispatched!'
The human-netherworld (<s>martyapātālīya</s>) —

children.text: "ārdrāvale!vraja na vetsyapakarṇa!karṇaṃ dviḥ sandadhāti na śaraṃ haraśiṣyaśiṣyaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'O <s>Ārdrāvala</s>! Go — you shall not know, O <s>Apakarṇa</s>, ear to ear — the disciple of the disciple of <s>Hara</s> does not place an arrow a second time on the string.',

children.text: tatsāmprataṃ samiti paśya kutūhalena martyaiḥ śarairapi kirīṭikirīṭamātham" //
children.translated_text: 'So now, behold in battle with curiosity — even with mortal arrows, [he strikes] the crown of the crowned one (<s>Kirīṭin</s>, i.e., <s>Arjuna</s>)!'

body.text: ihāpi pūrvavastamastamiśrabhedānugamaḥ /

children.translated_text: The divine-netherworld (<s>divyapātālīya</s>) —

children.text: "sa pātu vo yasya śikhāśmakarṇikaṃ svadehanālaṃ phaṇapatrasañcayam /
children.translated_text: 'May he protect you — he whose ear-serpent of <s>Pinākin</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) appears as a lotus:
the gem on the hood as the pericarp, his own body as the stalk, the spread of hoods as the petals, and the forked tongue as the filament.'

body.translated_text: Here too, the same mixed divisions as before apply.

children.translated_text: The divine-human-netherworld (<s>svargamartyapātālīya</s>) —

children.text: "āstīko 'sti muniḥ sma vismayakṛtaḥ pārīkṣitīyānmakhāt trātā takṣakalakṣmaṇaḥ phaṇabhṛtāṃ vaṃśasya śakrasya ca /
children.translated_text: 'There was the wondrous sage <s>Āstīka</s>, who from the sacrifice of <s>Parīkṣit</s>, saved <s>Takṣaka</s>, the ornament of the serpent race, and also [the honor of] <s>Śakra</s>'s lineage.
Even today, when the breeze sways the sandal-creepers of <s>Malaya</s> mountain, his fame is sung with graceful movements by the hosts of serpent-maidens.'

body.text:
so 'yamitthaṅkāramullikhyopajīvyamāno niḥsīmorthasārthaḥ sampadyate ityācāryāḥ /
"astu nāma niḥsīmorthasārthaḥ /
kintu dvirupa evāsau vicāritasustho 'vicāritaramaṇīyaśca /
tayoḥ pūrvamāśritāni śāstrāṇi taduttaraṃ kāvyāni" ityaudbhaṭāḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —
'To leap across the expanse of waters, yellowing the sky with his radiance,
<s>Hanumān</s>, of the hue of a blue lotus petal, sprang into the sky.'

body.translated_text: Thus, this boundless wealth of meaning, when traced and drawn upon in this manner, comes to fruition — say the teachers. 'Granted it is a boundless wealth of meaning; however, it is of two kinds only: that which is pleasing upon examination (<s>vicāritasustha</s>) and that which is pleasing without examination (<s>avicāritaramaṇīya</s>). Of these, the former is the domain of the <s>śāstras</s> (sciences), and the latter of <s>kāvya</s> (poetry)' — say the followers of <s>Udbhaṭa</s>.

children.translated_text: Or for instance —
'Those great sages, [rising] into the dark-blue sky,
reached the plateau of herbs, with the speed of mind.'

body.text:
yathā ca-
"tadeva vāri sindhūnāṃ mahatsthemārciṣāmiti" ityādi //
body.translated_text: And also — 'That very water of the rivers, the great firmness of flames' — and so on.

body.text:
"na svarupanibandhanamidaṃ rupamākāśasya sarilsalilādervā kintu pratibhāsanibandanam /
na ca pratibhāsastādatbhyena vastunyavatiṣṭhate, yadi tathā syātsūryācandramasormaṇḍale dṛṣṭyā paricchidyamānadvādaśāṅgulapramāṇe purāṇādyāgamaniveditadharāvalayamātre na staḥ iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
evaṃ nakṣatrādīnāṃ saritsalilādīnāmanyeṣāṃ ca /
yathāpratibhāsaṃ ca vastunaḥ svarupaṃ śāstrakāvyayornibandhopayogi" /

children.translated_text: In <s>śāstra</s> (science), for example —
'In the clear sky-water, bearing tranquil waters and mud-free,
with the association of star-lotuses, the moon moves like a swan.'

body.translated_text: 'This form of the sky, or of a river's water, is not based on [its] intrinsic nature, but rather on appearance. And appearance does not rest in a thing by identity with it. For if it were so, the discs of the sun and moon — perceived by the eye as measuring only twelve finger-breadths — would not actually be merely the size of the earth's surface as reported by the <s>Purāṇas</s> and other scriptures' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. 'Similarly for stars and other [celestial bodies], rivers' waters, and other things. And the form of a thing as it appears is useful for composition in both <s>śāstra</s> (science) and <s>kāvya</s> (poetry).'

body.text:
kāvyāni punaretanmayānyeva /
"astu nāma niḥsīmārthasārthaḥ /
kuntu rasavata eva nibandho yukto na nīrasasya" iti āparājitiḥ /

children.translated_text: As he states —
'A verse concerning bathing, flowers, the <s>avajaya</s> ceremony, twilight, moonrise, and the like —
even if it is charming, one should not compose it excessively, nor without connection to the principal <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion).

body.translated_text: Poetic compositions are entirely pervaded by this [principle of appearance]. 'Granted it is a boundless wealth of meaning; however, only the composition that possesses <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) is fitting, not that which is devoid of <s>rasa</s>' — says <s>Aparājita</s>.

children.translated_text: The effort that goes into describing rivers, mountains, oceans, cities, horses, chariots, and the like —

children.text: kaviśaktikhyātiphalo vitatadhiyāṃ no mataḥ sa iha" //
children.translated_text: that effort, whose fruit is the poet's power and fame, is not approved here by those of expansive intellect.'

body.text:
"ām" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
asti cānubhūyamāno rasasyānuguṇo viguṇaścārthaḥ, kāvye tu kavivacanāni rasayanti virasayanti ca nārthāḥ, anvayavyatirekābhyāṃ cetamupalabhyate /

children.translated_text: The aesthetic richness in the description of a river (<s>saridvarṇanarasavattā</s>) —
'Behold, O slender-waisted one, this river <s>Tāmraparṇī</s> — whose waters, like pearls drawn from opened oyster-shells in the ocean's depths,

children.text: yasyāḥ payāṃsi pariṇāhiṣu hāramūrttyā vāmabhruvāṃ pariṇamanti payodhareṣu" //
children.translated_text: transform upon the breasts of beautiful women into the form of a necklace.'

body.translated_text: 'Indeed so' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. 'And there exists meaning that is experienced as favorable or unfavorable to <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion). In poetry, however, it is the poet's words that produce or destroy <s>rasa</s>, not the subject matter itself — this is understood through [the method of] co-occurrence and non-co-occurrence.'

children.translated_text: The aesthetic richness in the description of a mountain (<s>adrivarṇanarasavattā</s>) —
'These are the rivers near <s>Malaya</s> mountain, born from the banks of doe-eyed waters, the beloved abode of practice for the bow of the blessed <s>Manmatha</s> (god of love) —

children.text: yāsu śyāmaniśāsu pītatamaso muktāmayīścandrikāḥ pīyante vivṛtordhdacañcu vicalatkaṇṭhaṃ cakorāṅganāḥ" //
children.translated_text: where, on dark nights when darkness is dispelled, the <s>cakora</s> hens drink the pearl-like moonbeams with upturned beaks and trembling throats.'
The aesthetic richness in the description of the ocean (<s>sāgaravarṇanarasavattā</s>) —

children.text: "dhatte yatkilakiñcitaikagurutāmeṇīdṛśāṃ vāruṇī vaidhuryaṃ vidadhāti dampatiruṣāṃ yaccandrikārdraṃ nabhaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'That which bestows upon the doe-eyed women a singular gravity of coquetry through <s>Vāruṇī</s> (wine), which creates fickleness in lovers' quarrels through the moon-moist sky,

children.text: yacca svargasadāṃ vayaḥ smarasuhṛnnityaṃ sadā sampadāṃ yallakṣmīradhidaivataṃ ca jaladhestatkāntamāceṣṭitam" //
children.translated_text: which is the eternal friend of <s>Smara</s> (the god of love) and the perpetual youth of the heavenly beings, which is ever the wealth of prosperity and whose presiding deity is <s>Lakṣmī</s> — such is the lovely play of the ocean.'

body.text: evaṃ puraturagādivarṇanarasavattāpi /

children.translated_text: Even in the context of love-in-separation (<s>vipralambha</s>), there is great aesthetic richness —
'Emotions contrary [to love], not sustaining through conduct guided by that [love]; others, due to similarity of form, producing vain eagerness and [yet] being the finest —

children.text: tataḥ svecchaṃ pūrveṣvasajaditarebhyaḥ pratihataṃ kva hīnaṃ preyasyā hṛdayamidamanyatra ramatām" //
children.translated_text: therefore, repelled from those former [objects] to which it was not attached of its own accord, where can this diminished heart of the beloved find rest elsewhere?'

body.translated_text: Similarly, aesthetic richness in the description of cities, horses, and so forth is also [possible].

children.translated_text: A bad poet destroys the aesthetic richness even in love-in-separation.

children.text: astu vastuṣu mā vā bhūtkavivāci rasaḥ sthitaḥ //
children.translated_text: Whether or not it resides in the subject matter, <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) abides in the poet's speech.

children.text: "yathā tathā vāstu vastuno rupaṃ, vaktaprakṛtiviśeṣāyattā tu rasavattā /
children.translated_text: 'Whatever may be the form of a thing, the aesthetic richness depends on the particular nature of the speaker.

children.text: tathā ca yamarthaṃ raktaḥ stauti taṃ virakto vinindati madhyasthastu tatraghodāste" iti pālyakīrtiḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, one who is enamored praises that very meaning; one who is disenchanted censures it; and one who is indifferent remains silent about it' — says <s>Pālyakīrti</s>.

children.text: "yeṣāṃ vallabhayā samaṃ kṣaṇamiva sphārā kṣapā kṣīyate teṣāṃ śītataraḥ śaśī virahiṇāmulkeva santāpakṛt /
children.translated_text: 'For those who [spend time] with their beloved, the vast night passes as if in a moment; for them the moon is cool — but for the love-sick, it burns like a meteor.

children.text: asmākaṃ na tu vallabhā na virahastenobhayabhraṃśinām indū rājati darpaṇākṛtirayaṃ noṣṇo na vā śītalaḥ" //
children.translated_text: But for us — there is neither a beloved nor separation — thus, falling from both states, this moon shines like a mirror: neither hot nor cold.'

body.text: "vidagdhabhaṇitibhaṅginivedyaṃ vastuno rupaṃ na niyatasvabhāvam" iti avantisundarī /

children.translated_text: Therefore it is said —
'The nature of a thing in this domain is [determined] by the poet; in poetry, merit and demerit are subject to expression.
One who praises binds the moon as a nectar-rayed [luminary]; one who censures calls it the source of faults — says the clever one.'

body.translated_text: 'The form of a thing is to be conveyed through the artful turns of witty expression, and is not of a fixed nature' — says <s>Avantisundarī</s>.

body.text:
"ubhayamupapannam" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
sa punardvidhā /
muktakaprabandhatriṣayatvena /
tāvapi pratyekaṃ pañcadhā /
śuddhaḥ, citraḥ, kathotthaḥ, saṃvidhānakabhūḥ, ākhyānakavāṃśca /
tatra muktetivṛttaḥ śuddhaḥ /
sa eva saprapañcaścitraḥ /
vṛttetivṛttaḥ kathotthaḥ /
sambhāvitetivṛttaḥ saṃvidhānakabhūḥ /
parikalpitetivṛttaḥ ākhyānakavān /
tatra /

children.translated_text: In <s>muktaka</s> (standalone verse) — the pure [type]:

children.text: "sā patyuḥ prathamāparādhakaraṇe śikṣopadeśaṃ vinā no janāti savibhramāṅgavalanā vakrokticitrāṃ gatim /
children.translated_text: 'She, upon committing the first offense against her husband, without any instruction or teaching, does not know the artful way of crooked speech accompanied by charming bodily movements;

children.text: svacchairacchakapolamūlamūlagalitaiḥ paryastanetrotpalā bālā kevalameva roditi luṭhallolodakairaśrubhiḥ" //
children.translated_text: with tears flowing purely from the roots of her fair cheeks, her lotus-eyes overturned, the young girl merely weeps with rolling, trembling teardrops.'

body.translated_text: 'Both are established' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. It [<s>artha</s> (meaning)] is again twofold, by the division into <s>muktaka</s> (standalone verse) and <s>prabandha</s> (composition). Each of these is again fivefold: <s>śuddha</s> (pure), <s>citra</s> (variegated), <s>kathotthaḥ</s> (story-based), <s>saṃvidhānakabhūḥ</s> (plot-originated), and <s>ākhyānakavān</s> (narrative-possessing). Among these, one that is free from narrative is <s>śuddha</s> (pure). The same, when elaborated, is <s>citra</s> (variegated). One based on a [known] narrative is <s>kathotthaḥ</s> (story-based). One based on a supposed narrative is <s>saṃvidhānakabhūḥ</s> (plot-originated). One based on an imagined narrative is <s>ākhyānakavān</s> (narrative-possessing). Among these:

children.translated_text: The variegated [type]:

children.text: "dūrādutsakamāgate vivasitaṃ sambhāṣiṇi sphāritaṃ saṃśliṣyatyaruṇaṃ gṛhītavasane kopāñcitabhrūtalam /
children.translated_text: 'When the beloved approaches eagerly from afar, a smile; when he speaks, widened eyes; when he embraces, a blush; when he grasps her garment, brows arched in anger;

children.text: māninyāścaraṇānativyatikare bāṣpāmbupūrṇāṃ kṣaṇāc cakṣurjātamaho prapañcacaturaṃ jātāgasi preyasi" //
children.translated_text: when the beloved who has transgressed stumbles at the proud woman's feet — in an instant, the eye becomes filled with tears of joy — ah, how skilled it is in deception!'
The story-based [type]:

children.text: "dattvā rudbhagatiḥ khasādhipataye devīṃ dhruvasvāminīṃ yasmātkhaṇḍitasāhaso nivavṛte śrīśarmagutpo nṛpaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Having given Queen <s>Dhruvasvāminī</s> to the lord of the <s>Khasas</s>, the king <s>Śrīśarmagutpa</s>, whose valor was broken, retreated because of that;

children.text: tasminneva himālaye guruguhākoṇakvaṇatkinnare gīyante tava kārttikeyanagarastrīṇāṃ gaṇaiḥ kīrttayaḥ" //
children.translated_text: in that very <s>Himālaya</s>, where <s>Kinnaras</s> sing in the recesses of great caves, your glories are sung by the groups of women of <s>Kārttikeyapura</s>.'
The plot-originated [type]:

children.text: "dṛṣṭravaikāsanasaṃsthite priyatame paścādupetyādarād ekasyā nayane nimīlya vihitakrīḍānubandhacchalaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Having seen the beloved seated on a single seat, approaching from behind with affection, closing the eyes of one woman under the pretext of initiating a game,

children.text: īṣadvakritakandharaḥ sapulakaḥ premollasanmānasām antarhāsalasatkapolaphalakāṃ dhūrto 'parāṃ cumbati" //
children.translated_text: with neck slightly turned, with hair standing on end, the rogue kisses another woman whose mind is elated with love, whose cheek-surface glistens with a suppressed smile.'
And also:

children.text: "kuvartyā kuṅkumābhbhaḥ kapiśitavapuṣaṃ yattadā rājahaṃsīṃ krīḍāhaṃśo mayāsāvajāni virahitaścakravākībhrameṇa /
children.translated_text: 'By a wicked twist of fate, I, the royal gander, mistaking the ruddy-brown-bodied royal goose colored like saffron for a <s>Cakravākī</s>, became separated from her;

children.text: tasyaitatpāpmano me pariṇamati phalaṃ yatpure premabandhād ekatrāvāṃ vasāvo na ca dayita dṛśāpyasti nau sannikarṣaḥ" //
children.translated_text: this fruit of that sin of mine has ripened — that though in the same city, out of the bond of love, we two dwell together, yet, O beloved, we have no proximity even by sight.'
The narrative-possessing [type]:
'With the tusks first fashioned from wild elephants sustained by those seeking wealth,
the beneficent one born in the <s>Haihaya</s> lineage made the abode of <s>Śambhu</s>.'
In <s>nibandha</s> (composition) — the pure [type]:
'Of those gazes — quietly blossoming, with playfully rising eyebrow-creepers, gently half-closed, expanding at the corners,
slightly contracted at each fall of the glance — for a long time I became the object of such glances.'
The variegated [type]:
'With languid, turning, charming, tender, motionless, gentle sidelong glances, their pupils shining within with expanding wonder and a smile —

children.text: hṛdayamaśaraṇaṃ me pakṣmalākṣyāḥ kaṭākṣair apahṛtamapaviddhaṃ pītamunmīlitaṃ ca" //
children.translated_text: my defenseless heart was stolen, cast away, consumed, and laid bare by the glances of the woman with beautiful eyelashes.'
The story-based [type]:
'<s>Prajāpati</s>, with his senses inflamed by desire toward his own daughter,
then, having restrained that passion, was cursed — and this was its fruit.'
The plot-originated [type]:

children.text: "krodhaṃ prabho saṃhara saṃhareti yāvadbhiraḥ rave marutāṃ caranti /
children.translated_text: '"Withdraw your anger, O Lord, withdraw it!" — while the <s>Maruts</s> (storm gods) were thus crying out,
that fire born from the eye of <s>Bhava</s> (Śiva) reduced <s>Madana</s> (the god of love) to mere ashes.'
The narrative-possessing [type]:
'"Touch the crescent moon on your husband's head with this" — so said a friend in jest;

children.text: sā rajjayitvā caraṇau kṛtāśīrmālyena tāṃ nirvacanaṃ jaghāna" //
children.translated_text: she, having bowed at his feet and offered a blessing, struck her [friend] speechless with a garland.'

body.text:
kiñca-
saṃskṛtavatsarvāsvapi bhāṣāsu yathāsāmarthyaṃ yathāruci yathā-
kautukaṃ cāvahitaḥ syāt /
śabdārthayoścābhidhānābhidheyavyāpārapraguṇatāmavabudhyeta /

children.translated_text: Thus it has been said:

children.text: eko 'rthaḥ saṃskṛtoktyā sa sukaviracanaḥ prākṛtenāparo 'smin anyo 'pabhraṃśagīrbhiḥ kimaparamaparo bhūtabhāṣākrameṇa /
children.translated_text: 'One meaning is expressed in Sanskrit composition by a good poet; another in <s>Prākṛta</s>; yet another through <s>Apabhraṃśa</s> speech; and still another by the sequence of <s>Bhūtabhāṣā</s> (regional languages);

children.text: dvitrābhiḥ ko 'pi vāgbhirbhavati catasṛbhiḥ kiñca kaścidvivektuṃ yasyetthaṃ dhīḥ prapannā snapayati sukavestasya kīrttirjaganti //
children.translated_text: some poets express it in two or three languages, some in four — and whoever's intellect has attained the capacity to discriminate thus, that good poet's fame bathes the worlds.'

body.translated_text: Moreover — one should be attentive to all languages just as to Sanskrit, according to one's ability, taste, and curiosity; and one should understand the excellence of the relation between word and meaning, between the signifier and the signified.

children.translated_text: When the mind of a poet is thus cultivated through dense and rich [learning],
even on a difficult path, <s>Sarasvatī</s> (the goddess of speech) does not falter.

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe arthānuśāsane (arthavyātpiḥ) navamo 'dhyāyaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the ninth chapter, entitled '<s>Arthānuśāsana</s>' (Instruction on Meaning) — [specifically] <s>Arthavyutpatti</s> (Erudition in Meaning) — in the first section of the <s>Kavirahasya</s> (Secrets of the Poet) in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.
Chapter 10

body.text:
10 kavicaryā rājacaryā ca /
gṛhītavidyopavidyaḥ kāvyakriyāyai prayateta /
nāmadhātupārāyaṇe, abhidhānakośaḥ, chandovicitaḥ, alaṅkāratantraṃ ca kāvyavidyāḥ /
kalāstu catuḥṣaṣṭirupavidyāḥ /
sujanopajīvyakavisannidhaḥ, deśavārtā, vidagdhavādo, lokayātrā, vidvadgoṣṭhyaśca kāvyamātaraḥ purātanakavinibandhāśca /

children.translated_text: Moreover:
'Good health, practice of <s>pratibhā</s> (creative intuition), devotion, conversation with the learned, extensive learning,
firmness of memory, and perseverance — these are the eight mothers of poetic art.'

body.translated_text: 10. <s>Kavicaryā</s> (Conduct of Poets) and <s>Rājacaryā</s> (Conduct of Kings). Having acquired the principal and subsidiary sciences, one should exert oneself in the composition of poetry. The study of noun-roots and verb-roots, lexicons (<s>abhidhānakośa</s>), knowledge of meters (<s>chandoviciti</s>), and the science of figures of speech (<s>alaṅkāratantra</s>) — these are the sciences of poetry. The sixty-four arts are the subsidiary sciences. Proximity to a poet patronized by the virtuous, knowledge of regional affairs, witty discourse, experience of worldly affairs, and assemblies of the learned — these are the mothers of poetry, along with the compositions of ancient poets.

body.text:
api ca nityaṃ śuciḥ syāt /
tridhā ca śaucaṃ vākśaucaṃ, manaḥ-śaucaṃ, kāyaśaucaṃ ca /
prathame śāstrajanmanī /
tārtīyīkaṃ tu sanakhacchedau pādau, satāmbūlaṃ mukhaṃ, savilepanamātraṃ vapuḥ, mahārhamanulbaṇaṃ ca vāsaḥ, sukusumaṃ śira iti /
śuciśīlanaṃ hi sarasvatyāḥ saṃvananamāmananti /
sa yatsvabhāvaḥ kavistakadanurupaṃ kāvyam /
yadṛśākāraścitrakārastādṛśākāramasya citramiti prāyovādaḥ /
smitapūrvamabhibhāṣaṇaṃ, sarvatroktigarbhamabhidhānaṃ, sarvato rahasyānveṣaṇaṃ, parakāvyadṣaṇavaimukhyamanabhihitasya abhihitasya tu yathārthamabhidhānam /
tasya bhavanaṃ susaṃmṛṣṭaṃ, ṛtuṣaṭkocitavividhasthānam, anekatarumūlakalpitāpāśrayavṛkṣavāṭikaṃ, sakrīḍāparvatakaṃ, sadīrdhikāpuṣkariṇīkaṃ, sasaritsamudrāvarttakaṃ, sakulyāpravāhaṃ, savirhiṇahariṇahāritaṃ, sasārasacakravākrahaṃsaṃ, sacakorakrauñcakuraraśukasārikaṃ, dharmaklānticauraṃ, sabhū(ti)midhārāgṛhayantralatāmaṇḍapakaṃ,, sadolāpreṅkhaṃ ca syāt /
kāvyābhiniveśakhinnasya manasastadvinirvedacchedāya ājñābhūkaparijanaṃ vijanaṃ vā tasya sthānam /
apabhraṃśabhāṣaṇapravaṇaḥ paricārakavargaḥ, samāgadhabhāṣābhiniveśinyaḥ paricārikāḥ /
prākṛtasaṃskṛtabhāṣāvida āntaḥpurikā, mitrāṇi cāsya sarvabhāṣāvindi bhaveyuḥ /
sadaḥsaṃskāraviśuddhyarthaṃ sarvabhāṣākuśalaḥ, śīghravāk, cārvakṣaraḥ, iṅgitākāravedī, nānālipijñaḥ, kaviḥ, lākṣaṇikaśca lekhakaḥ syāt /
tadasannidhāvatirātrādiṣu pūrvoktanāmanyatamaḥ /
svabhavane hi bhāṣāniyamaṃ yathā prabhurvidadhāti tathā bhavati /
śrūyate hi magadheṣu śiśunāgo nāma rājā;tena duruñcārānaṣṭau varṇānapāsya svāntaḥpura eva pravarttato niyamaḥ, ṭakārādayaścatvāro mūrdhdanyāstṛtīyavarjamūṣmāṇastrayaḥ kṣakāraśceti /
śrūyate ca sūraseneṣu kuvindo nāma rājā; tena paruṣasaṃyogākṣaravarjamantaḥpura eveti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
śrūyate ca kuntaleṣu sātavāhano nāma rājā; tena prākṛtabhāṣātmakamantaḥpura eveti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
śrūyate cojjayinyāṃ sāhasāṅko nāma rājā; tena ca saṃskṛtabhāṣātmakamantaḥpura eveti samānaṃ pūrveṇa /
tasya sampuṭikā saphalakakhaṭikā, samudgakaḥ, salekhanīkamaṣībhājanāni tāḍipatrāṇi bhūrjatvaco vā, salohakaṇṭakāni tāladalāni susabhmṛṣṭā bhittayaḥ, satatasannihitāḥ syuḥ /
"taddhi kāvyavidyāyāḥ parikaraḥ"iti ācāryāḥ /
"pratibhaiva parikaraḥ" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
kaviḥ prathamamātmānameva kalpayet /
kiyānme saṃskāraḥ, kva bhāṣāviṣaye śakto 'smi, kiṃ rucirlokaḥ, parivṛḍho vā, kīdṛśi goṣṭhyāṃ vinītaḥ, kvāsya vā cetaḥ saṃsajata iti buddhvā bhāṣāviśeṣamāśrayeta"iti ācāryāḥ /
"ekadeśakaveriyaṃ niyamatantraṇā, svatantraghasya punarekabhāṣāvatsarvā api bhāṣāḥ syuḥ" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
deśaviśeṣavaśena ca bhāṣāśrayaṇaṃ dṛśyate /

children.translated_text: Thus it has been said:

children.text: "gauḍādyāḥ saṃskṛtasthāḥ paricitarucayaḥ prākṛte lāṭadeśyāḥ sāpabhraṃśaprayogāḥ sakalamarubhuvaṣṭakkabhādānakāśca /
children.translated_text: 'The <s>Gauḍas</s> and others are established in Sanskrit, with cultivated taste; the <s>Lāṭas</s> are native to <s>Prākṛta</s>; those employing <s>Apabhraṃśa</s> are the <s>Ṭakka</s>, <s>Bhā</s>, <s>Dānaka</s> peoples of the entire desert region;

children.text: āvantyāḥ pāriyātrāḥ saha daśapurajairbhūtabhāṣāṃ bhajante yo madhyemadhyadeśaṃ nivasati sa kaviḥ sarvabhāṣāniṣaṇṇaḥ //
children.translated_text: the <s>Āvantyas</s> and <s>Pāriyātras</s>, along with those from <s>Daśapura</s>, cultivate <s>Bhūtabhāṣā</s> (regional languages). He who dwells in the middle, in <s>Madhyadeśa</s>, that poet is proficient in all languages.'

body.translated_text: Furthermore, one should always be pure. Purity is threefold: purity of speech, purity of mind, and purity of body. The first two arise from learning. As for the third [bodily purity]: feet with trimmed nails, mouth with betel, body with just a touch of fragrance, garments costly but not ostentatious, flowers on the head — thus. For the cultivation of purity is regarded as the propitiation of <s>Sarasvatī</s>. A poet's poetry corresponds to his nature. 'As is the appearance of the painter, so is the appearance of his painting' — this is a general saying. One should speak with a smile, express oneself with substance at all times, seek out secrets everywhere, turn away from examining others' poetry [unless asked], and of what is unsaid say nothing, but of what is said, speak truthfully. His dwelling should be well-swept, furnished with various quarters suited to the six seasons, with garden groves having trees arranged at the base of many trees, with pleasure-hills, with ponds and lotus-pools, with artificial streams and ocean-whirlpools, with water-channels, frequented by peacocks and deer and parrots, with <s>Sārasa</s> cranes, <s>Cakravāka</s> ducks, and geese, with <s>Cakora</s> birds, <s>Krauñca</s> herons, <s>Kurara</s> ospreys, parrots and <s>Sārikā</s> mynahs — a stealer of the weariness of <s>Dharma</s> — with fountain-houses, mechanical water-devices, and vine-pavilions, with swings and seesaws. For one weary of mind from devotion to poetry, to break that tedium, there should be a solitary place with obedient attendants, or a deserted spot. The group of male servants should be inclined to speaking <s>Apabhraṃśa</s>; the female attendants should be devoted to <s>Māgadhī</s> speech. The women of the inner quarters should know <s>Prākṛta</s> and Sanskrit, and his friends should know all languages. For the refinement of his assembly, the scribe should be proficient in all languages, quick of speech, beautiful in lettering, skilled in reading gestures and expressions, knowledgeable in various scripts, a poet, and a grammarian. In his absence, during overnight sessions and the like, any one of the aforementioned [attendants may serve]. For whatever linguistic regulation the master establishes in his household, so it becomes. It is heard that among the <s>Magadhas</s> there was a king named <s>Śiśunāga</s>; he, removing eight difficult-to-pronounce letters, established a regulation in his own inner quarters alone — the four cerebrals beginning with <s>ṭa</s>, the three sibilants except the third, and <s>kṣa</s>. And it is heard that among the <s>Sūrasenas</s> there was a king named <s>Kuvinda</s>; he [established a rule] excluding harsh consonant clusters — in the inner quarters alone, the same as the former. And it is heard that among the <s>Kuntalas</s> there was a king named <s>Sātavāhana</s>; he established <s>Prākṛta</s> speech — in the inner quarters alone, the same as the former. And it is heard that in <s>Ujjayinī</s> there was a king named <s>Sāhasāṅka</s>; he established Sanskrit speech — in the inner quarters alone, the same as the former. His [the poet's] writing materials — a case with a writing board, a box, pen-and-ink vessels, palm-leaves or birch-bark, metal styluses for palm-leaf strips, and well-cleaned walls — should always be at hand. 'These are the equipment of the science of poetry' — say the teachers. '<s>Pratibhā</s> (intuition) alone is the [true] equipment' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. A poet should first assess himself: 'How great is my training? In which domain of language am I capable? What does the public enjoy — the mature or the novel? In what kind of assembly am I accomplished? Where does my mind become engaged?' — having understood this, he should take up a particular language, say the teachers. 'This restriction of method is for the poet of limited scope; for the independent [poet], all languages should be as natural as Sanskrit' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. And the choice of language is also seen to depend on the particular region.

children.translated_text: 'A poet should know what is approved by the public and where he stands;
he should avoid what is disapproved and commit himself to what is approved.
One should not despise oneself merely because of popular censure;
one should know oneself, for the public is unrestrained.
People praise the poet who has passed away or who dwells in another land;

children.text: pratyakṣe tu kavau lokaḥ sāvajñaḥ sumahatyapi //
children.translated_text: but toward a poet who is present, the public is contemptuous, even toward a very great one.
The poetry of a poet who is present, the beauty of a wife of the household,
the knowledge of the family physician — who would appreciate these?
This indeed is laughable behavior — that one who merely follows the recitation of others' words
condemns poets who have attained the status of a treasury of fine sayings, with the mere pretense of poetic skill.

children.text: vacaḥ svādu satāṃ lehyaṃ leśasvādvapi kautukāt /
children.translated_text: The speech of the good is sweet and to be savored; even a small taste of it, out of curiosity,
passes from mouth to mouth among children, women, and the lowborn.
The poetry of poets, like those ready for the occasion of duty, like wandering ascetics, like kings —

children.text: kāvyaṃ sadyaḥ kavīnāṃ ca bhramatyahnā diśo daśa //
children.translated_text: in a single day traverses the ten directions.
The sons, disciples, and foot-soldiers of fathers, teachers, and kings

children.text: avivicyaiva kāvyāni stuvanti ca paṭhanti ca" //
children.translated_text: praise and recite their poetry without discrimination.'

na ca svakṛtiṃ bahumanyeta /
pakṣupāto hi guṇadoṣau viparyāsayati /

children.translated_text: Thus he says:

children.text: "idaṃ hi vaidagdhyarahasyamuttamaṃ paṭhenna sūktiṃ kavimāninaḥ puraḥ /
children.translated_text: 'This is the highest secret of refined wit: one should not recite a fine verse in the presence of one who fancies himself a poet;

children.text: na kevalaṃ tāṃ na vibhāvayatyasau svakāvyabandhena vināśayatyapi" //
children.translated_text: not only does he fail to appreciate it, but he destroys it with his own poetic composition.'

body.translated_text: 'Moreover, one should not recite a half-completed work — the result is like that of unground [grain]' — this is the <s>Kavirahasya</s> (Secret of the Poet). One should not [recite] a new [work] alone in the presence [of another poet]. For he, while speaking his own [verse], by what witness would he be defeated? Nor should one overvalue one's own composition, for partiality distorts both merits and faults. Nor should one be arrogant, for even a trace of pride destroys all refinement. And one should have it examined by others; for the general saying is: what one views with detachment, one does not [necessarily] practice. But one should please the self-proclaimed poet by following his meter. For before one who considers himself a poet, a fine saying would be like a cry in the wilderness — it would be wasted.

children.translated_text: As they say in this regard —
"Depositing for safekeeping, selling, giving away, leaving the country, short lifespan,
damage, fire, and flooding — these are the causes of a composition's destruction.

body.translated_text: Activities at irregular times become disrupted; therefore one should divide the day and night into four parts according to the sequence of watches. Having risen at dawn and performed the twilight worship, he should recite a <s>Sārasvata</s> hymn of praise. Then, seated comfortably in the study hall, he should practice the sciences of poetry and the auxiliary sciences until the end of the first watch; for there is no other cause of <s>pratibhā</s> (poetic inspiration) like fresh learning. In the second watch, he should engage in poetic composition. Toward midday he should bathe and eat food that is not harmful. After the meal, he should initiate a literary discussion. And sometimes he should engage in question-and-answer exchanges. Verse-completion exercises (<s>kāvyasamasyā</s>), memory drills (<s>dhāraṇā</s>), and practice of the <s>mātṛkā</s> alphabet, and <s>citrā yogāḥ</s> (pictorial puzzles) — these are the three forms of exercise. In the fourth watch, either alone or with a limited assembly, he should review the poetry composed during the morning. When composing poetry absorbed in <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment), one's critical eye does not function; therefore one should re-examine afterward. Removing what is excessive, filling in what is deficient, altering what is misplaced, and recovering what has been forgotten — this is the daily routine. In the evening he should perform the twilight worship and honor <s>Sarasvatī</s>. Then he should write out the poetry reviewed during the day, until nightfall. He should enjoy the company of a woman as need dictates. He should sleep well during the second and third watches. Proper sleep is the supreme health of the body. In the fourth watch he should awaken with effort. In the <s>Brāhma muhūrta</s> (the hour before dawn), the mind becomes clear — he contemplates those various subjects. This is the daily-and-nightly routine. And this routine is of four kinds: the <s>asūryampaśya</s> (one who does not see the sun), the <s>niṣaṇṇa</s> (the sedentary), the <s>dattāvasara</s> (one who finds occasion), and the <s>prāyojanika</s> (the purposeful). He who composes as a lifelong vocation by entering caves, underground chambers, houses and the like — he is the <s>asūryampaśya</s>; for him, all times are suitable. He who is deeply absorbed in poetic composition and composes, but is not a lifelong practitioner — he is the <s>niṣaṇṇa</s>; for him too, all those times apply. He who composes without abandoning service and other duties — he is the <s>dattāvasara</s>; for him, only certain times are suitable: the last half of the fourth watch of the night, for that is the <s>Sārasvata muhūrta</s> (the hour of <s>Sarasvatī</s>); the time after meals, for satisfaction brings well-being; the time after lovemaking, for when distress has subsided there is single-pointed concentration; and during travel by palanquin or chariot, for a mind withdrawn from other objects, wherever it is directed, adheres to it like a <s>guhūcīlā</s> creeper. And whenever one contemplates the transience of one's own existence — that is the time for poetic creation. He who composes with a specific dramatic plot in view — he is the <s>prāyojanika</s>; his schedule is determined by the purpose at hand. This is the rule-pattern for those of natural and acquired intelligence. But for one who has received instruction, mere will suffices for all times, and all rule-patterns apply. Just like men, women too can become poets; for <s>saṃskāra</s> (refinement) resides in the self and does not require the distinction of female or male. One hears of and sees princesses, daughters of ministers, courtesans, and wives of artisans who are learned in the <s>śāstras</s> and are poets. And one should make copies of a completed composition and deposit them in multiple repositories.

children.translated_text: Poverty, addiction to vices, disrespect, ill fortune,

children.text: duṣṭe dviṣṭe ca viśvāsaḥ pañca kāvyamahāpadaḥ" //
children.translated_text: and trusting the wicked and the hostile — these are the five great calamities of poetry."

punaḥ samāpayiṣyāmi, punaḥ saṃskariṣyāmi, suhṛdbhiḥ saha vivecayiṣyāmīti karturākulatā rāṣṭropaplavaśca prabandhavināśakāraṇāni /
"aharniśāvibhāgena ya itthaṃ kavate kṛtī /ekāvalīva tatkāvyaṃ satāṃ kaṇṭheṣu lambate //
body.translated_text: "I will finish it later, I will revise it later, I will discuss it with friends later" — the author's procrastination and political upheaval in the kingdom are also causes of a composition's destruction. "He who composes thus, dividing day and night in this manner, his poetry hangs like a single-strand pearl necklace (<s>ekāvalī</s>) upon the necks of the virtuous."

children.translated_text: "The more practice and refinement a poet has,
the greater, by degrees, is the beauty of his compositions.
In standalone verses (<s>muktaka</s>), poets are countless; in anthologies (<s>saṅghāta</s>), poets number in hundreds;
but in a great composition (<s>mahāprabandha</s>), there is one poet, two are rare, three are impossible to find."
To this they further say —
"Much scattered verse may be uttered freely at will,
but a sustained composition (<s>prabandha</s>) with unbroken coherence of meaning is hard to produce.

children.text: rītiṃ vicintya vigaṇayya guṇānvigāhya śabdārthasārthamanusṛtya ca sūktimudrāḥ /
children.translated_text: Having considered the <s>rīti</s> (style), having calculated the <s>guṇas</s> (poetic qualities), having plunged into them, having followed the treasury of word and meaning, and the seals of fine expression —

children.text: kāryo nibandhaviṣaye viduṣā prayatnaḥ ke potayantrarahitā jaladhau plavante //
children.translated_text: a learned person must exert effort in the domain of sustained composition; who can float upon the ocean without a ship's mechanism?

children.text: līḍhābhidhopaniṣadāṃ savidhe budhānām abhyasyataḥ pratidinaṃ bahudṛśvano 'pi /
children.translated_text: Even for one who has studied closely with the wise who have mastered the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, who practices daily and has seen much,

children.text: kiñcitkadācana kathañcana sūktipākād vāk-tattvamunmiṣati kasyacideva puṃsaḥ //
children.translated_text: only rarely, somehow, through the ripening of poetic expression, does the true essence of speech reveal itself to some rare person.
Thus, to him whose mental activity is directed to nothing else, in the complete course of his creative work,
the goddess <s>Sarasvatī</s> observes a vow of fidelity to a single husband toward the poet.

children.text: siddhiḥ sūktiṣu sā tasya jāyate jagaduttarā /
children.translated_text: That perfection in fine verses which arises for him becomes supreme in the world;

children.text: mūlacchāyāṃ na jānāti yasyāḥ so 'pi girāṃ guruḥ" //
children.translated_text: even <s>Bṛhaspati</s>, the preceptor of the gods, does not know the root and shadow of that perfection."
