children.translated_text: It is heard that in <s>Ujjayinī</s> there was an examination of poets —
"Here <s>Kālidāsa</s>, <s>Meṇṭha</s>, and <s>Atrāmarūpasūrabhāravi</s> —
<s>Haricandra</s> and <s>Candragupta</s> were examined here in <s>Viśālā</s>."

body.translated_text: A king who is a poet should establish a literary assembly (<s>kavisamāja</s>). When the king is a poet, everyone in the realm becomes a poet. He should build an assembly hall (<s>sabhā</s>) for the examination of poetry. It should be furnished with sixteen pillars, four doors, and eight <s>mattavāraṇī</s> (elephant-ornament brackets). Attached to it should be the king's pleasure-chamber. In the middle of the hall, between four pillars, there should be a raised platform (<s>vedikā</s>) of level jeweled floor, one <s>hasta</s> (cubit) in height. Upon it should be the king's seat. To the north of it, the <s>Saṃskṛta</s> poets should be seated. Among multilingual poets, whoever is most proficient in a particular language is designated by that language. But one who is proficient in several should move about and sit in each place in turn. Beyond them should be seated the Vedic scholars, the logicians (<s>prāmāṇika</s>), the <s>Paurāṇikas</s> (reciters of <s>Purāṇas</s>), the <s>Smārtas</s> (experts in <s>Smṛti</s>), physicians, astrologers, and others of similar kind. To the east, the <s>Prākṛta</s> poets; beyond them, actors, dancers, singers, instrumentalists, reciters, <s>kuśīlava</s> performers, <s>tālāpacara</s> rhythm-keepers, and others of similar kind. To the west, the <s>Apabhraṃśa</s> poets; beyond them, painters, jewel-setters, mimics (<s>vaikaṭika</s>), goldsmiths, carpenters, metalworkers, and others of similar kind. To the south, the <s>Bhūtabhāṣā</s> poets; beyond them, snake-charmers, swimmers, conjurers, acrobats, wrestlers, those who live by weapons, and others of similar kind. Seated there comfortably, the king should initiate literary discussions, encourage poetic composition, and examine poetry. He should emulate all the great literary patrons such as <s>Vāsudeva</s>, <s>Sātavāhana</s>, <s>Śūdraka</s>, and <s>Sāhasāṅka</s> through gifts and honors. His assembly members should be well-nourished and prosperous, and should receive rewards at appropriate times. For extraordinary poetry, there should be fitting honor for the poet. From time to time, amid the literary discussions, he should also permit philosophical debates. Even honey does not taste good without a sting. When weary of poetry and <s>śāstra</s>, he should take delight in the company of learned people. He should arrange through other means for scholars who have come from distant lands to meet with him, and should honor them appropriately for the duration of their stay. He should support those who seek patronage, and gather them to himself. The king alone is the ocean that receives the jewels among men. And those who depend on the king should also emulate the king's conduct; for it is indeed to the king's benefit that his dependents be refined. In great cities he should establish learned assemblies (<s>brahmasabhā</s>) for the examination of poetry and <s>śāstra</s>. Those who pass the examination there should receive a chariot procession and a turban-binding ceremony (<s>paṭṭabandha</s>).

children.translated_text: And it is heard that in <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> there was an examination of <s>śāstra</s> authors —
"Here <s>Upavarṣa</s> and <s>Varṣa</s>, here <s>Pāṇini</s> and <s>Piṅgala</s>, here <s>Vyāḍi</s>,
here <s>Vararuci</s> and <s>Patañjali</s> — having been examined, they attained fame."
He who, having become the lord of the assembly, examines poetry in this manner —

children.text: vaśastasya jagadvayāpi sa sukhī tatra tatra ca //
children.translated_text: the world is under his sway, and he is happy both here and hereafter.

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe kavicaryā rājacaryāṃ ca daśamo 'dhyāyaḥ
body.translated_text: Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the daily routine of the poet and the conduct of the king (<s>kavicaryā</s> and <s>rājacaryā</s>), in the first section of the <s>Kavirahasyam</s> in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.

children.translated_text: An example of stealing a <s>śleṣa</s> (pun) by means of another <s>śleṣa</s> word —
"Are these not <s>Kirātas</s> with their long-drawn arrows flying crosswise? Or are these not <s>palāśa</s> trees with faces smeared in yellow and red?

children.text: pānthāḥ kesariṇaṃ na paśyata puropyenaṃ vasantaṃ vane mūḍhā rakṣata jīvitāni śaraṇaṃ yāta priyāṃ devatām" //
children.translated_text: O travelers, do you not see the lion dwelling in this very forest in spring? Fools, protect your lives — take refuge in your beloved deity!"

body.translated_text: The methods of stealing words and meanings, and the distinctions among poets. First, the methods of stealing words. The methods of word-theft (<s>śabdaharaṇa</s>). The incorporation of words and meanings used by another poet is called <s>haraṇa</s> (literary theft). It is of two kinds: that which must be abandoned (<s>parityājya</s>) and that which may be accepted (<s>anugrāhya</s>). Of these, word-theft itself is fivefold: by a single word (<s>padataḥ</s>), by a quarter-verse (<s>pādataḥ</s>), by a half-verse (<s>arddhataḥ</s>), by a full verse (<s>vṛttataḥ</s>), and by an entire composition (<s>prabandhataḥ</s>). "The borrowing of a single word is not a fault" — so say the <s>Ācāryas</s> (teachers). "Except when it is a word with double meaning" — so says the follower of <s>Yāyāvara</s>.

children.translated_text: And similarly —
"O traveler, do not go! Having abandoned your beloved, a long-drawn arrow

children.text: sthitaṃ panthānamāvṛtya kiṃ kirātaṃ na paśyasi" //
children.translated_text: stands blocking the path — do you not see the <s>Kirāta</s>?"
An example of stealing by borrowing part of a <s>śleṣa</s> compound —
"It is no wonder that this ignoble one has affection for me;
how could a person free from hunger make use of flesh (<s>māṃsa</s>)?"
And similarly —

children.text: "kopānmānini kiṃ sphuratyatitarāṃ śobhādharaste 'dharaḥ kiṃ vā cumbanakāraṇāddayita no vāyorvikārādayam /
children.translated_text: "O proud one, why does your lower lip tremble so much from anger? Or is it, beloved, for the sake of a kiss? No, it is merely an agitation of the wind.

children.text: tasmātsubhru sugandhimāhitarasaṃ snigdhaṃ bhajasvādarān mugdhe māṃsarasaṃ bruvantiti tayā gāḍhaṃ samāliṅgitaḥ" //
children.translated_text: Therefore, O fair-browed one, partake lovingly of the lip that is fragrant, full of flavor, and tender — O innocent one, 'partake of the meat broth,' they say" — and so saying, he was tightly embraced by her.
An example of stealing a <s>śleṣa</s> by means of <s>yamaka</s> (paronomasia) —
"By him who wielded the plough, vast as the ocean, striking in the battlefield —
his own fame, spotless as the digits of the moon, was spread forth, throwing the <s>Asuras</s> into confusion."
And similarly —
"By him who shattered the frenzied army with arrows,

children.text: daśasu dikṣu ca tena yaśaḥ sitaṃ niravadhīritamākulamāsuram" //
children.translated_text: his fame, white in the ten directions, was spread forth, throwing the <s>Asuras</s> into confusion."

body.text:
śliṣṭasya praśnottareṇa haraṇam-
"yasyāṃ bhujaṅgavargaḥ karṇoyatekṣaṇaṃ kāminīvavadanaṃ ca" //
body.translated_text: An example of stealing a <s>śleṣa</s> by means of question-and-answer — "In which [place] there is a multitude of serpents, an eye extending to the ear, and a face like that of a beautiful woman."

children.translated_text: And similarly —
"What does a lover do, and for how long, in the house of a courtesan?
What kind of face does he behold — one with eyes extending to the ears?"
An example of stealing a <s>yamaka</s> by means of another <s>yamaka</s> —

children.text: "varadāya namo haraye patati jano 'yaṃ smarannapi na moharaye /
children.translated_text: "Obeisance to <s>Hari</s>, the boon-giver — even remembering him, this person does not fall into delusion;

children.text: bahuśaścakranda hatā manasi ditiryena daityacakraṃ dahatā" //
children.translated_text: <s>Diti</s>, whose demon-host was destroyed, cried out many times in her mind, struck by him who burns the wheel [of enemies]."
And similarly —

children.text: cakraṃ dahatāraṃ cakranda hatāraṃ khaṅgena tavājau rājannarinārī /
children.translated_text: "O king, in battle your sword burned the enemy wheel, made the enemy women cry out — [employing the same <s>yamaka</s> pattern of] <s>cakraṃ dahatāraṃ</s> and <s>cakranda hatāraṃ</s>."
In this manner, through mutual correspondence, there are other varieties as well.
Is this not something that can only be taught by instruction?
As they say in this regard —
"Other kinds of theft by a person decay with the passage of time,

children.text: api putreṣu pautreṣu vākcauryaṃ ca na śīryati" //
children.translated_text: but the theft of words does not decay, even down to sons and grandsons."

body.text: "ayamaprasiddhaḥ prasiddhimānahamṣa, ayamapratiṣṭhaḥ pratiṣṭhāvānaham, aprakrāntamidamasya saṃvidhānakaṃ prakrāntaṃ mama, gūḍūcīvacano 'yaṃ mṛdvīkāvacano 'ham, anādṛtabhāṣāviśṣo 'yamahamādṛtabhāṣāviśeṣaḥ, praśāntajñātṛkamidaṃ, deśāntaritakarttṛkamidam, ucchannanibandhanamūlamidaṃ, mlecchitakopanibandhamūlamidamityevamādi bhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ śabdaharaṇe 'rthaharaṇe cābhirameta" //
body.translated_text: "This one is unknown while I am famous; this one is without standing while I have standing; his dramatic plot is unfinished while mine is complete; his language is like that of the <s>guḍūcī</s> (bitter creeper) while mine is like that of the grape (<s>mṛdvīkā</s>); he disregards linguistic distinction while I honor linguistic distinction; the knowers of this work have died out; the author belongs to a distant land; the original text of this composition has been lost; the source of this composition is in a foreign language" — by such justifications as these, one indulges in the theft of words and the theft of meanings.

body.text:
ity avantisundarī /
"tribhyaḥ padebhyaḥ prabhṛti tvaśliśṭebhyo haraṇam"
iti ācāryāḥ-

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "sa pātu vo yasya jaṭākalāpe sthitaḥ śaśāṅkaḥ sphuṭahāragauraḥ /
children.translated_text: 'May he protect you, in whose matted locks the moon rests, bright as a clear pearl necklace,
like a sleeping swan in autumn upon a cluster of blue lotus stalks.'

body.translated_text:
— says <s>Avantisundarī</s>.
'From three <s>pādas</s> (verse-quarters) onward, taking from non-cohesive [verses] constitutes <s>haraṇa</s> (literary theft)'
— say the teachers.

children.translated_text: And as:
'May he protect you, whose [enemies] were slain leaving only remnants — even in the lotus-eyes of their own beloved women, colored with collyrium of the same hue,
though endowed with beauty, the <s>Daityas</s> (demons) tremble.'

body.text:
"na" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
ullekhavānpadasandarbhaḥ pariharaṇīyo nāpratyabhijñāyātaḥ pādo 'pi /
tasyāpi sāmye na kiñcana dṛṣṭaṃ syāt /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
'Having thus spoken, setting his mind — delightful in the particular manner of expression — upon the attainment of victory,
the noble-minded king spoke to <s>Dvaipāyana</s> these equally noble words.'

body.translated_text:
'No' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>.
A verse-composition that bears a resemblance should be avoided; even a <s>pāda</s> (verse-quarter) that is not recognized [as borrowed] should not [be taken].
Even in the case of similarity, nothing wrong would be seen.

children.translated_text: And as:
'Having thus spoken — delightful in the particular manner of expression — the proud brother of <s>Rāma</s> fell silent,

children.text: saṃkṣitpamātpāvasaraṃ ca vākyaṃ sevāvidhijñaiḥ purataḥ prabhūṇām" //
children.translated_text: and [spoke] a brief yet fitting speech, as is [proper] before lords by those versed in the duties of service.'
An example with resemblance:
'Obeisance to the one who dispenses both the poison and the nectar of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) and <s>nirvāṇa</s> (liberation),
to <s>Śaṅkara</s>, the ocean of milk, [whose] waves are the hosts of the virtuous.'
And as:
'To the one whose nature is pure nectar, with flowing drops and resonance,
obeisance to <s>Śaṅkara</s>, the ocean of milk, of infinite radiance.'

body.text: "pāda evānyathātvakaraṇakāraṇaṃ na haraṇam, api tu svīkaraṇam" iti ācāryāḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
'Those devoted to <s>tyāga</s> (renunciation) attain heaven; those devoid of <s>tyāga</s> go to hell.

children.text: na tyāgināṃ kiñcidasādhyamasti tyāgo hi sarvavyasanāni hanti" //
children.translated_text: Nothing is unachievable for the renouncer — for <s>tyāga</s> destroys all vices.'

body.translated_text: 'Merely altering a <s>pāda</s> (verse-quarter) is not <s>haraṇa</s> (theft), but rather <s>svīkaraṇa</s> (appropriation)' — say the teachers.

children.translated_text: And as:
'"<s>Tyāga</s> (renunciation) destroys all vices" — this notion is widely accepted in the world as false,
for all vices have arisen through the <s>tyāga</s> (abandonment) of that doe-eyed woman by me.'

body.text:
tadidaṃ svīkaraṇāparanāmadheyaṃ haraṇameva (iti yāyāvarīyaḥ-) /
tadvadardhdaprayoge 'pi /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "pādaste naravara dakṣiṇe samudre pādo 'nyo himavati hemakūṭalagne /
children.translated_text: 'One foot of yours, O best of men, is in the southern ocean; the other foot rests on the <s>Himālaya</s>, touching <s>Hemakūṭa</s>.

children.text: ākrāmatyalaghu mahītalaṃ tvayītthaṃ bhūpālāḥ praṇatimapāsya kinnu kuryuḥ" //
children.translated_text: As you thus stride powerfully across the earth, what can the kings do except offer prostration?'

body.translated_text:
'This so-called <s>svīkaraṇa</s> (appropriation) is indeed <s>haraṇa</s> (theft) by another name' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>.
Likewise in the case of borrowing a half-verse:

body.text:
yathā cottarārddhe-
"itthaṃ te vidhṛtapadadvayasya rājan nāścaryaṃ kathamiva sīvanī na bhinnā" //
body.translated_text:
And as, in the latter half:
'Thus, O king, as you hold both feet [on the earth], how is it not amazing that the seam [of the earth] is not split!'

body.text: evaṃ vyastārddhaprayoge 'pi /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
'The moon's radiance is greater only so long as the orb of the fierce-rayed [sun] has not risen;

children.text: abhyudgate sakaladhāmanidhau tu tasmin nindoḥ sitābhraśakalasya ca ko viśeṣaḥ" //
children.translated_text: but when that repository of all light has risen, what difference is there between the moon and a piece of white cloud?'

body.translated_text: Likewise in the case of using separated halves:

children.translated_text: And as:

children.text: "tattāvadeva śaśinaḥ sphiritaṃ mahīyo yāvanna kiñcidapi gauritarā hasanti /
children.translated_text: 'The moon's radiance is greater only so long as certain fairer women do not laugh;

children.text: tābhiḥ punarvihasitānanapaṅkajābhir indoḥ sitābhraśakalasya ca ko viśeṣaḥ" //
children.translated_text: but when they laugh, their faces [blooming] like lotuses — what difference is there between the moon and a piece of white cloud?'

body.text: pāda evānyathātvakaraṇaṃ na svīkaraṇaṃ pādonaharaṇaṃ vā /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
'In a wilderness, in a desolate place, at night, inside a house, in a robbery,
and in the denial of a deposit — a divine ordeal takes place.'

body.translated_text: Merely altering a <s>pāda</s> (verse-quarter) is neither <s>svīkaraṇa</s> (appropriation) nor <s>pādonaharaṇa</s> (theft-minus-a-quarter).

body.text:
yathā cottarārddhe-
"tanvaṅgī yadī labhyeta divyā sambhagavati kriyā" /

children.translated_text: Or as:
'He in whose hair are the clouds, in whose every limb are the rivers,
in whose belly are the four oceans — obeisance to that one whose essence is water!'

body.translated_text:
And as, in the latter half:
'If a slender-limbed woman were to be obtained — a divine ordeal indeed takes place!'

body.text:
yathā cottarārddhe---
"kukṣau samudrāścatvāraḥ sa saheta smarānalam" /
bhinnārthānāṃ tu pādānāmekena pādenānvayanaṃ kavitvameva /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "kimiha kimapi dṛṣṭaṃ sthānamasti śrutaṃ vā vrajati dinakaro 'yaṃ yanna nāstaṃ kadācit /
children.translated_text: '"Is there any place seen here, or heard of, where this sun does not set?" —
thus asking the flocks of birds, the wretched <s>Cakravāka</s> (ruddy shelduck), frightened of separation at night, wanders about.'

body.translated_text:
And as, in the latter half:
'In whose belly are the four oceans — he would endure the fire of <s>Smara</s> (Love).'
But the joining of <s>pādas</s> (verse-quarters) of different meaning into a single <s>pāda</s> is itself poetic skill.

children.translated_text: And as:
'Victorious is <s>Pinākī</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), wearing the white and trembling serpent as sacred thread, with the stream of <s>Gaṅgā</s> water within his dense tawny matted locks,
bearing the crescent moon unknowingly, his dark throat like that of a mature peacock.'
And as:
'The lotus grove wilts, the splendid lotus cluster [blooms]; the owl grows intoxicated, the <s>Cakravāka</s> rejoices;

children.text: udayamahimaraśmiryāti śītāṃsurastaṃ hatavidhilalitānāṃ hī vicitro vipākaḥ //
children.translated_text: the cool-rayed moon sets as the sun of mighty radiance rises — indeed, wonderful is the fruition of those whose fortune is destroyed!'
And as:

children.text: "kimiha kimapi dṛṣṭaṃ sthānamasti śrutaṃ vā ghanakapilajaṭāntarbhrāntagaṅgājalaudhaḥ /
children.translated_text: '"Is there any place seen here, or heard of?" — With the stream of <s>Gaṅgā</s> water within his dense tawny matted locks,

children.text: nivasati sa pinākī yatra yāyāṃ tadasmin hatavidhilalitānāṃ hī vicitro vipākaḥ" //
children.translated_text: that <s>Pinākī</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) dwells wherever he goes — indeed, wonderful is the fruition of those whose fortune is destroyed!'
The use of a few words short of a full <s>pāda</s> (verse-quarter) — as [illustrated by]:

children.text: "yā vyāpāravatī rasān rasayituṃ kācitkavīnāṃ navā dṛṣṭiryā pariniṣṭhitārthaviṣayonmeṣā ca vaipaścitī /
children.translated_text: 'That certain fresh vision of poets which is active in savoring the <s>rasas</s> (aesthetic emotions), and that scholarly insight whose domain is established meaning —

children.text: te dve apyavalambya viśvamaniśaṃ nirvārṇayanto vayaṃ śrāntā naiva labdhamabdhiśayana tvadbhaktitulyaṃ sukham" //
children.translated_text: relying on both of these and constantly examining the universe, we have grown weary, yet have not found, O reclining-on-the-ocean [<s>Viṣṇu</s>], a happiness equal to devotion to you.'

body.text:
yathā ca caturthapāde-
"śrāntā naiva ca labdhamutpaladṛśāṃ premṇaḥ samānaṃ sukham" //
body.translated_text:
And as, in the fourth <s>pāda</s>:
'We have grown weary, yet have not found a happiness equal to the love of lotus-eyed women.'

children.translated_text: Even the non-taking of a portion of a <s>pāda</s> may serve as an indication of a portion of a word — as [illustrated by]:
'As if washed by radiance due to incomplete laughter, with eyes half-closed revealing ear-lotuses,

children.text: pibati madhusugandhīnyānanāni priyāṇāṃ tvayi vinihitabhāraḥ kuntalānāmadhīśaḥ" //
children.translated_text: the lord of the <s>Kuntalas</s>, having placed his burden upon you, drinks the honey-fragrant faces of his beloveds.'

body.text:
yathā cottarārdhe-
"pibatu madhusugandhīnyānanāni priyāṇāṃ mayi vinihitabhāraḥ kuntalānāmadhīśaḥ" /
vākyasyānyathā vyākhyānamapi na svīkaraṇaṃ haraṇaṃ vā /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "subhru!tvaṃ kupitetyapāstamaśanaṃ tyaktā kathā yoṣitāṃ dūrādeva mayojbhphatāḥ surabhayaḥ sragdāmadhūpādayaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'O fair-browed one! Since you are angry, food has been set aside, talk of women abandoned; from afar I have cast away garlands, fragrant wreaths, and incense.

children.text: kopaṃ rāgiṇi muñca mayyavanate dṛṣṭe prasīdādhunā sadyastvadvirahādbhavanti dayite sarvā mamāndhā diśaḥ" //
children.translated_text: O passionate one, release your anger — now that I bow before you, seeing me, be gracious! For immediately upon separation from you, O beloved, all directions become dark to me.'

body.translated_text:
And as, in the latter half:
'Let the lord of the <s>Kuntalas</s>, having placed his burden upon me, drink the honey-fragrant faces of his beloveds.'
Even interpreting a sentence differently is neither <s>svīkaraṇa</s> (appropriation) nor <s>haraṇa</s> (theft).

body.text:
etañca kāntāprasādanaparaṃ vākyaṃ kupitadṛṣṭiparatayā vyakhyātaṃ, na svīkṛtaṃ hṛtaṃ vā /
yattu parakīyaṃ svīyamiti proktānāmanyatamena kāraṇena vilapanti, tanna kevalaṃ haraṇam, api tu doṣodāharaṇam /
muktakaprabandhaviṣayaṃ tat /
mūlyakrayo 'pi haraṇameva /
varamaprātpiryaśaso na punarduryaśaḥ /
(sabhāpatistu dvidhā, upajīvya, upajīvakaśca /
tatropajīvanamātreṇa na kaściddoṣaḥ /
yataḥ sarvo 'pi parebhya eva vyutpadyate, kevalaṃ tatra samudāyo guruḥ) "tadvahaktiharaṇam" iti ācāryāḥ /
yathā -
"ūrudvayaṃ sarasakadalīkāṇḍasabrahmacāri" /

children.translated_text: And as:
'The pair of thighs is of the same lineage as the plantain and the lily stem; the hips are arranged like a companion of stone slabs;

children.text: vakṣaḥ stanadvitayatāḍitakumbhaśobhaṃ sabrahmacāri śaśisaśca mukhaṃ mṛgākṣyāḥ" //
children.translated_text: the chest is beautiful with the pair of breasts striking [like] water pots — a companion-in-celibacy of the moon is the face of the deer-eyed woman.'

body.translated_text:
And this sentence, intended for appeasing a beloved, has been interpreted as referring to an angry glance — it is neither appropriated nor stolen.
But when people lament for one of the stated reasons that another's [work] is [presented as] their own — that is not merely <s>haraṇa</s> (theft), but rather an illustration of a fault.
That pertains to the domain of <s>muktaka</s> (standalone verse) anthologies.
Purchasing [verses] for a price is also indeed <s>haraṇa</s> (theft).
Better the non-attainment of fame than infamy.
(The patron is of two kinds: the one who is supported, and the supporter.
In that, there is no fault in merely being supported,
since everyone indeed learns from others — only there, the collective is the teacher.)
'That is <s>bhaktiharaṇa</s> (theft of a composition's structure)' — say the teachers.
As [illustrated by]:
'The pair of thighs is a companion-in-celibacy of the succulent plantain stalk.'

children.text: uktayo hyarthāntarasaṅkrāntā na pratyabhiyājñante, svadante ca; tadarthastu haraṇādapi haraṇaṃ syuḥ" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Expressions that have migrated to a different meaning are not recognized [as stolen], and they please; but those [taken] for the same meaning — they would be theft upon theft' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>.
'There is no poet who is not a thief, no merchant who is not a thief;

children.text: sa nandati vinā vācyaṃ yo jānāt nigūhitum //
children.translated_text: he rejoices without reproach who knows how to conceal [his borrowing].
One poet is a creator, another is a transformer,
yet another is a concealer, and still another is a compiler.
He who, in the matter of words, meanings, and expressions, can devise something new here
and indicate something from the ancients — let him be considered a <s>mahākavi</s> (great poet).'

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe ekādaśo 'dhyāyaḥ śabdaharaṇāni //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the eleventh chapter, entitled '<s>Śabdaharaṇāni</s>' (Verbal Thefts), in the first section of the <s>Kavirahasya</s> (Secrets of the Poet) in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.
Chapter 12

body.text: dvadaśo 'dhyāyaḥ 12
body.translated_text: Twelfth chapter, 12.

body.text: arthaharaṇopāyāḥ, kaviprabhedāḥ, pratibimba-kalpavikalpasya samīkṣā ca /

children.text: "purāṇakavikṣuṇṇe vartmani durāpamaspṛṣṭaṃ vastu, tataśca tadeva saṃskṛrtuṃ prayateta" iti ācāryāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'On the path well-trodden by ancient poets, untouched matter is difficult to obtain; therefore one should endeavor to refine that very [existing material]' — say the teachers.
'No' — says <s>Vākpatirāja</s>.
'Though its essence has been taken daily by noble poets since the beginning of <s>saṃsāra</s> (the world),
the overflow of speech still shines today with its seal unbroken.'

body.translated_text: <s>Arthaharaṇopāyāḥ</s> (Means of Borrowing Meaning), <s>Kaviprabhedāḥ</s> (Distinctions among Poets), and the Examination of <s>Pratibimba-kalpa-vikalpa</s> (Reflection-Replica Theory).

body.text:
tatpratibhāsāya ca paraprabandheṣvavadadhīta /
"tadavagāhane hi tadekayonayo 'rthāḥ pṛthak pṛthak prathante" ityeke /
"tatratyānāmarthānāṃ chāyayā parivṛttiḥ phalam" ityapare /
mahātmanāṃ hi saṃvādinyo buddhaya ekamevārthamupasthāpayanti, tatparityāgāyatānādriyeta iti ca kecit /
"na" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
sārasvataṃ cakṣuravāṅmanasagocareṇa praṇidhānena dṛṣṭamadṛṣṭaṃ cārthajātaṃ svayaṃ vibhajati /
tadāhuḥ-
sutpasyāpi mahākaveḥ śabdārthau sarasvatī darśayati /
taditarasya tatra jāgrato 'pyandhaṃ cakṣuḥ /
anyadṛṣṭacare hyarthe mahākavayo jātyandhāstadviparīte tu divyadṛśaḥ /
na tat tryakṣāḥ sahasrokṣo vā yañcarmacakṣuṣo 'pi kavayaḥ paśyanti /
madidarpaṇe kavīnāṃ viśvaṃ pratiphalati /
kathaṃ nu vayaṃ dṛśyāmaha iti mahātmanāmahampūrvikayaiva śabdārthāḥ puro dhāvanti /
yatsiddhapraṇidhānā yoginaḥ paśyanti, tatra vācā vicaranti kavayaḥ ityanantā mahākaviṣu sūktayaḥ (iti) /
"samastamarsti" kintu tripathamarthamadhyagīṣmahi /
iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
yadutānyayonirnihṇutayonirayoniśca /
tatrānyayonidvidhā pratibimbakalpaḥ, ālekhyayaprakhyaśca /
nihnutayonirapi dvidhā tulyadehitulyaḥ parapurapraveśasadṛśca /
ayoniḥ punarekādṛśa eva /

children.translated_text: Among these:

children.text: arthaḥ sa eva sarvo vākyāntaraviracanāparaṃ yatra /
children.translated_text: Where the meaning is entirely the same, [only] recast into a different sentence,
that poetry, different [only] in the other [surface] meaning, would be of the <s>pratibimbakalpa</s> (reflection-type).

body.translated_text:
And in order to manifest that [poetic vision], one should study the compositions of others.
'For upon immersing oneself in those, ideas born from the same source spread out separately' — say some.
'The result is a transformation [of meaning] through the shadow of the ideas found therein' — say others.
For the minds of great souls are concordant — they bring forth the very same meaning; therefore one should not be inclined toward rejecting that — say some.
'No' — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>.
The eye of <s>Sarasvatī</s>, through concentration beyond the reach of speech and mind, distributes both seen and unseen subject matter by itself.
Thus they say:
Even for a sleeping <s>mahākavi</s> (great poet), <s>Sarasvatī</s> reveals words and meanings.
For anyone else, even when awake there, the eye is blind.
For in subject matter seen by others, great poets are born blind; but in the opposite [i.e., unseen matter], they possess divine sight.
What poets with mere fleshly eyes see — that neither the three-eyed [<s>Śiva</s>] nor the thousand-eyed [<s>Indra</s>] see.
In the mirror of the mind of poets, the entire universe is reflected.
'How indeed are we perceived?' — with this ego-driven [curiosity], words and meanings rush forth before the great souls.
What accomplished <s>yogins</s> see through concentration — in that [realm], poets roam through speech. Thus there are endless fine sayings about great poets.
'All of this exists' — but we shall examine the threefold path of meaning,
says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>.
Namely: <s>anyayoni</s> (born from another), <s>nihnutayoni</s> (born from concealment), and <s>ayoni</s> (without source).
Among these, <s>anyayoni</s> is twofold: <s>pratibimbakalpa</s> (reflection-type) and <s>ālekhyaprakhya</s> (painting-like).
<s>Nihnutayoni</s> is also twofold: <s>tulyadehitulya</s> (identical-body type) and <s>parapurapraveśasadṛśa</s> (entering-another's-city type).
<s>Ayoni</s> (without source) is simply of one kind.

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "te pāntu vaḥ paśupateralinīlabhāsaḥ kaṇṭhapradeśaghaṭitāḥ phaṇinaḥ sphurantaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'May they protect you — the serpents of <s>Paśupati</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), dark-blue as bees, fastened at the region of his throat, quivering,
by whom the <s>Kālakūṭa</s> (poison) appears adorned as if with sprouts nourished by the sprinkling of cool moon-nectar drops.'
And as:
'Victorious are the great dark serpents on the throat of <s>Nīlakaṇṭha</s> (<s>Śiva</s>),
appearing like sprouts of <s>Kālakūṭa</s> (poison) watered by the flowing waters of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>.'
Where, through a certain degree of transformative effort, the subject appears as if different —
that, the learned in meaning call <s>ālekhyaprakhya</s> (painting-like) poetry.
In that very subject, as [illustrated by]:
'Victorious are the white serpents hanging from the matted locks of <s>Śambhu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>),
appearing like sprouts from the bulb of the moon, watered by the flowing waters of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>.'
Where, despite difference in subject matter, there is a perception of non-difference due to extreme similarity —
that, even the wise compose as <s>tulyadehitulya</s> (identical-body type) poetry.
As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "avīnādau kṛtvā bhavati turago yāvadavadhiḥ paśurdhanyastāvatprativasati yo jīvati sukham /
children.translated_text: 'A horse is fortunate only until it is yoked at the beginning of a battle; a domestic animal is blessed so long as it dwells [peacefully] and lives happily.

children.text: amīṣāṃ nirmāṇaṃ kimapi tadabhūddagdhakariṇāṃ vanaṃ vā kṣeṇībhṛdbhavanamathavā yena śaraṇam" //
children.translated_text: What was it that led to the creation of those burnt elephants — whether the forest, the king's palace, or wherever their shelter was?'
In this [same] subject:
'In every house there is the same treatment of fodder; because of their utility they are valued and honored.

children.text: sphurati hatamaṇīnāṃ kintu taddhāma yena kṣitipatibhavane vā svākare vā nivāsaḥ" //
children.translated_text: But the splendor of slain gems — whether their dwelling was in the king's palace or in their own mine — that alone shines forth.'
Where the root [idea] would be the same, but the elaboration is manifoldly different from afar —
that poetry, resembling the entering of another's city, is to be discerned by good poets.
As [illustrated by]:
'She, whose enemy's wife, looking all around at the sky during the rainy season, with the rumbling thunder overpowering the sound of the ocean, amidst the agitation of dense cloud-masses,
with eyes slightly narrowed, with tears of joy clearly expressing the fear of the abandoned forceful assault, repeatedly smelled the <s>kadamba</s>-scented breeze.'
The same meaning [expressed differently] —

children.text: "ācchidya priyataḥ kadambakusumaṃ yasyāridārairnavaṃ yātrābhaṅgavidhāyino jalamucāṃ kālasya cihnaṃ mahat /
children.translated_text: 'Having snatched from her beloved a fresh <s>kadamba</s> flower — the great sign of the season of rain-clouds that disrupts [military] expeditions,

children.text: hṛṣyadbhiḥ paricumbutaṃ nayanayornyastaṃ hṛdi sthāpitaṃ sīmante nihitaṃ kathañcana tataḥ kārṇāvataṃsīkṛtam //
children.translated_text: joyfully it was kissed, placed before the eyes, held to the heart, set upon the hair-parting, and then somehow made an ear-ornament.'

body.text:
" tadetaccatuṣṭayanibandhanāśca kavīnāṃ dvātriṃśaddharaṇopāyāḥ /
amīṣāṃ cārthānāmanvarthā ayaskāntavañcatvāraḥ kavayaḥ pañcamaścādṛṣṭacarārthadarśī /

children.translated_text: Thus they say —
'The bewilderer (<s>bhrāmaka</s>), the kisser (<s>cumbaka</s>), the puller (<s>karṣaka</s>), and the melter (<s>drāvaka</s>) —
such a poet is worldly; but the other, [who is like] a <s>cintāmaṇi</s> (wish-fulfilling gem), is extraordinary.

body.translated_text: And these thirty-two methods of appropriation by poets are based on these four categories. And corresponding to these meanings, there are four types of poets, like loadstones, and a fifth who perceives unseen meanings.

children.translated_text: He who creates the appearance of never-before-seenness even in an ancient subject-matter,
dazzling with unprecedented brilliance and the like — he is the bewildering (<s>bhrāmaka</s>) poet.
He who kisses another's meaning with his own captivating expression,
imparting a slight new shade with little alteration — he is considered the kissing (<s>cumbaka</s>) poet.
He who draws out another's meaning and expression and settles them in his own speech

children.text: samullekena kenāpi sa smṛtaḥ karṣakaḥ kaviḥ //
children.translated_text: with some fresh embellishment — he is known as the pulling (<s>karṣaka</s>) poet.
He who melts down the original meaning and gives it novelty in his own expression

children.text: yo drāvayitvā mūlārthaṃ drāvakaḥ sa bhavetkaviḥ //
children.translated_text: so that it is unrecognizable — he is the melting (<s>drāvaka</s>) poet.
He whose host of meanings arises like a wonderful form, producing <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) alone, simultaneous with thought,

children.text: adṛṣṭapūrvo nipuṇaiḥ purāṇaiḥ kaviḥ sa cintāmaṇiradvitīyaḥ" //
children.translated_text: never before seen by any skilled ancient — that poet is a <s>cintāmaṇi</s> (wish-fulfilling gem), without a second.'

body.text:
tasya cāconirarthaḥ /
sa ca tridhā laukikālaukikabhedena, tayormiśratvena ca /

children.translated_text: Worldly —

children.text: "mā kośakāralatike vaha varṇagarvaṃ kiṃ ḍambareṇa caṇike tava kausumena /
children.translated_text: 'Do not bear the pride of your coloring, O <s>kośakāra</s> (cochineal) creeper! What is the use of your floral display, O <s>caṇikā</s> (chickpea)?

children.text: puṇḍrekṣuyaṣṭiriyamekatarā cakāstu yā syandate rasamṛte 'pi hi yantrayogāt" //
children.translated_text: Let this single <s>pauṇḍra</s> sugarcane stalk shine forth, for it flows with juice even without the aid of a press.'

body.translated_text: And his meaning is unprecedented. And that is of three kinds: worldly, extraordinary, and a mixture of both.

children.translated_text: Extraordinary —

children.text: "devī putramasūna nṛtyata gaṇāḥ kiṃ tiṣṭhatetyudbhuje" harṣādbhṛṅgiriṭāvudāḥ hṛtagirā cāmuṇḍayāliṅgite /
children.translated_text: 'The Goddess has borne a son! Dance, O <s>Gaṇas</s>! Why are you standing?' — at this, with arms upraised, when <s>Cāmuṇḍā</s> embraced [them], with words uttered by <s>Bhṛṅgiriṭa</s> in his ecstasy,

may the sound protect you — [a sound] arising from the mutual impact of their bodies, born from the rattling of their massive bones, overpowering even the rumbling music of the divine <s>dundubhi</s> drums.'
Mixed —
'When the slayer of <s>Mura</s> resides within the womb, the mother's exhalations — releasing showers of pollen from the lotus of her navel —

children.text: nipātāḥ sānandaṃ racitaphaṇacakreṇa halinā lamantādasyāsuḥ pratidivasamenāṃsi bhavataḥ" //
children.translated_text: whose falls are joyfully [received] by <s>Halāyudha</s> (<s>Balarāma</s>) with his expanded serpent-hood — may the daily growing [months of pregnancy] of this [<s>Devakī</s>] be auspicious to you!'
And for each of these four types of meaning —

children.text: catvāra ete kathitā mayaiva ye 'rthāḥ kavīnāṃ haraṇopadeśe /
children.translated_text: These four meanings in the instruction on poetic appropriation have been described by me;
by virtue of eight subdivisions for each, they are followed by thirty-two varieties in all.

body.text:
tatra pratibimbakalpavikalpāḥ /
sa evārthaḥ paurvāparyaviparyāsād vyastakaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —
'Having seen another elephant and produced excitement, considering the driver's command as mere straw,

children.text: gacchandaghre nāgarājaḥ kariṇyā premṇā tulyaṃ bandhanaṃ nāsti jantoḥ" //
children.translated_text: the bull-elephant, approaching the she-elephant at the front — for a creature, there is no bond equal to the bond of love.'

body.translated_text: Among these, the <s>pratibimbakalpa</s> (mirror-image) variations: the same meaning, by reversal of the sequence, becomes <s>vyastaka</s> (rearranged).

children.translated_text: The same meaning [in different form] —
'Even for a creature devoid of discrimination, the bond of love is an unfettered chain;
toward which, the bull-elephant, heading toward each she-elephant, was long restrained by the female elephant.'
The expression of half of a larger meaning is <s>khaṇḍa</s> (fragmentary).

children.text: "purā pāṇḍuprāyaṃ tadanu kapiśinmā kṛtapadaṃ tataḥ pākodrekāraruṇaguṇasaṃvargitavapuḥ /
children.translated_text: 'First mostly pale, then brownish, then with a body suffused with reddish-crimson quality from the excess of ripening,

children.text: śanaiḥ śoṣārambhe sthapuṭanijaviṣkambhaviṣamaṃ vane vītāmodaṃ badaramarasatvaṃ kalayati" //
children.translated_text: then slowly at the onset of drying, uneven with its own natural expanded shell, the <s>badara</s> (jujube) fruit in the forest assumes its juiceless state, devoid of fragrance.'

body.text:
atrārthe-
"pākakriyāparicayapraguṇīkṛtena saṃvarddhitāruṇaguṇaṃ vapuṣā nijena /āpāditasthapuṭasaṃsyitiśoṣapoṣādetadvane virasatāṃ badaraṃ bibhartti" //
body.translated_text: The same meaning — 'With a body made smooth through familiarity with the process of cooking, its crimson quality enhanced, with its own form having attained the drying and nourishing of the expanded shell — this jujube in the forest bears its juiceless state.'

body.text: saṃkṣitpārthavistareṇa tailabinduḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —
'By the weight of whose web of strings reaching to the bottom of the netherworld,
the Earth once again remembered the tusk of the Great Boar (<s>Mahāvarāha</s>).'

body.translated_text: The expansion of a condensed meaning is <s>tailabindu</s> (oil-drop).

children.translated_text: The same meaning [expanded] —

'As the earth sank, plunging under the weight of the web of strings, with broad gem-slabs as thorns swaying at the tip of [the serpent's] hoods, exhausted, the boundary of the massive pillar-like pillars of the moving-and-unmoving world —
the Earth remembered again the tusk-tip of that <s>Hiraṇyākṣa</s>-slayer, sharpened on the whetstone-rows of the massive chest-bones, fierce though whitened by the broad moonlight-like radiance.'

body.text: anyatamabhāṣānibanddhaṃ bhāṣāntareṇa parivarttyata iti naṭanepathyam /

children.translated_text: For example —
[Prakrit:] 'The crow, fearing a snare, does not accept even the morsel given by the traveler's wife,
the morsel placed in the middle of a bangle that keeps slipping from her constantly [raised] hand.'

body.translated_text: What is composed in one language and transformed into another is <s>naṭanepathya</s> (theatrical costume).

children.translated_text: [Sanskrit rendering:] 'The crow, fearing a snare, does not accept even the morsel given by the traveler's wife,
the morsel placed in the middle of a bangle that keeps slipping from her constantly [raised] hand.'
The same meaning [in Sanskrit verse] —

children.text: "dattaṃ piṇḍaṃ nayanasalilakṣālanādhautagaṇḍaṃ dvāropānte kathamapi tayā saṅgamāśānubandhāt /
children.translated_text: 'The morsel given by her at the doorstep, its cheek washed with the bathing of her tears, offered somehow out of the longing for her lover's return —

children.text: vakragrīvaścalanataśirāḥ pārśrasañcāricakṣuḥ pāśāśaṅkī galitavalayaṃ nainamaśnāti kākaḥ" //
children.translated_text: with neck bent, head shaking, eyes roving to the sides, the crow, fearing a snare, does not eat it, [seeing] the bangle that has slipped from her [thin wrist].'

body.text: chandasā parivṛttiśchandovinimayaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —

children.text: "kānte talpamupāgate vigalitā nīvī svayaṃ bandhanāt tadvāsaḥ ślathamekhalāguṇadhṛtaṃ kiñcinnitambe sthitam /
children.translated_text: 'When the beloved came to the bed, the girdle-knot loosened by itself; that garment, held loosely by the string of the girdle, stayed just a little upon the hips;

children.text: etāvatsakhi vedmi kevalamahaṃ tasyāṅgasaṅge punaḥ ko 'sau kāsmi rataṃ nu kiṃ kathamiti svalpāpi me na smṛtiḥ" //
children.translated_text: this much alone I know, dear friend — but further, in his bodily embrace: who was he, who was I, was there pleasure, how — I have not the slightest memory.'

body.translated_text: Transformation through metre is <s>chandovinimaya</s> (metrical exchange).

children.translated_text: The same meaning [in a different metre] —
'Blessed are you who can narrate even during the union with the beloved, hundreds of confident, sweet words between the intervals of lovemaking;

children.text: nīvīṃ prati praṇihite tu kare priyeṇa sakhyaḥ śapāmi yadi kiñcidapi smarāmi" //
children.translated_text: but when my beloved placed his hand upon my girdle-string, dear friends, I swear — I do not remember even a little.'

body.text: kāraṇaparāvṛttyā hetuvyatyayaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —
'Then the moon, its radiance made faint by the red glow of dawn,
in the foreground [displayed] the pallor of the cheek of a woman emaciated by <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love).'

body.translated_text: By the reversal of the cause, there is <s>hetuvyatyaya</s> (change of cause).

children.translated_text: The same meaning —
'Together with the flower-bowed one (<s>Kāma</s>), with the pallor of a pregnant woman's cheek,
the moon placed its step upon the crest of the eastern mountain.'

body.text: dṛṣṭasya vastuno 'nyatra saṃkramitiḥ saṅkrāntakam /

children.translated_text: For example —
'Now, with their braids loosened after bathing, swaying wet, the hip-burden has become familiar with the sprout-like locks of hair;

children.text: apyetebhyo nabhasi patataḥ paṅkiśo vāribindūn sthitvodgrīvaṃ kuvalayadṛśāṃ kolihaṃsāḥ pibanti" //
children.translated_text: even from these [drops] falling from the sky — the <s>kolihaṃsa</s> (bar-headed geese), standing with necks upraised, drink the muddy water-drops of the lotus-eyed women.'

body.translated_text: The transfer of a perceived object elsewhere is <s>saṅkrāntaka</s> (transference).

children.translated_text: The same meaning —
'The water-drops dripping from the matted lock-tips of freshly bathed ascetics intent on <s>japa</s> (prayer) are eagerly drunk by young deer, distressed with thirst, with faces upturned;

children.text: etāṃ premabharālasāṃ ca sahasā śuṣyanmukhīmākulaḥ śliṣyan rakṣati pakṣasampuṭakṛtacchāyaḥ śakuntaḥ priyām" //
children.translated_text: and her — languid with the weight of love, her face suddenly drying — the agitated bird protects, embracing [her], creating shade with the cup of his wings, [protecting] his beloved.'

body.text: ubhayavākyārthopādānaṃ sampuṭaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —

children.text: "vindhyasyādreḥ parisaranadī narmadā subhru saiṣā yādobharttuḥ prathamagṛhiṇīṃ yāṃ viduḥ paścimasya /
children.translated_text: 'O beautiful-browed one, this is the river <s>Narmadā</s>, flowing from the environs of Mount <s>Vindhya</s>, whom they know as the first wife of the Lord of Waters, the western [ocean];

children.text: yasyāmantaḥ sphuritaśapharatrāsahāsākulākṣī svairaṃ svairaṃ kathamapi mayā tīramṛttāritāsi" //
children.translated_text: in whose waters, with eyes trembling and playful with the startled darting of fish — somehow, leisurely, I pulled you to the bank.'

body.translated_text: The incorporation of meaning from both [original and new] statements is <s>sampuṭa</s> (amalgamation).

children.translated_text: And also —

'Entering the cave-like hollow of the navel, the <s>Revā</s> (<s>Narmadā</s>) waters with their moving waves producing sweet sounds of <s>kukkubha</s> (a bird) through the audible, dripping, [gurgling] noise,
are copiously embraced by the women of <s>Lāṭa</s> during their afternoon baths.'
The same meaning [amalgamating both] —

'The river waters that were entered by women [whose play] in each direction alarmed [the fish] with the splashing of heavy, deep whirlpools, disrupting and startling [them], during the campaigns of conquest over the directions,

with waves rolling in playful alternation of swallowing the deep navel-cave-hollows and releasing [them], producing bewildered, startled, resonant <s>kukkubha</s>-bird sounds — [these waters were entered] by the women.'

body.text: so 'yaṃ kaverakavitvadāyī sarvathā pratibimbakalpaḥ pariharaṇīyaḥ /

children.translated_text: Because —
'People do not separately grasp a thing that exists in another's poem;
people do not separately grasp their own form when it is reflected.'

body.translated_text: This <s>pratibimbakalpa</s> (mirror-image technique), which bestows non-poetry upon a poet, is in all cases to be avoided.

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaṇe śabdārthaharaṇopāyāḥ kaviprabhedāḥ pratibimbakalpavikalpasya samīkṣā dvādaśo 'dhyāyaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the twelfth chapter, entitled 'The Methods of Appropriation of Words and Meanings, Types of Poets, and Examination of Mirror-Image Variations,' in the first section of the <s>Kavirahsya</s> (Secrets of the Poet) in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.
Chapter 13

body.text:
rājacaryā trayodaśo 'dhyāyaḥ 13 arthaharaṇeṣvālekhyaprakhyādibhedāḥ ālekhyaprakhyaparisaṅkhyāḥ /
sadṛśañcāraṇaṃ samakramaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —
'In the western mansion of the setting mountain, the disc of the lord of rays, somewhat reddish,
from the lady of the western direction who had somehow loosely taken her position sideways, shone like one cheek smeared with <s>kuṅkuma</s> (saffron) paste.' (1)

body.translated_text: The Conduct of Kings. Thirteenth chapter, section 13. In the matter of appropriation of meanings: the varieties such as <s>ālekhyaprakhya</s> (painting-like) and others. The enumeration of <s>ālekhyaprakhya</s> [techniques]. And <s>sadṛśacāraṇa</s> (similar portrayal) is <s>samakrama</s> (equal sequence).

children.translated_text: And also —
'Of the eastern direction that shines as an ornament at the forehead, with a cheek-surface reddened with <s>kuṅkuma</s>,
the moon with its rising blush equals [her beauty] — behold, O beautiful one, the cool-rayed one!'

body.text: alaṅkṛtamanalaṅkṛtyābhidhīyata iti vibhūṣaṇamoṣaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —

children.text: "kuvalayasiti mūle bālacandrāṅkurābhaṃ tadanu khalu tato 'gre pākapītāmrapītam /
children.translated_text: 'At the base [resembling] a blue lotus, then [colored like] a young crescent moon sprout, then at the top golden-yellow like a ripened mango,

children.text: abhinavaravirocirdhūmadhūbhraṃ śikhāyām iti vivadhavikāraṃ didyute daipamarciḥ" //
children.translated_text: smoke-grey like the rays of the new sun at the tip — thus the lamp-flame shone with varied transformations.'

body.translated_text: When an adorned [object] is described without the ornament, it is <s>vibhūṣaṇamoṣa</s> (theft of ornament).

children.translated_text: The same meaning —

children.text: "manāṅmūle nīlaṃ tadanu kapiśonmeṣamudare tataḥ pāṇḍu stokaṃ sphuradaruṇalekhaṃ ca tadanu /
children.translated_text: 'Slightly blue at the base, then tawny-brown flashing in the middle, then slightly pale, and then with a faint red streak,

children.text: śikhāyāmādhūbhraṃ dhṛtavividhavarṇakramamiti kṣaṇādarcirdaipaṃ dalayati tamaḥ puñjitamapi" //
children.translated_text: smoke-grey at the tip, bearing a succession of various colors in sequence — the lamp-flame in an instant destroys even accumulated darkness.'

body.text: krameṇābhihitasyārthasya viparītābhidhānaṃ vyutkramaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example, in the same [context] —

children.text: "śyāmaṃ śikhābhuvi manāgaruṇaṃ tato 'dhaḥ stokāvapāṇḍuradhanaṃ ca tato 'pyadhastāt /
children.translated_text: 'Dark at the tip of the flame, then slightly red below that, then faintly pale and rich further below,

children.text: āpiñjaraṃ tadanu tasya tale ca nīlam andhaṃ tamaḥ paṭalamarddati daipamarciḥ" //
children.translated_text: tawny-brown after that, and blue at its base — the lamp-flame destroys the thick curtain of darkness.'

body.translated_text: The reversed statement of a meaning that was described in sequence is <s>vyutkrama</s> (inversion of order).

body.text: sāmānyanibandhe viśeṣābhidhānaṃ viśeṣoktiḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —
'Thus when the moon rose, by the women with eyes and minds stirred by the conversation of charming, dear messengers,
the act of adornment was begun — [an adornment] at which the circle of friends laughed because of the reversed placement of ornaments.'

body.translated_text: The statement of a particular in a general description is <s>viśeṣokti</s> (particular expression).

children.translated_text: The same meaning —
'One woman placed the girdle-band upon the expanse of her breasts marked with white sandalwood,

children.text: priyaṃ prati preṣitacittavṛttirnitambabimbe ca babandha hāram" //
children.translated_text: and upon the globe of her buttocks — her mind dispatched toward her beloved — she fastened the necklace.'

body.text: upasarjanasyārthasya pradhānatāyāmuttaṃsaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example —
'Then, illuminating the sky with floods of rays, fair as a cloud reddened with <s>kuṅkuma</s>,
like a golden pitcher, the cool-rayed moon slowly rose from the crest of the eastern ocean.'

body.translated_text: When a subordinate meaning is given prominence, it is <s>uttaṃsa</s> (crest-ornament).

children.translated_text: The same meaning —
'Then, slightly tearing the dark garment-bodice of darkness, [something] became visible within —
the beautiful remaining <s>kuṅkuma</s> on the breast of the night's youth — the full [beauty] of the moon.'

body.text: tadeva vastūktivaśādanyathā kriyata iti naṭanepathyam /

children.translated_text: For example —
'The <s>tilaka</s> mark that was lovingly placed on the cheek of her moon-spotted face,
O beloved — [was later] washed away by the tears of the one whose <s>tilaka</s> had become smudged, after the violation of the appointed time.'

body.translated_text: When the same subject is made different through the force of expression, it is <s>naṭanepathya</s> (theatrical disguise).

children.translated_text: The same meaning —
'On the cheeks of the women whose days [of waiting] had been broken, moistened with tears of grief,
the leaf-ornaments, when the beloved delayed, became short-lived.'
When the accompaniments are the same but the principal object is different, it is <s>ekaparikārya</s> (single-object variation).

children.text: avyādgajendravadanaḥ sa imāṃ trilokīṃ yasyodgatena gagane mahatā kareṇa /
children.translated_text: May the elephant-faced one (<s>Gaṇeśa</s>) protect this triple world, by whose great trunk raised in the sky,
with <s>bīsa</s> (lotus-stalk) sprouts seized at the root by his tusk, the disc of the sun became as if stalked like a lotus.'
The same meaning —
'The trunk of the elephant-bodied Almighty (<s>Gaṇeśa</s>) triumphs, [like] a straight arm-staff [forming] the stalk,
with the lotus-root stalks at the base, where the single tusk became [like a lotus root].'

body.text: vikṛteḥ prakṛtiprāpaṇaṃ pratyāpattiḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"The moon, whose beauty has been transferred to the sun, whose disc is covered by frost,
does not shine, like a mirror blinded by breath."

body.translated_text: The restoration of a modified thing to its original form is <s>pratyāpatti</s> (reversion).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"Her face, suddenly freed from the sorrow caused by rivalry with her co-wife, shone forth,
like a personal mirror that, when the mist of sighs and tears has cleared, reveals its own clarity."

body.text:
tā imā ālekhyaprakhyasya bhidāḥ /
so 'yamanugrāhyo mārgaḥ /

children.translated_text: And they say:
"This entire expanse of subject matter, through the variety of expression,
like an actor on the stage of description, assumes ever-changing forms."

body.translated_text:
These are the varieties of <s>ālekhyaprakhya</s> (painting-like composition).
This is the <s>anugrāhya</s> (favored) path.

body.text:
atha tulyadehitulyasya bhidāḥ /
tasyaiva vastuno viṣayāntarayojanādanyarupāpattirviśayaparivarttiḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "ye sīmantitagātrabhasmarajaso ye kumbhakadveṣiṇo ye līḍhāḥ śravaṇāśrayeṇa phaṇinā ye candraśaityadruhaḥ /
children.translated_text: "Those [breaths] that have parted the ash-dust on his body, that are hostile to breath-retention, that have been licked by the serpent dwelling at his ear, that are enemies of the moon's coolness —

those breaths of <s>Sthāṇu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), who shares his body with the angry <s>Girijā</s> (<s>Pārvatī</s>), witnesses to his mental anguish, issuing from the right nostril-cavity — may they protect you!"

body.translated_text:
Now, the varieties of <s>tulyadehitulya</s> (equivalence of identical subject).
The assumption of a different form by the same subject through connection with a different domain is <s>viṣayaparivṛtti</s> (domain-transference).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:

children.text: "ye kīrṇākvathitodarābjamadhavo te mlāpitoraḥ strajo ye tāpāttaralena talpaphaṇinā pītapratāpobhphijtāḥ /
children.translated_text: "Those [breaths] that have scattered the honey of the lotus in his agitated belly, that have wilted the garlands on his chest, that have been drunk of their heat by the restless serpent on his bed —

children.text: te rādhāsmṛtisākṣiṇaḥ kamalayā sāsūyamākarṇitā gāḍhāntardavathoḥ pratatpasaralāḥ śvāsā hareḥ pāntu vaḥ" //
children.translated_text: those breaths of <s>Hari</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), witnesses to the memory of <s>Rādhā</s>, heard jealously by <s>Kamalā</s> (<s>Lakṣmī</s>), deeply burning within, hot and flowing — may they protect you!"

body.text: dvirupasya vastuno 'nyatararupopādānaṃ dvandvavicchittiḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "utkleśaṃ keśabandhaḥ kusumaśararipoḥ kalmaṣaṃ vaḥ sa muṣyād yatrendanaṃ vīkṣya gaṅgājalabharalulitaṃ bālabhāvādabhūtām /
children.translated_text: "May the hair-knot of the enemy of the flower-arrowed one (<s>Śiva</s>) steal away your sin, wherein seeing the fuel [of the sacrificial fire] swept away by the flood of <s>Gaṅgā</s> water, she (<s>Gaṅgā</s>) became childlike [in confusion];

and the enemy of <s>Krauñca</s> (<s>Skanda</s>), with eyes rolling in bewilderment like darting fish in churned waters, and the elephant-faced one (<s>Gaṇeśa</s>), his trunk playfully grasping fresh lotus stalks."

body.translated_text: The selection of one form of a two-formed subject is <s>dvandvavicchitti</s> (pair-splitting).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:

children.text: "diśyāddhūrjaṭijūṭakoṭisariti jyotsnālavodbhāsinī śāśāṅkī kalikā jalabhramivaśād drāga dṛṣṭanaṣṭā sukham /
children.translated_text: "May the crescent moonbeam-gleaming bud atop the matted locks of <s>Dhūrjaṭi</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), appearing and vanishing in the swirl of water, bring you happiness —
that [bud] which the serpent, confused in his aim, tries to seize with contracting and extending [coils], closing his hoods repeatedly due to the darting movement of a fish."

body.text: pūrvorthānāmarthāntarairantaraṇaṃ ratnamālā /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "kapole mārjāraḥ paya iti karāṃlleḍhi śaśinas tarucchidraprotānbisamiti kareṇuḥ kalayati /
children.translated_text: "On the cheek, a cat licks his paws thinking 'milk'; through the gaps in the trees, an elephant grasps thinking 'lotus fiber';

children.text: ratānte talpasthānharati vanitāpyaṃśukamiti prabhāmattaścandro jagadidamaho vibhramayati" //
children.translated_text: after lovemaking, a woman snatches from the bed thinking 'garment' — ah, the intoxicated moon thus bewilders this world with its radiance!"

body.translated_text: The interweaving of earlier meanings with additional meanings is <s>ratnamālā</s> (jewel-garland).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:

children.text: "jyotsnārcirdugdhabuddhyā kavalitamasakṛdbhājane rājahaṃsaiḥ svāṃse karpūrapāṃsucchuraṇarabhasataḥ sambhṛtaṃ sundarībhiḥ /
children.translated_text: "Repeatedly swallowed by royal geese in their bowls thinking it milk; gathered eagerly by beautiful women on their shoulders thinking it the shimmer of camphor dust;

children.text: pubhbhirvyastaṃ stanāntātsicayamiti rahaḥ sambhrame vallabhānāṃ līḍhaṃ drāksindhuvāreṣvabhinavasumanolampaṭaiḥ ṣaṭpadaiśca" //
children.translated_text: wiped from their breasts by lovers in secret confusion thinking it a powder-offering; and licked at the <s>Sindhu</s>-berry bushes by bees fond of fresh blossoms — [such is the moonlight]."

body.text: saṅkhyāvaiṣamyeṇārthapraṇayanaṃ saṅkhyollekhaḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"The nails of the feet of the bowing <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, illumined by his radiance,
serve you like ten moons to your crest-jewel, O <s>Rudra</s>."

body.translated_text: The presentation of meaning through numerical incongruity is <s>saṅkhyollekha</s> (numerical suggestion).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"At the meeting of heads, the moon, gleaming on the toenail of <s>Umā</s>'s one lotus-foot, of one who committed an offense,

children.text: ṣaḍātmatāmāśrayatīva candramāḥ sa nīlakaṇṭhaḥ priyamātanotu vaḥ" //
children.translated_text: seems to assume a sixfold nature — may that <s>Nīlakaṇṭha</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) extend to you what is dear!"

body.text:
samamabhidhāyādhikasyopanyāsaścūlikā /
dvidhā ca sā saṃvādinī visaṃvādinī ca /

children.translated_text: Of these, the first, as [illustrated by]:
"On the courtyard anointed with moonbeams, seeing a royal goose resembling a cluster of moon-rays,
the timid goose-lady cries out with a voice choked with tears."

body.translated_text:
The introduction of something additional after stating what is equal is <s>cūlikā</s> (crest).
And it is twofold: <s>saṃvādinī</s> (concordant) and <s>visaṃvādinī</s> (discordant).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"On the palace terrace bathed in moonlight, the royal house-goose could not discern his mate, whose wing-tips were indistinguishable [in the whiteness];
confused in hearing, he did not recognize even her who was speaking before him, by the sound of her tinkling anklets."
The second, on the same subject, as [illustrated by]:
"On the palace terrace bathing in a flood of moonlight, the goose-lady, with her body bright as a heap of loose pearls,
somehow recognized her mate by the faint sounds of the tips of his crest-feathers rustling."

body.text: niṣedhasya vidhinā nibandho vidhānāpahāraḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "kurabaka kucāghātakrīḍārasena viyujyase bakulaviṭapin smarttavyaṃ te mukhāsavasecanam /
children.translated_text: "O <s>kurabaka</s> (tree), you will be deprived of the pleasure of being struck by her breasts; O <s>bakula</s> tree, you must remember the sprinkling of her mouth-wine; O <s>aśoka</s>, bereft of the touch of her feet, you will attain sorrow — thus did the women of his enemies speak when he departed from his own city."

children.text: caraṇaghaṭanāśūnyo yāsyasyaśoka saśokatām iti nijapuratyāge yasya dviṣāṃ jagaduḥ striyaḥ" //

body.translated_text: The binding of a prohibition through a positive injunction is <s>vidhānāpahāra</s> (injunction-negation).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"The <s>bakula</s> tree by her mouth-wine, the crimson <s>aśoka</s> by her foot-placement, the <s>tilaka</s> tree by her graceful glances —

children.text: jalanidhitaṭīkāntārāṇāṃ kramātkakubhāṃ jaye jhagiti gamitā yadvargyābhirvikāsamahotsavam" //
children.translated_text: the trees in the wilderness of the ocean-shore quarters were made to burst into a great festival of blossoming by the women of his retinue, one after another, at the conquest of the directions."

body.text: bahūnāmarthānāmekatropasaṃhāro māṇikyapujjaḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"The Earth-bride, under the guise of a mountain, stretching out her own long arm,
seems to apply a moon-<s>tilaka</s> mark on her face with the help of her friend the Night."

body.translated_text: The gathering of many meanings into one is <s>māṇikyapuñja</s> (heap of gems).

children.translated_text: And as [illustrated by]:
"Seeing the moon-lion, resting on the peak of the rising mountain, beautiful with clusters of fully-bloomed <s>atimuktaka</s> flowers, with radiating rays as its mane —
the herds of elephants of darkness, irresistible, were instantly scattered."
And as [illustrated by]:
"The moon, with its streaming flood of rays, marked by the sign applied by the lady Night,
appears like a silver pitcher with a lotus on top, as if to arrange the <s>abhiṣeka</s> (consecration) of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love)."
And as [illustrated by]:
"Behold, O slender-waisted one, it rises — with rays that are like streams of milk from a cracked bark,
this crest-jewel of the eastern mountain, the beloved of <s>Rohiṇī</s> (the moon), has risen!"
And as [illustrated by]:
"Pale as a ball of fresh butter, touching the lotus-groves with the tips of its rays,
with a resounding laugh upon the slope of the eastern mountain, the moon rises — a face-mirror for the bride of Night."
And as [illustrated by]:
"In this [sky], with the moon-goose as his emissary, <s>Madana</s> (the god of love) bathed as it were in the waters of darkness,
in the pond of the sky, smiling with star-lotuses."
On this very subject:
"A forehead-mark for the lady Night, a lion among the elephant-herds of darkness, a silver consecration-pitcher for the king of the flower-weaponed god (<s>Kāma</s>),

children.text: ayamudayācalaikacūḍāmaṇirabhinavadarpaṇo diśām udayati gaganasarasi haṃsasya hasanniva vibhramaṃ śaśī" //
children.translated_text: the sole crest-jewel of the eastern mountain, a fresh mirror for the directions — the moon rises in the lake of the sky, as if laughing at the swan's confusion."

body.text: kandabhūto 'rthaḥ kandalāyamānairviśeṣairabhidhīyata iti kandaḥ /

children.translated_text: And as [illustrated by]:
"In the openings of streets it spreads, on the crests of palaces it accumulates,
in the lotus-ponds it blossoms — the moonlight poured from the pitcher of the moon."

body.translated_text: A meaning that is like a bulb, being expressed through proliferating particulars, is called <s>kanda</s> (bulb).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:

children.text: "viyati visarpatīva kumudeṣu bahūbhavatīva yoṣitāṃ pratiphalatīva jaraṭhaśarakāṇḍuṣu gaṇḍabhittiṣu /
children.translated_text: "In the sky it seems to spread, in the lotuses it seems to multiply, on the cheek-surfaces of old <s>śara</s>-reed arrow-shafts it seems to be reflected,

children.text: ambhasi vikasatīva lasatīva sudhādhavaleṣu dhāmasu dhvajapaṭapallaveṣu lalatīva samīracaleṣu candrikā" //
children.translated_text: in the water it seems to blossom, in the dwellings white as nectar it seems to gleam, on the banner-cloth leaves it seems to flutter, stirred by the breeze — the moonlight."
Like a crystal pitcher the moon — its lid, as it were, is its dark spot;

children.text: kṣarati ciraṃ yena yathā jyotsnā ghanasāradhūliriva //
children.translated_text: from which the moonlight flows for long, like dust of camphor.
From the white gem-pitcher of the moon, with its lid of the deer's green grass-covering, the spilled [rays] —
the maidservant of Night sprinkles the courtyard of the sky with moonlight-waters.
The moon, with its streaming flood of rays, marked by the sign applied by the lady Night,
appears like a silver pitcher with a lotus on top, as if to arrange the <s>abhiṣeka</s> (consecration) of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love)."

body.text:
tā imāstulyadehitulyasya parisaṃkhyāḥ" /
so 'yamullekhavānanugrāhyo mārgaḥ" iti surānandaḥ /

children.translated_text: Therefore he says:

children.text: "sarasvatī sā jayati prakāmaṃ devī śrutiḥ svastyayanaṃ kavīnām /
children.translated_text: "That goddess <s>Sarasvatī</s> triumphs completely — she who is the divine speech, the well-being of poets,
who, by sketching anything here in her own manner, brings it to priceless value — that art-jewel."

body.translated_text:
These are the enumerated varieties of <s>tulyadehitulya</s> (equivalence of identical subject)."
This is the <s>ullekhavān anugrāhya</s> (descriptive favored) path" — thus says <s>Surānanda</s>.

body.text:
atha parapurapraveśasaddaśasya bhidāḥ /
upanibaddhasya vastuno yuktimatī parivṛttirhuṅḍayuddham /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"How does he not attain bodilessness, he whose discrimination is destroyed, whose pride is slain,

children.text: praharataḥ kadalīdalakomale bhavati yasya dayā na vadhūjane" //
children.translated_text: he who strikes at the young bride-folk, tender as a plantain leaf, and has no compassion?"

body.translated_text:
Now, the varieties of <s>parapurapraveśasaddaśa</s> (the mode of entering another's city).
The skilful transformation of a bound subject is <s>huṇḍayuddha</s> (ram-battle).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"How is that <s>Madana</s> (god of love), the banner-bearer of the <s>makara</s> (crocodile), who stands firm in discrimination, not to be worshipped,
when he strikes with his flower-born arrows the bodies of doe-eyed women, graceful as plantain [leaves]?"

body.text: prakārāntareṇa visadṛśaṃ yadvastu tasya nibandhaḥ pratikañcukam /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"Bearing a stream of honey falling from the intoxicated <s>cakora</s> bird's eye-like radiance,
the crescent moon shone like a goose-lady, lovely with a lotus-stalk grasped at the tip of her beak."

body.translated_text: The composition of a dissimilar subject in a different manner is <s>pratikañcuka</s> (counter-armor).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"A certain woman shone, offering wine through a coral-tube,
as if a pet parrot held in her cupped hands was holding a <s>vallūra</s>-creeper in its beak."

body.text: upamānasyopamānāntaraparivṛttirvastusaṃcāraḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "aviralamiva dāmnā pauṇḍarīkeṇa baddhaḥ snapita iva ca dugdhasrotasā nirbhareṇa /
children.translated_text: "As if tightly bound by a garland of white lotuses, as if bathed by an overflowing stream of milk,

children.text: kavalita iva kṛtsnaścakṣuṣā sphāritena prasabhamamṛtamegheneva sāndreṇa siktaḥ" //
children.translated_text: as if entirely swallowed by a wide-open eye, as if forcibly sprinkled by a dense cloud of nectar."

body.translated_text: The replacement of one simile by another simile is <s>vastusaṃcāra</s> (subject-transference).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:

children.text: "muktānāmiva rajjavo himarucermālāḥ kalānāmiva kṣīrābdheriva vīcayaḥ klamamuṣaḥ pīyūṣadhārā iva /
children.translated_text: "Like strings of pearls, like garlands of the moon's digits, like waves of the milk-ocean, like streams of fatigue-destroying nectar —

children.text: dīrghāpāṅganadīṃ vilaṅdhya sahasā līlānubhāvāñcitāḥ sadyaḥ premabharollasā bhṛgadṛśo māmabhyaṣiñcandṛśaḥ" //
children.translated_text: suddenly crossing the river of long side-glances, adorned with playful grace, overflowing with the surge of love, the glances of the doe-eyed one anointed me."

body.text: śabdālaṅkārasyārthālaṅkāreṇānyathātvaṃ dhātuvādaḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"Victorious are [the dust particles] cherished by the crowns of <s>Bāṇāsura</s>, kissing the crest-jewels of the ten-headed one (<s>Rāvaṇa</s>),
resting atop the crests of the lords of gods and demons — the dust of the feet of <s>Tryambaka</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), the destroyer of worldly existence!"

body.translated_text: The transformation of a verbal ornament into a meaning-ornament is <s>dhātuvāda</s> (element-discourse).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"Making beings humble through the majesty of revealing the true path,
victorious are the dust-particles of the feet of the enemy of <s>Pura</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), of unprecedented power!"

body.text: tasyaiva vastuna utkarṣeṇānyathākaraṇaṃ satkāraḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"Now, with the loosened hair-braids still wet from bathing, the weight of their hips familiar with the tendrils of their tresses,

children.text: apyetebhyo nabhasi patataḥ paṅktiśo vāribindūn sthitvodgrīvaṃ kuvalayadṛśāṃ kelihaṃsāḥ pibanti" //
children.translated_text: even so, stretching their necks upward, the pet geese of the lotus-eyed women drink the raindrops falling in rows from the sky."

body.translated_text: The transformation of the same subject through elevation is <s>satkāra</s> (honoring).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:

children.text: "lakṣmyāḥ kṣīranidherudaktavapuṣo veṇīlatāgracyutā ye muktāgrathanāmasūtrasubhagāḥ prātpāḥ payobindavaḥ /
children.translated_text: "Those drops of water that fell from the tips of the vine-like braids of <s>Lakṣmī</s>, she whose body emerged from the milk-ocean, beautiful as strings of threaded pearls —

children.text: te vaḥ pāntu viśeṣasaspṛhaddaśā dṛṣṭāściraṃ śārṅgiṇā helodgrīvajaleśahaṃsavanitālīḍhāḥ sudhāsvādavaḥ" //
children.translated_text: may they protect you, gazed upon longingly by <s>Śārṅgin</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), licked as if tasting nectar by the goose-ladies who raised their necks playfully from the water!"

body.text: pūrvaṃ sadṛśaḥ paścādbhinno jīvañcīvakaḥ /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"In her eyes, belly, cheek, and on the radiant clusters of gems in her ornaments,
with the reflected moon-disc everywhere, a certain woman appeared as if adorned with a hundred-moon ornament."

body.translated_text: That which is similar at first but different afterwards is <s>jīvañcīvaka</s> (the living and the living).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"With the moon reflected in the brilliant cheek-surface, earrings, pearl-necklace,
fine girdle-gems — the lovely woman shines as if attended upon by the moon, whose splendor is overpowered by the beauty of her charming face."

body.text: prāktanavākyābhiprāyanibandho bhāvamudrā /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:
"On the <s>Malaya</s> mountain slopes where betel-vines embrace areca palms, where <s>elā</s> (cardamom) creepers cling to sandalwood trees,
on beds spread with <s>tamāla</s> leaves — please be gracious and sport there."

body.translated_text: The composition based on the intention of a preceding statement is <s>bhāvamudrā</s> (seal of intent).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:
"Surely <s>Madana</s> (the god of love) presides over this place, bestowing the union of yoga even upon the dispassionate,
for here the <s>elā</s> (cardamom) has embraced the sandalwood, and the <s>nāga</s> (betel) creeper climbs the areca tree."

body.text: pūrvārthaparipanthinī vasturacanā tadvirodhī (dhinī) /

children.translated_text: As [illustrated by]:

children.text: "hāro vakṣasi dantapatraviśadaṃ karṇe dalaṃ kaumudaṃ mālā mūrdhni dukūlinī tanulatā karpūraśuklau stanau /
children.translated_text: "A necklace on the breast, a petal-earring bright as ivory on the ear, a garland on the head, a fine silk creeper on the slender body, breasts white as camphor,

children.text: vaktre candanabindurindudhavalaṃ bālaṃ mṛṇālaṃ kare veṣaḥ kiṃ sita eṣa sundari śaraścandrāttvayā śikṣitaḥ" //
children.translated_text: a sandalwood dot on the face, a tender lotus-stalk white as the moon in the hand — O beautiful one, is this your white attire, or has the moon-rayed [autumn] been trained by you?"

body.translated_text: The composition of subject matter that opposes the preceding meaning is <s>tadvirodhī</s> (that which contradicts).

children.translated_text: On this very subject:

children.text: "mūrtirnīladukūlinī mṛgamadaiḥ pratyaṅgapatrakriyā vāhū mecakaratnakaṅkaṇabhṛtau kaṇṭhe masārāvalī /
children.translated_text: "A form clad in blue silk, with musk-leaf designs on every limb, arms bearing bracelets of dark gems, a string of sapphires on the neck,

children.text: vyālambālakavallarīkamalikaṃ kāntābhisārotsave yatsatyaṃ tamasā mṛgākṣi vihitaṃ veṣe tavācāryakam" //
children.translated_text: with a jasmine crown on the creeper-like hanging locks — at the festival of the beloved's tryst, O doe-eyed one, in truth, darkness has served as your instructor in matters of disguise."
Thus thirty-two methods of appropriating meaning have been demonstrated.
Poetic skill, in my view, lies in the knowledge of what to discard and what to adopt.
Moreover, these methods of appropriation should be known together with their counterparts;
the counterpart is to be recognized by the reversal of meaning.
Furthermore —

children.text: śabdārthaśāsanavidaḥ kati no kavante yadvāṅmayaṃ śrutidhanasya cakāsti cakṣuḥ /
children.translated_text: How few among those who know the science of word and meaning truly compose poetry — that speech which shines as the eye of one whose wealth is learning! But he who has something new to say in his words, stringing together fine sayings — his speech stands at the forefront, and is sacred.

children.text: kintvasti yadvacasi vastu navaṃ sadukti-sandarbhiṇāṃ sa dhuri tasya giraḥ pavitrāḥ //

body.text: iti rājaśekharakṛtau kāvyamīmāṃsāyāṃ kavirahasye prathame 'dhikaraṇe arthaharaṇeṣvālekhyaprakhyādibhedāstrayodaśo 'dhyāyaḥ //
body.translated_text: Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, entitled "The Types such as Painting and Semblance in the Appropriation of Meaning," in the first section of the <s>Kavirahsya</s> (Secrets of the Poet) in the <s>Kāvyamīmāṃsā</s> composed by <s>Rājaśekhara</s>.

body.text: caturdaśo 'dhyāyaḥ 14
body.translated_text: Chapter 14

body.text:
kavisamayaḥ jātidravyakriyāsamayasthāpanā /
aśāstrīyamalaukikaṃ ca paramparāyātaṃ yamarthamupanibadhnanti kavayaḥ sa kavisamayaḥ /

children.translated_text: "But surely this is a fault!
How then is it worthy of being employed?" — say the teachers.
"How can that which supports the path of poets be a fault?" — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>.
"Then the reason should be stated" — say the teachers.

body.translated_text: Poetic Convention (<s>Kavisamaya</s>): Establishing Conventions of Genus, Substance, and Action. That meaning which poets employ, which is neither sanctioned by scripture nor found in the world, but has been handed down by tradition — that is <s>kavisamaya</s> (poetic convention).

body.text:
"idamabhidhīyate" iti yāyāvarīyaḥ /
pūrve hi vidvāṃsaḥ sahasraśākhaṃ sāṅgaṃ ca vedamavagāhya, śāstrāṇi cāvabudhya, deśānterāṇi dvīpāntarāṇi ca paribhramya, yānarthānupalabhya praṇītavantasteṣāṃ deśakālāntaravaśena anyathātve 'pi tathātvenopanibandho yaḥ sa kavisamayaḥ /
kavisamayaśabdaścāyaṃ mūlamapaśyadbhiḥ prayogamātradaśibhiḥ prayukto rūḍhaśca /
tatra kaścidādyatvena vyavasthitaḥ kavisamayenārthaḥ, kaścitparasyaropakramārthaṃ svārthāya dhūrttaiḥ pravarttitaḥ /
sa ca tridhā svargyo bhaumaḥ pātālīyaśca /
svargyapātālīyayorbhaumaḥ pradhānaḥ /
sa hi mahāviṣayakaḥ /
sa ca caturddhā jātidravyaguṇakriyārupārthatayā /
te 'pi pratyakṣaṃ tridhā asato nibandhanāt, satopyanibandhanāt, niyamataśca /
tatra sāmānyasyāsato nibandhanam, yathā--nadīṣu padmotpalādīni, jalāśayamātre 'pi haṃsādayo, yatra tatra parvateṣu suvarṇaratnādikaṃ ca /

children.translated_text: Lotuses in rivers, for example —
"Prolonging the melodious cry of <s>sārasa</s> cranes with a sharp, intoxicating note, bitter-sweet with the fragrance of blossoming lotuses at dawn,

children.text: yatra strīṇāṃ harati surataglānimaṅgānukūlaḥ śiprāvātaḥ priyatama iva prārthanācāṭukāraḥ" //
children.translated_text: where the breeze of the <s>Śiprā</s>, like a most beloved one with flattering entreaties, soothes the languor of lovemaking, agreeable to the limbs."

body.translated_text: "This is what is meant" — says <s>Yāyāvarīya</s>. For the ancient learned ones, having plunged into the <s>Veda</s> of a thousand branches with its ancillary texts, having understood the <s>śāstras</s>, having traveled to various countries and islands, composed [poetry] based on the meanings they perceived; the binding of those [meanings] as they are, even when they have changed due to differences of place and time — that is <s>kavisamaya</s> (poetic convention). And this term <s>kavisamaya</s> was used and became established by those who, not seeing the original basis, saw only the usage. Among these, some meanings are established as conventions from the beginning, while some have been introduced by rogues for their own purposes under the guise of serving others. And it is threefold: celestial, terrestrial, and subterranean. Among the celestial and subterranean, the terrestrial is primary, for it has the widest scope. And it is fourfold, having the nature of genus (<s>jāti</s>), substance (<s>dravya</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), and action (<s>kriyā</s>). These too are manifestly threefold: by the binding of what does not exist, by the non-binding of what does exist, and by restriction. Among these, the binding of what does not generally exist — for example: lotuses and blue lotuses in rivers, swans etc. in any body of water whatsoever, and gold and gems on any mountain whatsoever.

children.translated_text: Blue lotuses in rivers —
"Removing with gentle breezes the drops of perspiration from those who sport in the sky, acquired during their play of flying through the heavens,
he beheld the <s>Jāhnavī</s> (<s>Gaṅgā</s>), with the beauty of a grove of blue lotuses, as if she were the daughter of the Sun (<s>Yamunā</s>) with her cheek-ornaments clearly displayed."

body.text: evaṃ nadīkumudādyapi /

children.translated_text: Swans in any body of water, for example —

children.text: "āsīdasti bhaviṣyatīha sa jano dhanyo dhanī dhārmikaḥ yaḥ kṣīkeśavavatkariṣyati punaḥ śrīmatkuḍuṅgeśvaram /
children.translated_text: "There was, there is, and there will be that blessed, wealthy, and righteous person who will again make the glorious <s>Kuḍuṅgeśvara</s> [temple] like <s>Kṣīrakeśava</s> —
thus, as it were, the new river proclaims with its waters, resonant with the cackling cries of the flocks of swans and <s>sārasa</s> cranes swaying playfully."

body.translated_text: Similarly, night-lotuses (<s>kumuda</s>) and other [flowers] in rivers.

children.translated_text: Gold on any mountain, for example —
"The abode of serpents, delightful with colorful ships, with the circle of directions spread wide with abundance of gold,
having entered friendship with the ocean through their similarity — he is thus famed as <s>Jīmūtabhartā</s> (Bearer of Clouds)."
Gems, for example —
"Amidst the cliff-sides, where sprays of spray-mist released from the trumpeting of great elephants mingle with the arrays of blue sapphire rays,
peacocks, with their necks stretched straight, gaze with delight, mistaking them for rain-clouds, and begin to dance."

body.text:
evamanyadapi /
sato 'pyanibandhanam, tadyathā-na mānatī vasante, na puṣpaphalaṃ candanadrumeṣu, na phalamaśokeṣu /

children.translated_text: The first of these —
"<s>Caitra</s> (spring month), averse to <s>mālatī</s>, is [yet] the blossomer of the wealth of flowers —
how wondrous that one devoid of good birth should have flowers (<s>sumanasaḥ</s>, also "good-minded ones") as friends!"

body.translated_text: And similarly other [conventions]. The non-binding of what does exist — for example: <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine) does not [bloom] in spring, sandal trees have no flowers or fruit, and <s>aśoka</s> trees have no fruit.

children.translated_text: The second —
